papers.abstract: Quantization-aware training (QAT) is the most reliable way to obtain accurate low-bit large language models (LLMs), but training with AdamW keeps two dense FP32 states for every weight matrix. We find that low-rank memory-efficient optimizers such as GaLore and LDAdam degrade substantially in QAT. A considerable part of the QAT momentum lies outside its top-r singular subspace, and projection-based methods discard this part at every step. We further observe that this residual remains useful when only its sign is kept. Based on these observations, we propose ResQAdam. It keeps a single BF16 momentum, applies Adam only to the r x r coordinates of the principal subspace, and adds a normalized sign update computed from the residual. We evaluate ResQAdam with two from-scratch QAT methods and three QAT fine-tuning pipelines, with weights quantized down to 2 bits. It reduces optimizer-state memory by 71% to 74% relative to AdamW, stays close to AdamW in most settings, and lowers training throughput by less than 2%.
authors: Liqun Ma, Shengkun Tang, Liangyu Wang, Lin Zhao, Wei Luo, Xinjun Niu, Spandan Tiwari, Ashish Sirasao, Kun Zhang, Zhiqiang Shen
bullets: Addresses the memory cost of AdamW’s two dense FP32 optimizer states in quantization-aware training.
Uses Adam updates in a low-rank principal subspace plus a normalized sign update from the residual momentum.
Evaluated across two from-scratch QAT methods and three QAT fine-tuning pipelines, including weights quantized to 2 bits.
Reduces optimizer-state memory by 71–74% relative to AdamW and keeps throughput loss below 2%.
Performance remains close to AdamW in most tested settings.

papers.abstract: As long-horizon agents increasingly rely on multi-step tool interactions to accomplish complex tasks, their execution trajectories continuously accumulate structured outputs and intermediate artifacts, leading to growing context overhead. Existing compression methods primarily rely on text importance or fixed truncation rules, often overlooking cross-step dependencies within workflows and potentially discarding critical information required for subsequent task execution. To address this challenge, we propose WAAC, a workflow-aware framework for agent trajectory compression. WAAC structurally models successful historical trajectories to extract reusable workflow compression experience and incorporates online backward dependency analysis to dynamically identify information retention requirements. By combining current dependency constraints with historical experience, WAAC selects appropriate compression strategies for different types of historical information. Experiments on PinchBench and Odysseys demonstrate that WAAC achieves an overall score of 87.6 and a perfect completion rate of 19.0%, respectively, while reducing execution costs by 19.7% and 29.1% compared with the strongest baseline methods. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of workflow-aware trajectory compression in improving task performance and cost efficiency for long-horizon agents. Code and resources are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/waac-6527/.
authors: Qijia Zhuang, Rui Liu, Yuxiang Ren
bullets: Long-horizon tool use creates growing context overhead from structured outputs and intermediate artifacts.
Existing text-importance and truncation methods may discard information needed by later workflow steps.
WAAC models successful trajectories to learn reusable compression experience and performs online backward dependency analysis.
It combines historical experience with current dependency constraints to choose compression strategies for different information types.
On PinchBench and Odysseys, WAAC reports an overall score of 87.6, a 19.0% perfect completion rate, and execution-cost reductions of 19.7% and 29.1% versus the strongest baselines.

Before each online model invocation, WAAC derives requirements from outstanding obligations, retrieves compatible historical policies, and combines them through a conservative join. The resulting projection changes the model-visible history while retaining original events and artifacts in runtime storage.

papers.title: Rethinking Agent Trajectory Compression: A Workflow-Aware Perspective
papers.tldr: WAAC compresses long-horizon agent trajectories by preserving workflow-critical information, improving task performance while reducing execution costs.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models perform versatile manipulation tasks from language instructions, but their inference cost limits how fast a robot can respond in closed-loop control. Visual token pruning reduces this cost; however, prior methods estimate token redundancy from encoded visual embeddings or attention, only after the visual encoder has processed the entire observation. We propose \ours, a training-free token pruning method that moves the pruning decision ahead of the vision encoder by grounding it in a geometric prior derived from the robot's own action. The action chunk predicted at the previous control step is already available before the current observation is encoded, and it specifies the end-effector and camera motion between consecutive observations. The same action affects the two standard camera views asymmetrically: in the fixed third-person view, \ours retains patches along the projected end-effector trajectory together with semantic anchors, while in the wrist view, it prunes patches that remain unchanged after compensating for the action-induced camera motion. Extensive experiments on two simulation environments (LIBERO and VLABench) and four real-robot tasks demonstrate that \ours achieves up to 1.61 $\times$ speedup and 59.5\% FLOPs reduction with negligible degradation in success rates.
authors: Sungwon Moon, Minji Kim, Hyemin Boo, Daeun Song, Jiyoung Lee
bullets: Targets slow closed-loop robot response caused by expensive visual processing.
Training-free pruning uses the predicted prior action as a geometric prior before the vision encoder runs.
In the fixed third-person view, it keeps patches along the projected end-effector path and semantic anchors.
In the wrist view, it removes patches that remain unchanged after compensating for action-induced camera motion.
Evaluated in LIBERO, VLABench, and four real-robot tasks, achieving up to 1.61× speedup and 59.5% FLOPs reduction with negligible success-rate degradation.

papers.selection_reason: Action-grounded visual token pruning for efficient VLA inference, combining embodied action priors with token efficiency.
papers.title: ActPrune: Action-Grounded Visual Token Pruning for Efficient Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: ActPrune uses the robot’s previous action to prune visual tokens before encoding, reducing VLA inference cost with minimal impact on task success.

papers.abstract: Most LLM architectures have fixed compute demands determined at training time. We propose a novel architecture that combines the Mixture-of-Experts architecture with shallow experts and a novel dynamic-depth system to make the extent of a forward pass dynamically adjustable. Our approach lets the model automatically determine the compute needed for a given task, paired with a system to scale it down after training without retraining when the execution environment demands faster or cheaper inference. To achieve this, we introduce an iterative computation mechanism, sequence-level depth-based routing steered by a halting mechanism within the experts, a depth encoding that lets the model track its progress in the chain, and a regularization mechanism that incentivizes the model to use allocated compute efficiently. We present initial benchmarks and discuss future research directions.
bullets: Targets the fixed compute demands of conventional LLM architectures.
Uses shallow experts with iterative computation and sequence-level depth routing.
Employs learned halting within experts to determine how much computation each task needs.
Adds depth encoding and compute-efficiency regularization to support dynamic execution.
Reports initial benchmarks, while leaving broader evaluation and future research open.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding has become a standard way to accelerate LLM inference: a lightweight drafter proposes tokens that the target verifies in one parallel pass. Existing drafters face trade-offs that limits their speedups: autoregressive drafters generate tokens one at a time, so drafting cost grows with draft length, while diffusion drafters generate tokens in parallel but predict each position independently, ignoring inter-token dependencies. We introduce ChainFlow, a new speculative decoding paradigm and the first flow-matching drafter conditioned on the target's hidden states. ChainFlow treats drafting as a short transport over hidden states, needing one or two flow steps instead of the many denoising steps of generation from noise. A variational autoencoder compresses these states so drafting cost barely grows with target size, lightweight feedback heads restore inter-token dependencies, and tree drafting raises acceptance. On Qwen3.5 models, at matched drafter size and training data, ChainFlow outperforms EAGLE-3 and DFlash in vLLM by 39% and 11%, respectively. These gains further widen as drafters are adapted to new languages sequentially. Our ablations cover drafter design and concurrent serving, and we open-source our code and drafter models.
authors: Selim Aktas, Yusuf Erdem Erdem, Ahmed Zeer, Himmet Toprak Kesgin, Muzaffer Kaan Yuce, Mehmet Fatih Amasyali
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between slow autoregressive drafters and parallel drafters that ignore inter-token dependencies.
Conditions drafting on the target model’s hidden states and uses a variational autoencoder to compress them.
Uses lightweight feedback heads to restore token dependencies and tree drafting to improve acceptance.
On Qwen3.5 models, it outperforms EAGLE-3 and DFlash in vLLM by 39% and 11%, respectively, under matched drafter size and training data.
The abstract reports further widening gains during sequential adaptation to new languages; code and drafter models are released.

papers.selection_reason: Flow-matching drafter for speculative decoding to accelerate LLM inference.
papers.title: ChainFlow: Few-Step Latent Flow Matching for Speculative Decoding
papers.tldr: ChainFlow accelerates speculative decoding with a compact flow-matching drafter that generates dependent token sequences in one or two hidden-state transport steps.

papers.abstract: Medical vision--language models can interpret volumetric images, but processing full volumes is costly because hundreds of slices produce long, redundant visual-token sequences. Existing compression methods often couple content selection with budget determination. We observe that neighboring slices share visual features and that attention concentration varies across visual encoders. We propose VoluCompose, a training-free, model-agnostic framework that separates what visual content to retain from how many tokens to allocate. Its hyperbolic token composition module groups contiguous slices into ordered support units and uses the Lorentz distance to account for feature magnitude and direction during token allocation, anchor selection, and refinement. Its capacity control module uses visual-encoder attention entropy to allocate more tokens when attention is more dispersed. We evaluate VoluCompose on two tasks across three datasets and four backbones. Across nine calibrated settings, VoluCompose attains the highest mean quality--retention hypervolume among the compared methods. It achieves a mean relative quality of 121.68\% against the uncompressed references while retaining 22.78% of visual tokens on average. Compression remains robust even at a 10% token budget. Across settings, the lowest ROUGE-L ratio to the uncompressed reference is 96.4\% for VoluCompose. The corresponding minima for the compression baselines range from 15.0% to 70.5%. Code is available at https://github.com/yezanting/VoluCompose.
authors: Zanting Ye, Yunrui Lin, Shengyuan Liu, Jing Hao, Chen Hu, Yefeng Zheng, Lijun Lu
bullets: Addresses the high cost and redundancy of processing hundreds of volume slices in medical vision–language models.
Separates visual-content selection from token-budget allocation instead of coupling them.
Groups contiguous slices into ordered units and uses Lorentz distance for token allocation, anchor selection, and refinement.
Uses visual-encoder attention entropy to assign more tokens where attention is more dispersed.
Across nine settings, retains 22.78% of tokens on average while achieving 121.68% mean relative quality and robust performance at a 10% budget.

The hyperbolic token composition module groups contiguous slices into ordered support units, allocates tokens across units, selects distinctive anchors with the Lorentz distance, and refines them with related context while preserving source order. The attention-calibrated capacity control module determines the total budget 𝐵 from a prescribed retention fraction or normalized attention entropy. The compact token sequence is supplied to the language decoder for downstream tasks.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes VoluCompose, a training-free framework for compressing volumetric medical images by separating content selection from token allocation, improving efficiency for vision-language models.
papers.title: VoluCompose: Constructing Compact Volumetric Visual Representations for Medical Image Understanding
papers.tldr: VoluCompose is a training-free, model-agnostic method that compresses volumetric medical images into compact visual-token sequences while preserving understanding quality.

papers.abstract: Camera-based driving models build a dense bird's-eye-view (BEV) grid and spend the same computation on every cell of it, although the vehicle crosses only a few of those cells within the planning horizon. We present BEVCast, a two-stage BEV whose resolution adapts to the predicted driving path. A coarse pass encodes the whole scene on a grid of 4.096 m cells. A heat head trained on the recorded path assigns a heat to every coarse cell and the cells with the highest heat are refined into 1.024 m cells under a fixed budget. The remaining cells keep their coarse resolution, so the trajectory head reads a mixed-resolution BEV that still covers the entire scene and needs neither an HD map nor a navigation command. Against a full grid of 1.024 m cells with the same architecture and training recipe, BEVCast at a 10% refinement budget encodes 28% of the BEV queries and needs 66% of the BEV encoder time at batch size 1. On nuScenes its mean displacement error is 1.078 m against 1.149 m and its drivable area violation rate is 1.46% against 2.29%. On NAVSIM navtest its mean displacement error is 0.577 m against 0.598 m and its extended predictive driver model score is 82.51 against 81.28. Next to published planners BEVCast reaches a comparable error on both benchmarks without a navigation command. The resolution of a driving BEV can therefore follow the task instead of the grid.
authors: Qiren Wang, Mingyu Guo, Zixuan Wang, Weisong Shi
bullets: Dense BEV grids waste computation on regions the vehicle will not traverse.
A coarse scene encoding predicts path-related heat, then selectively refines high-heat cells under a fixed budget.
The mixed-resolution BEV covers the full scene and requires neither an HD map nor a navigation command.
With 10% refinement, it uses 28% of BEV queries and 66% of encoder time versus a full fine grid, while achieving lower reported errors on nuScenes and NAVSIM navtest.
The approach is evaluated on two benchmarks and is intended for path-focused, efficient end-to-end driving.

papers.selection_reason: Path-adaptive BEV refinement for end-to-end autonomous driving; fits learned navigation policies and token/cell selection for efficiency.
papers.title: BEVCast: Path-Adaptive BEV for Efficient End-to-End Autonomous Driving
papers.tldr: BEVCast reduces BEV computation by refining only cells near the predicted driving path while maintaining or improving planning performance.

papers.abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) are the dominant architecture for video generation, but their quadratic attention complexity results in substantial computational cost and latency. Permuted block-sparse attention (PBSA) offers a promising approach to reducing this cost by selectively computing blocks of a semantically permuted attention matrix. However, existing approaches typically select only the top few key blocks for each query block, following a top-$p$ paradigm. We find that top-$p$ selection can be highly sample inefficient in high-entropy attention regimes, which are common in video generation. In these regimes, we show that sampling can provide substantially better approximations under the same computational budget. More generally, we cast block selection as importance sampling, where the top-scoring keys form an exact set that is computed in full and the remaining keys are represented by a sample drawn in proportion to their estimated attention and reweighted by inverse sampling probability. Building on this formulation, we present InstaGen, which can be parameterized by any PBSA method: it replaces the method's block selection with an exact set plus a weighted sample. Each query cluster draws one sample shared by all its queries, so the sampled keys form blocks amenable to efficient GPU execution. In this paper, we take the SVG family of PBSA methods and show that, on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B and Wan2.1-T2V-14B, InstaGen parameterized by SVG2 improves PSNR over SVG2 by 3.4 dB and 2 dB, respectively, at matched attention density, and by 1.6 dB and 2.2 dB at matched wall-clock time. On Wan2.1-T2V-14B, InstaGen also beats SVG-EAR by 1.1 dB PSNR at nearly the same density while running faster (1.65x against 1.48x over dense).
authors: Kislay Aditya Oj, Kumar Krishna Agrawal, Sri Surya Varma Datla, Aditya Desai
bullets: Top-p block selection can be sample-inefficient when video attention has high entropy.
It treats block selection as importance sampling: exact computation for top-scoring keys and inverse-probability-weighted samples for the rest.
Each query cluster shares a sampled set, preserving block structure for efficient GPU execution.
With SVG2, InstaGen improves PSNR at matched attention density and wall-clock time on Wan2.1-T2V models.
It also outperforms SVG-EAR on Wan2.1-T2V-14B while running faster at nearly the same density.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of InstaGen. (a) Queries and keys are clustered into groups. (b) Centroid scores give each key group a probability π of being used by each query group. (c) The top key group is always kept; the remaining keys are sampled in proportion to π and weighted by 1/π. (d) Queries in a group share the same keys, so attention runs over dense blocks in one kernel.

Figure 4: InstaGen approximates attention more accurately than prior sparse methods. Left: relative L2 error of one self-attention call from Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B against exact attention. Importance sampling gives the lowest error at every density, several times below SVG2. Right: per-block, per-head error over one full generation averaged across all steps. InstaGen (uniform, 16+16, no warm-up) keeps the error low everywhere at 32% density, while SVG2 (p=0.9, warm-up counted as zero error) leaves large errors in individual heads and layers despite computing 46%.

Figure 5: Warmup ablations on Wan2.1-T2V-14B (720p, 81 frames, 50 steps). InstaGen with uniform sampling runs its first 0, 5, 10 or 15 of 50 steps at full attention (warmup), ranging from 4+4% to 32+32% budget. SVG2 runs at its paper configurations at top-p 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9 and 0.99. A 5–10 step warmup matches or beats the 15 steps SVG2 uses. The hollow diamond is SVG2 without its one-layer warmup; the InstaGen runs have none. The prompt used is svg2 ex1, Appendix A.1.

Figure 6: InstaGen with importance sampling matches SVG2’s quality at much lower density. (a) PSNR against overall attention density (warm-up steps count as dense), averaged over 22 VBench prompts on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B (720p, 81 frames, 50 steps). SVG2 in its paper configuration (p=0.9) reaches 25.03 dB at 44.1%; InstaGen (importance sampling) reaches the same PSNR at 34.0% with the same 30% warm-up, and at 20.0% with no warm-up. (b) Denoising time against the number of frames on one H100 SXM, on one prompt (svg2 ex1, Appendix A.1; VAE decoding excluded), with InstaGen (importance sampling) at 4+4% with the 30% warm-up and at 14+14% with no warm-up, budgets at which it beats SVG2 (p=0.9) on PSNR, SSIM and LPIPS on this prompt at 81 frames. At 561 frames dense takes 162 min, SVG2 82.8 min (1.97×), and InstaGen 61.9 min (2.62×) with warm-up and 57.3 min (2.83×) without.

Figure 2: InstaGen gives higher quality than SVG2 at both matched density and matched latency on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B. Left: PSNR against generation time per video. Right: PSNR against attention density, the share of attention computed over the whole generation. SVG2 uses the configuration from its paper (Cq=100, Ck=500, full attention for the first 30% of steps, key floor 0.1) at top-p 0.5, 0.75, 0.9 and 0.95. InstaGen runs exact + sampled budgets from 4+4% to 32+32% at two clustering configurations for uniform and one for importance, with the same warmup and without it.

Table 1: Main results on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B and 14B. PSNR, SSIM and LPIPS compare each video with the dense video from the same seed, and all quality metrics are averaged over the 22 VBench prompts. E+S: exact and sampled share of keys per sparse call with dense warmup, as prescribed by each baseline’s paper; InstaGen uses SVG2’s (first 30% of steps and 3% of layers). Density is overall, counting warmup calls as full attention. Speedup is end-to-end wall-clock on one H100 against a dense run. Bold: best sparse method in each column.

papers.selection_reason: Improves diffusion-based video generation with sparse/block attention and importance sampling, fitting video diffusion and efficient attention.
papers.title: InstaGen: Group-Shared Importance Sampling for Fast Video Generation
papers.tldr: InstaGen accelerates video diffusion by replacing inefficient top-block selection with group-shared importance sampling, improving reconstruction quality at comparable compute.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are attractive rerankers for recommendation. Running an expensive model on every request is costly, and for users with sparse interaction histories it often lowers quality. We present CascadeRec, a two-tier LLM reranking cascade deployed in production at a large financial planning and analysis (FP&A) SaaS provider. It serves content recommendations to enterprise tenants on AWS EKS and GKE. A lightweight Tier-1 model reranks every request. A router escalates only the requests where extra inference-time compute is likely to help, and sends them to a more expensive Tier-2 procedure (self-consistency sampling, multi-path reasoning, or a larger model). The system has run in a production A/B experiment for over a month. Compared with uniform use of the expensive tier, CascadeRec has reduced inference cost by about 10%, with minimal latency impact and no quality regression observed to date. Tenant data cannot be released, so we also evaluate the pipeline on public benchmarks (MovieLens-1M and Amazon-Electronics). Segment-level analysis with paired-bootstrap confidence intervals shows that uniform LLM reranking lowers NDCG@10 for sparse-history users by up to 30%, and its only statistically significant gain appears on the segment with the longest histories. Escalating cold users can make the loss larger instead of repairing it. Which segments benefit from escalation depends on the domain, and this motivates the segment-gated rollout we use in production. We describe the deployment architecture, the measured benefits, and lessons learned, including inter-tenant load imbalance as a driver for cascading and the handling of LLM output-parsing failures at the serving layer.
authors: Kai Zhao, Guilin Zhang, Xiang Cheng, Xiquan Cui, Henry Heng, Xu Chu, Alet Blanken
bullets: Uniform expensive LLM reranking can hurt sparse-history users, lowering NDCG@10 by up to 30% on public benchmarks.
A lightweight Tier-1 reranks every request, while a router sends potentially beneficial cases to a more expensive Tier-2 procedure.
The production system runs across multi-tenant AWS EKS and GKE deployments with minimal latency impact reported.
Escalation benefits vary by user segment and domain; cold-user escalation can worsen performance, motivating segment-gated rollout.
The deployment addresses practical serving issues including inter-tenant load imbalance and LLM output-parsing failures.

Figure 2: Production request path. The router escalates a minority of requests to the Tier-2 pool. Any LLM failure falls back to the best earlier ranking (dashed red). Orange boxes are LLM inference.
Figure 3: Cost and quality on MovieLens-1M: aggregate NDCG@10 against average tokens per user, with values from Table 2. The dashed line marks B0.
Table 2: Aggregate results (1,000 users per dataset). Bold: best NDCG@10 per dataset. Underline: best within each LLM group. Esc.: share of escalated users. Tok: average tokens per user.
Table 1: NDCG@10 by cold-start bin (200 users per bin). ∗: the 95% paired-bootstrap CI of the delta vs. B0 excludes zero. CR uses τ=5, so bins with k ≤ 5 are escalated.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a cascade architecture for LLM reranking that reduces inference cost by routing requests based on user history, demonstrating a practical efficiency strategy.
papers.title: CascadeRec: Deployed Adaptive LLM Compute Allocation for Multi-Tenant Content Recommendation
papers.tldr: CascadeRec reduces costly LLM reranking by selectively escalating requests to a stronger tier, cutting production inference cost by about 10% without observed quality loss.

papers.abstract: To train a sparse autoencoder (SAE), you need a massive cache of model activations. We look into the effects that compression has on an SAE in two ways: we keep the original fp32-trained SAE and pass the compressed cache into the same SAE to see how many feature activations stay the same (the frozen-SAE test), and we retrain an SAE on the compressed cache and see how many of the original features still exist (the retraining test). We found that in the retraining test, there is no clear scale for retained features. On a GPT-2 cache, rounding everything to fp16 keeps 60.6% of features, but changing one value in a million by the smallest step fp32 allows (a change eight orders of magnitude smaller) keeps only 70.5%. Meanwhile, changing the random seed keeps 23.0%. For the frozen-SAE test, the frozen SAE's correlation with the original increases in order of how precise the codecs are, but plain $L_2$ distance gives nearly the same ordering. We also see the same frozen reading correspond to different percentages retained at different sites. This leaves the question of the right measurement. We build one by calibrating: retraining on identical bytes sets the ceiling, and a reseed sets the floor. We then measure the effect of each compressed codec against its own site's floor. With TopK SAEs on GPT-2 small and Pythia-1.4B at research-scale budgets, na\"ive per-token int4 loses more features than a reseed everywhere we tested, as do PCA and random projection on GPT-2. Standardizing each channel before quantizing brings int4 back above the floor in terms of retained features, at the same raw file size. At our smallest budget, a bf16 forward pass, which some pipelines use to save memory, loses slightly more features than rotated 8-bit storage. Calibrating a site costs four training runs and two evaluation passes.
bullets: The study tests compression by evaluating both a frozen SAE on compressed activations and an SAE retrained on them.
Feature retention after retraining has no clear universal scale: compression effects can be smaller or larger than changing the random seed.
Frozen-SAE correlation broadly follows codec precision, but simple L2 distance gives nearly the same ranking and does not transfer consistently across sites.
The authors calibrate each site using identical-byte retraining as a ceiling and reseeding as a floor, requiring four training runs and two evaluation passes.

At research-scale budgets, naive per-token int4, PCA, and random projection can underperform reseeding; channel standardization improves int4, while bf16 can lose slightly more features than rotated 8-bit storage.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Retrained agreement against perturbation size. Blue: calibrated isotropic noise, fp32 on both sides; orange: real codecs; star and diamond: one ulp on one scalar and on a millionth of them; the shaded band marks fp32’s own precision, below which no dense fp32 noise can go. Retraining barely responds to the size of tiny perturbations but separates the real codecs clearly. GPT-2 L6, seed 0; the fp16-scale noise and the millionth-of-values change were each run three times and are plotted at their original run.

Figure 3: Agreement as a multiple of each site’s own seed floor, against measured bits per dimension, 1× budget (33M token-visits on GPT-2, 24.6M on Pythia). Filled markers: fp16 and the rotated codecs; hollow: naïve per-token at the same rate. The dotted riser is the effect of standardizing and rotating at identical bytes (on GPT-2, standardizing alone gives the same, Table 18), and at 4 bits it spans the floor at every site. Read the ordering, not the levels: at 10× budget rot-int4’s ratio is 1.09×. Pythia’s fp16 is its own bf16 master, so it is omitted there.

Figure 4: Agreement on a fixed-size stable set (N = 774, the 1× tier’s stable-feature count, taking the top N by cross-seed stability at each budget) against training budget; error bars are binomial standard errors. fp16 is flat; the rotated codecs improve, so the gap does not widen.

Figure 5: The frozen-SAE reading against the retraining it stands in for, at three sites; the x axis is frozen disagreement 1 − r, log scale, improving rightward. Every series is monotone (the frozen SAE ranks codecs correctly), but the series are offset from each other (the same reading corresponds to different retained percentages at different sites); the viable codecs crowd into a span a linear axis would collapse to a point. Dotted lines are each site’s seed floor. Pythia’s fp16 point is omitted: the bf16 master makes it bit-lossless.

Figure 1: GPT-2 layer 6, seed 0: one ulp on a millionth of values already costs three quarters of fp16’s loss, so the count needs a floor. Bars: alive features a retrained SAE recovers at best match r > 0.9 (grey: control; blue: tiny perturbations; orange: real codecs); dashed line: seed floor.

Table 1: Full GPT-2 codec panel. ± rows are three-seed means (± half the range), bare cells seed 0, so fp16 reads 59.3 ± 1.1 here and 60.6 (seed 0) in the text. survived: best match above r = 0.9 against fp32 at the same seed; FVU: fraction of variance unexplained; mean r: the retrained SAE’s best-match correlation, averaged over alive features (not the frozen reading); stable: survival among the 774 features reproduced in both other fp32 seeds; Hung. cos: mean matched encoder and decoder cosine over all latents, dead ones included; frozen: the thresholded reading through the frozen fp32 SAE. FVU is flat across every viable codec (0.1355 to 0.1361) while seed-0 agreement falls from 60.6 to 37.6%. The floor row’s FVU is the fp32 reference’s own, and its Hungarian cosine averages the two seed-0 pairs.
Table 13: Ratio to floor as the counting threshold moves. Levels change with the threshold; the ordering and the below-floor verdict for naïve int4 do not.

Table 14: The noise levels and sparse changes (seed 0; pp/decade is the change in agreement per decade of relative L2 to the next row): isotropic noise at an exact relative L2 and one-ulp changes to a fixed count of values, all stored in fp32 on both sides. Everything from n = 77 to 15,335 is flat; the one-value change also differs in when it reaches training (Appendix J). The fp16-scale noise and the millionth-of-values change were re-run twice with fresh randomness (60.6/60.4/60.8 and 70.5/69.7/71.6%); the table prints the original runs.

Table 16: How far the two smallest perturbations sit above the seed floor at each counting threshold. The margin is positive everywhere (11–43 pp dense, 12–47 sparse) but its size is thresholddependent.

Table 22: Predicting per-feature survival from fp32 statistics. CV AUC: a logistic model on all three, 5-fold cross-validated; the other columns are single-statistic AUCs. Mean activation is the strongest single predictor, unlike the peak activation reported for weight quantization.

Table 28: The frozen-SAE test explained by TopK margins (GPT-2 layer 6, the frozen test’s own SAE and tokens). model: Spearman correlation, over alive features, between predicted and measured frozen disagreement 1 − r; the prediction uses only the second moment of the codec’s error, estimated on held-out tokens, and the SAE’s margins on clean activations. statistic: the largest |ρ| of log firing rate, log mean or log peak activation with 1− r. crossing %: median share of a degraded or damaged feature’s squared error that comes from tokens where it is active on one side only (–: not reported for the noise-like codecs, which have at most 6 degraded or damaged features each). Below the rule, codecs that remove part of the signal rather than add noise. Sources: geom_margins.json, geom_summary.json.

Table 29: Predicting from one SAE which features retraining recovers (GPT-2 layer 6, AUC). Above the rule the target is seed stability (best match r > 0.9 in both other seeds); the logistic model is fit once on the 1×, k = 32 SAE (its row is cross-validated) and applied unchanged to the other regimes’ own SAEs. Below the rule, the same seed-fit model predicts which features survive retraining on each codec. positive %: seed-stable or retained share of alive features. statistics: log firing rate, log mean and log peak activation. geometry: co-firing share with the best partner, decoder coherence, co-firing of the nearest decoder atom, TopK margin relative to the activation, encoder-decoder cosine. Predictors use held-out eval tokens. Source: geom_identifiability.json.

Table 8: The alive cut, swept. Tightening it raises agreement and the floor together and lowers rotint4’s ratio monotonically (1.63 to 1.13× on GPT-2); our 0.001 cut is the loosest of the five. rot-int4 only, so this bounds a ratio, not an ordering; the floor here averages the two seed-0 pairs at each site (23.1 against the three-pair 23.0 on GPT-2).

Table 7: Linear probes: accuracy change against the fp32-trained probe, and learned-direction cosine, each scored against a seven-split resample floor (0.008/0.002 accuracy and 0.80/0.77 cosine on sst2/ag_news, mean over splits, with cosine minima 0.788/0.759; probe_floor.json). Accuracy resolution is one validation example, so read the deltas as counts. PCA-256 keeps accuracy on sst2 but not on ag_news (its drop there is outside the floor) while its directions collapse to about 0.5 on both; int4-o16 fails the sst2 direction floor (0.778 against a floor minimum of 0.788) on a test the retraining test passes. The two other codecs with probe runs, int8 and rot-int6, clear both floors on both tasks (0.991/0.995 and 0.998/0.998 cosine) and are omitted for width.

Table 2: Pythia-1.4B layer 8, same construction as Table 1. Codec runs are seed 0 only, so gaps under the 2 pp tie band are unresolved; the bracketed intervals resample features against the seed0/seed-1 floor pair, not seeds. fp16 is bit-lossless under the bf16 master, so its row is a same-seed ceiling.

Table 4: Frozen-SAE mean r beside retrained agreement at three sites. Within a site the frozen SAE ranks the codecs as retraining does; across sites the same reading carries no level (rot-int8 reads within 0.00005 everywhere and retrains to 2.09–2.73× the local floor). Codec rows are seed 0; floors are three-pair means.
Table 3: Pythia-1.4B layer 16. Identical construction, interval convention and bit-identical fp16 ceiling reading to Table 2. Source: runs_m4_L16/eval.

Table 5: JumpReLU panel (GPT-2, calibrated λ = 8.68). The viable codecs land within a few points of the floor (fp16 26.4, rot-int4 26.1, rot-int8 25.3 against 23.7 to 24.2), too close together for a graded verdict. mean r: the retrained best-match correlation averaged over alive features. The fp32 and viable-codec runs end with about a third of latents dead (the naïve int4 run about a quarter), and the naïve int4 run converged to L0 = 38.2 against fp32’s 18.6, so its row is shown but excluded from any verdict as confounded.

Table 10: A treatment that is not a storage codec: computing the cache with a bf16 forward (stored in fp32) beside the storage codecs. Over three seeds the bf16 forward retains 49.7–51.2% against rot-int8’s 51.6–53.8, disjoint but with n = 3 (a sign test cannot go below p = 0.25; within-seed deltas −2.7, −1.8, −3.0 pp). At 3× budget the comparison reads 44.4 against 45.3% (one seed each), inside the tie band. It runs 2.21× faster.

Table 12: Serial loader throughput per store (prefetch = 0, warm page cache, one Apple M5). The 1× training run consumes 10,017 tokens/s, so even the slowest store (int4-o16, 55k tokens/s) outruns training; the standardize-and-rotate decode path costs real time (rot-int8 reads at 64% of int8’s rate). One-machine numbers. In a paired idle-machine measurement (two interleaved runs each), std-int4 decodes at 88 MB/s against rot-int4’s 89; our std-int4 keeps the rotation matmul with an identity matrix, so this does not isolate the rotation’s own cost.

Table 11: Lossless zstd-3 over the quantized payloads, measured on one shard per codec. Rotated codecs compress only 1.04–1.26× further; naïve scaling leaves headroom that zstd recovers. Standardization without the rotation lands with the rotated codec (303.8 against 307.5B/token).

Table 17: The causal test: a difference-in-means steering vector injected into the residual stream, scored against the variation between two disjoint halves of the same data (the half-versus-half floor runs about twice a full-data comparison, so it is conservative only for a fail; the like-for-like referent is half the floor). Naïve int4 fails at least 399 of 400 resample splits on both tasks; PCA-256 passes on average but fails 51 of 400 ag_news splits against the like-for-like referent; task-matched prompts and a strength sweep leave every verdict unchanged.

Table 15: The noise levels and codecs on the seed-stable stratum (n = 774) beside all alive features. The response is flatter still on the stable stratum (0.35 pp per decade from noise 10−7 to 10−4, against 2.6 from fp16 to rot-int4), and the ratio of the two rates depends on the window, so we quote no single ratio.

Table 27: Training throughput on an A100 (thousand tokens/s, full 1× run, mean of two fresh containers) by cache format and where the loader decodes; busy is the share of training time the loader spent reading, decoding and shuffling. Every decode path of a format trains bit-identical weights. Best std-int4 over best fp32: 1.09 from local disk, 1.04 from the network volume, under the pre-registered 1.10 for a material gain. Volume reads varied 60–840 MB/s between runs.

Table 30: In this run, when a perturbation reaches training decides its cost (GPT-2 layer 6, seed 0, one run per row). Each perturbed run is a copy of the reference run, which reproduces Table 1’s fp32 seed-0 SAE bit for bit, that receives the change at the listed step(s) and trains on the same batches. agreement: the paper’s retained percentage against the reference. distance: relative Frobenius distance of the decoder from the reference’s, at the end and 2,000 steps after the change. The one-ulp row replays the one-scalar experiment (its altered value enters training twice; the weights are bit-identical to the reference at every logged step from 130 until the second entry; optimizer moments were not compared) and reproduces that SAE bit for bit. The last row is not a copy: it is the separately trained noise7 SAE of Table 14, where every batch carries the change, scored against the same reference. Sources: geom_summary.json, pair_geomdyn_*.json.
Table 9: Sparsity moves the floor without touching a byte: over a 1.95× swing in the floor, rot-int8’s ratio spreads 1.72–3.23× while its survival among seed-stable features spreads only 92.8–97.1%.

Table 6: Budget scaling on a fixed stable set (N = 774 features at every tier, binomial SE about 1.1 pp). fp16 is flat, the rotated codecs improve. fp16’s count is 741 of 774 at all three tiers by coincidence: the three pairs are distinct runs whose all-alive agreement is 60.6, 49.2 and 50.6%. Budget was scaled by re-reading one 20M-token cache (up to about 16 passes over the same tokens), so this isolates optimization from data diversity but not from convergence on a fixed corpus; at 3×, fresh text gives the same floor (Table 25).

Table 18: Which step repairs 4-bit. std-int4 is byte-identical to rot-int4 with the rotation set to the identity, so the two differ by exactly the rotation: standardization alone gives 38.0 ± 0.9%, adding the rotation 37.7 ± 0.3%, inside the tie band. All three arms are three-seed means over same-seed pairs. The ablation keeps the rotation matmul, so it isolates the rotation’s effect, not its decode cost.

Table 19: Is codec damage a shared bias or seed-like noise? On the fp32 seed-stable set (n = 774), losses are enriched above independence for every codec, so a shared component exists, but under rot-int8 only 0.13% of seed-stable features are lost in all three seeds against 24.2% under naïve int4. Recomputed from released pair files; no training.

Table 20: Survival among seed-stable / seed-unstable features under four definitions of stability: activation-space matching at three thresholds, and weight-space Hungarian matching on encoder+decoder cosine. Under every definition the viable codecs keep far more of the stable features than of the unstable ones (stable 62.9 to 98.8%, unstable 19.9 to 57.9%), and naïve int4 is lowest on both; the levels move with the definition, so a stratified percentage is only interpretable with its definition attached. On Pythia the viable codecs keep 18.6 to 38.3% of the unstable features (runs_m4_L8, runs_m4_L16 stability files). GPT-2 L6, seed 0. Sources: stability_fp32_s0_t0p*.json, stability_hungarian.json.

Table 21: Spearman rank agreement of three cheap readings with retrained agreement over every released condition per site. The 15 GPT-2 conditions are the 13 storage codecs of Table 1 plus the bf16 forward and the std-int4 ablation. None of the three needs a retrained SAE, and none ranks better than the others.

Table 23: Do matched features do the same thing? 300 sampled alive fp32 features, each removed from the residual stream on its 32 strongest held-out rows, then its best match in each retrained SAE on the same rows. Same effect: cosine above 0.9 between the two changes in next-token log-probabilities; the last three columns are medians. std-int4 exceeds reseeding by 15.7 pp (95% CI 10.5 to 20.8); among pairs matched at r > 0.9 its effects are as close as a reseed’s (median difference +0.014, CI −0.018 to +0.042). Seed 0, one sample.

Share of alive fp32 features recovered on held-out tokens by a least-squares map from their m best-correlated partners (R2 > 0.81, so m=1 is the retraining count re-scored on these tokens). Recovering from four partners keeps std-int4 13.4 pp above reseeding (three seeds each). Stable: features matched above r = 0.9 in both other fp32 seeds of the same regime; fixed-774: the top 774 by cross-seed agreement, as in Table 6. The fresh floor sits +0.09 pp from the replay floor and std-int4 keeps the same lead in both regimes.

Table 26: Equal stored bytes at 3×: fp16 on the 20M-token cache against std-int4 on the first 79.0M tokens of the fresh store, in 99.76% of fp16’s bytes. Agreement is cross-seed against fresh fp32 (six pairs per candidate, mean and range), so no candidate shares an initialization or data order with its reference; the reference row is fresh fp32 against itself across seeds (three pairs). The two candidates differ by +0.02 pp: a tie. †Post-hoc resolution check, not pre-registered (naïve int4: seed 0 only, two pairs).

papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses memory-efficiency in AI by studying activation-cache compression for SAE training, fitting the efficient-AI and memory-efficiency subtopic.
papers.title: How Small Can We Go? Calibrating Activation-Cache Compression for SAE Training
papers.tldr: A calibrated evaluation framework shows that activation-cache compression can severely alter SAE features, while channel-standardized int4 preserves more features than naive int4 at the same storage cost.

papers.abstract: Wafer-scale accelerators promise ultra-low-latency AI inference, but current system stacks still carry an unsustainably high cost premium. The reason is that many current and emerging inference techniques, such as batching and MoE, introduce runtime dynamism that existing wafer-scale systems cannot support efficiently. As a result, they must choose between two unsatisfactory options: accept suboptimal latency, or preserve low latency by restricting dynamic techniques, thereby limiting the models they can support and reducing aggregate throughput. This tradeoff significantly increases the cost of low-latency serving. We present MeshRT, the first wafer-scale system to achieve both ultra-low latency and high throughput for LLM inference. MeshRT achieves this via a novel system architecture, which we call compile-time governance of runtime dynamism. This architecture features new system abstractions and mechanisms that enable MeshRT to compile dynamic events arising from LLM inference directly into per-core schedules, enabling asynchronous and decentralized execution with low runtime overhead. Implemented on a commodity wafer-scale accelerator, MeshRT preserves ultra-low latency while improving throughput by up to 56$\times$ over the state-of-the-art system for wafer-scale accelerators. Against measured single-instance SGLang results on H200, MeshRT achieves 4.5-7.0$\times$ lower latency. Under ideal linear scaling of those GPU measurements to an approximately power-matched H200 cluster, MeshRT achieves 1.7-13.0$\times$ higher decode system throughput in the low-latency regime.
authors: Congjie He, Le Xu, Zhan Lu, Yeqi Huang, Haocheng Xiao, Cheng Deng, Lingxiao Ma, Ziming Miao, Fan Yang, Luo Mai
bullets: Addresses the tension between low latency and dynamic techniques such as batching and mixture-of-experts (MoE) inference.
Introduces “compile-time governance of runtime dynamism,” compiling inference events into per-core schedules.
Enables asynchronous, decentralized execution with low runtime overhead on a commodity wafer-scale accelerator.
Reports up to 56× higher throughput than the prior state of the art for wafer-scale accelerators.
Achieves 4.5–7.0× lower latency than measured single-instance SGLang on H200; GPU-cluster throughput comparisons use ideal linear scaling assumptions.

figures.caption: Figure 4.MeshRT system overview. Given a computation graph and mapping choices, MeshRT synthesizes dynamismaware per-core event tables (§4.2), partitions them into segments that fit hardware resource limits (§4.3), and deploys the result onto the wafer-scale accelerator.

Figure 9. System throughput vs. single-user throughput on WSE-3 at 4K context for prefill (top) and decode (bottom). Comparing each system’s peak over the evaluated micro-batches, MeshRT improves system throughput by 4.0–6.6× during prefill and by up to 55.8× during decode. Decode points do not apply workload-level padding correction.

Figure 8. MeshRT system boundary. The host compiles and installs per-core schedules once (top left). During serving (bottom left), it asynchronously pushes prefill contexts and decode KV caches. All per-step execution, continuous batching, and dynamism resolution proceed on chip without host involvement (right).
Figure 2. Padding compute ratios across different models increase with serving batch size.

Figure 1. Wafer-scale accelerators as a distinct runtime setting. Host-mediated control incurs expensive round trips. Cores form a neighbor-only mesh of𝑀 × 𝑁 cores, so chipwide synchronization takes 𝑂 (𝑀+𝑁 ) hops and grows with physical distance. Each core exposes only bounded local resources, including local SRAM, finite routing-table state, and simple local branching rather than a general scheduler. These properties limit design choices.

Figure 6. Synthesized per-core sub-schedules for continuous batching. The last-layer core prepends batch-state metainfo to outgoing data; the first-layer core parses it and updates its local request table to select active slots.

Figure 5. Per-core schedule synthesis for an AllReduce kernel mapped to one row of cores. The kernel function and mapping determine role-specific event-action tables: edge cores receive a partial sum, accumulate locally, forward it, and later receive the broadcast result; mid cores relay and accumulate; and the root reduces and broadcasts.

Figure 3. MeshRT design intuition: compile-time governance of runtime dynamism. Instead of deferring dynamic decisions to host control, MeshRT compiles them directly into per-core schedules as control events that execute alongside data events entirely on chip. Each core then runs its own schedule asynchronously, coordinating only through data arrival.

papers.selection_reason: Wafer-scale runtime that reduces LLM inference latency and improves throughput, fitting the efficiency-oriented scope of Efficient AI.
papers.title: MeshRT: Compile-Time Governed Wafer-Scale Runtime for Low-Latency High-Throughput Inference

papers.abstract: Decision models such as Jev have emerged as a highly promising paradigm for LLM agent systems, providing lightweight and reliable categorical reasoning for rapid System One execution. However, existing generation-oriented inference engines fail to support these workloads effectively, suffering from severe prefix recomputation overheads or distorted output probabilities. To address this challenge, we propose Flide, an efficient and exact inference engine that decouples the logical tree structure of a decision request from its physical execution within a single flattened token stream. Through ForkAttention, Flide navigates request dependencies using GPU-resident indices across both standard attention and recurrent Gated DeltaNet layers, guaranteeing in exact arithmetic that every query branch evaluates identically to an isolated forward pass. By expressing branch topologies directly in GPU-resident metadata, Flide accommodates diverse request mixtures with a compact set of pre-recorded execution graphs while enabling expanding agent histories to resume from checkpoints saved in earlier passes. Extensive evaluations on public hybrid and decision models demonstrate that Flide answers queries up to 9.5 times faster than vLLM and SGLang while staying closest to a float32 reference in total variation distance. By unifying physical execution throughput with mathematical exactness, Flide establishes a principled foundation for scalable, latency-critical decision intelligence in agent systems.
bullets: Targets prefix recomputation and probability distortion in existing generation-oriented inference engines.
Uses ForkAttention with GPU-resident indices to represent logical request trees across standard attention and recurrent Gated DeltaNet layers.
Ensures each query branch matches an isolated forward pass in exact arithmetic.
Supports diverse request mixtures through compact pre-recorded execution graphs and checkpoint-based resumption of expanding agent histories.
Evaluations on public hybrid and decision models report up to 9.5× faster queries than vLLM and SGLang, with outputs closest to a float32 reference in total variation distance.

papers.abstract: Local online training on resource-constrained platforms requires low computational and training-state overhead. We study the numerical stability and computational efficiency of half-precision proximal policy optimization (PPO) on commodity GPUs. Directly converting PPO training to FP16 is unreliable because numerical errors feed back through policy updates and subsequent data collection, while PPO repeatedly compares a current policy with a fixed behavior policy. We propose PPO-FP16 with three structure-aware modules. Global scalar protection stabilizes statistics shared across a minibatch or parameter update. Policy-change residual protection extracts and preserves small differences between the current and behavior policies. Efficient persistent-update protection stabilizes optimizer state and parameter writeback while reducing state storage. These changes preserve the PPO objective, hyperparameters, and training budget. Across six continuous-control tasks and five seeds, PPO-FP16 achieves the lowest mean return-AUC rank (1.90) among the four methods and ranks first in 17 of 30 environment-seed comparisons. Eight of nine performance configurations yield PPO update speedups ranging from 1.16 to 2.03 times. Relative to Full FP32 Adam, optimizer-state memory is reduced by 71.7 to 74.9 percent, and peak allocated GPU memory is reduced by up to 44.5 percent. The results show that protecting a small set of structurally important quantities can deliver stable, efficient FP16 PPO without retuning.
bullets: Direct FP16 PPO is unstable because numerical errors influence later policy updates and data collection.
Three protections target shared scalars, small current-versus-behavior policy differences, and persistent optimizer/parameter updates.
Across six continuous-control tasks and five seeds, PPO-FP16 had the best mean return-AUC rank and ranked first in 17 of 30 environment-seed comparisons.
Update speed improved by 1.16–2.03× in eight of nine configurations, while optimizer-state and peak GPU memory were substantially reduced.
The approach is evaluated for stable local training on commodity GPUs and does not require retuning PPO hyperparameters.

papers.selection_reason: Half-precision PPO with memory and compute reduction fits efficient AI, though no specific subtopic.
papers.title: Structure-Aware Numerical Stabilization for Half-Precision Proximal Policy Optimization
papers.tldr: PPO-FP16 enables stable, faster, and more memory-efficient half-precision PPO by protecting structurally important numerical quantities without changing PPO settings.

papers.abstract: Real-time video generation, interactive world models, and on-device image synthesis are almost a reality. Diffusion Transformers (DiT) achieve excellent sample quality, shifting the bottleneck to the throughput of the models themselves. Natural images are inherently sparse, as large portions of an image are often background, contribute little to the scene content, and are easy to denoise. DiTs fail to exploit this sparsity, as they process image tokens statically and uniformly. We propose MoDDiT, a simple architecture modification that learns to route tokens through both MLP and self-attention operations. By routing tokens through both blocks independently, MoDDiT allows for dynamic compute allocation in MLPs that varies across tokens, images, and denoising timesteps. Using MoDDiT to train image generation models from scratch significantly reduces computational costs of training and inference, processing as few as 12.5% of the tokens. By increasing sparsity and model depth, MoDDiT reduces costs and improves generation performance over unrouted baselines. The learned allocation is interpretable, revealing how computation varies with visual content and noise level. We also use MoDDiT to train video generation models, where allocation correlates with motion, and to distill a dense bidirectional video model into a sparse autoregressive student.
bullets: Targets DiTs’ inefficient uniform processing of mostly sparse visual content.
Routes tokens independently through MLP and self-attention operations, adapting compute by token, image, and denoising timestep.
Processes as few as 12.5% of tokens, substantially reducing training and inference costs.
Higher sparsity and model depth improve generation performance over unrouted baselines.
Token allocation is interpretable, correlating with visual content, noise level, and video motion.

papers.abstract: Activation memory, not compute, limits CNN inference on constrained hardware such as microcontrollers. Direct in-place convolution removes the dual-buffer cost, but the memory-optimal formulation of Gural and Murmann assumes valid padding, unit stride, unit dilation, and odd square kernels, and needs a non-sequential traversal costing $2\times$ inference time in transposes. We identify two regimes in which their published closed form does not hold: (1) an under-allocation of exactly $(k-1)C_{in} \bmod (C_{out}-C_{in})$ scalars, active on every convolutional layer of their own deployed network and manifesting as a silent corruption of still-live input; (2) an unbounded overestimate, up to $2{,}432\times$, once the critical leg leaves the output grid. We correct both and generalize to arbitrary stride, dilation, padding, and rectangular kernels. We then propose Right In-Place (RiP) convolution, a bit-identical operation in which every layer reads its input right-aligned in a shared workspace and writes its output left-aligned from index zero. The debt is piecewise affine in the output pixel index, so evaluating its breakpoints in $O(1)$ yields the minimum safe gap without enumerating the output grid, with row-major access preserved. Across $10{,}000$ random layers RiP produced no corruption, and across 84 convolutional layers from 25 architectures it matches the herringbone workspace exactly on 58 and within 5% on 81, using 24.8% less memory than dual buffering on average. Written into TinyEngine's kernels and deployed to a Raspberry Pi Pico 1 and Pico 2, it cuts peak activation memory across eleven MCUNet models by 12.5 to 33.3% at unchanged cycle counts and bit-identical outputs, raising the number of models that fit the Pico 1's 256 KB SRAM from six to nine.
bullets: Addresses activation-memory limits caused by dual-buffer CNN inference on microcontrollers.
Corrects flaws in prior memory-optimal formulations and generalizes them to arbitrary stride, dilation, padding, and rectangular kernels.
Uses right-aligned inputs, left-aligned outputs, and O(1) breakpoint analysis to find the minimum safe workspace gap while preserving row-major access.
Matches the exact herringbone workspace on 58 of 84 layers and comes within 5% on 81; it uses 24.8% less memory than dual buffering on average.
On Raspberry Pi Pico devices, it reduces peak activation memory by 12.5–33.3% with unchanged cycles and bit-identical outputs, increasing fitting models from 6 to 9 on the Pico 1.

papers.selection_reason: Focuses on memory-efficient CNN inference (RiP convolution) to reduce activation memory on constrained hardware, directly addressing a key challenge in Efficient AI.
papers.title: Right In-Place (RiP) Convolution: A Simple, General, and Near-Optimal Strategy for Memory-Efficient CNN Inference
papers.tldr: RiP convolution enables safe, near-minimal in-place CNN inference for constrained devices while preserving speed and bit-identical outputs.

papers.abstract: LLM agents use context compaction to manage growing interaction histories, but summarizing long histories with large models can introduce substantial delays. Compaction therefore requires balancing information retention against latency. We observe that structured summary slots can retain information when generated independently. Based on this observation, we present SpecCompact, a framework that accelerates compaction through slot-parallel semantic speculation. SpecCompact fine-tunes a small drafter and generates slots in parallel. The target model verifies each proposed line and repairs rejected content, while subsequent drafting uses the updated slot prefix. System optimizations further reduce repeated context processing and model calls. Across AppWorld and $\tau^3$ benchmarks with two target models, SpecCompact achieves $2.04$--$5.63\times$ compaction speedups over Hermes-style summarization. Separate downstream evaluations reveal model- and task-dependent performance trade-offs. A user study within Hermes further shows an $8.68\times$ median compaction speedup.
authors: Yulu An, Yifei Feng, Xiangyang Yin
bullets: Addresses the latency of summarizing growing agent histories while preserving important information.
Uses a small fine-tuned drafter to propose structured summary slots in parallel.
A target model verifies each proposed line, repairs rejected content, and guides subsequent drafting.
Reports 2.04–5.63× speedups on AppWorld and τ³ with two target models, plus an 8.68× median speedup in a Hermes user study.
Downstream quality shows model- and task-dependent trade-offs.

papers.selection_reason: Accelerates LLM agent context compaction via speculative verification, directly relevant to long-context and memory efficiency.
papers.title: SpecCompact: Accelerating LLM Agent Context Compaction with Slot-Parallel Semantic Speculative Verification

papers.abstract: Computer-use agents (CUAs) have recently achieved superhuman performance on several long-horizon benchmarks. However, their computational cost limits their use in long-horizon tasks and real-time domains such as video games. A key bottleneck is representing each screenshot as thousands of visual tokens, which accumulate into long contexts as agents reason over extended interaction histories. We observe that most of these visual tokens are either semantically irrelevant to the agent's next action or temporally redundant across screenshots. Building on this observation, we introduce Visual Token Routing (VTR), a joint training framework for learning sparse visual representations that preserve the information needed for action prediction. In VTR, we train the vision-language model together with a lightweight spatio-temporal router that examines each image region in the current and previous screenshots and decides whether its visual token enters the language model. We optimize the router using an adaptive loss to keep the number of visual tokens as small as possible while minimizing performance degradation. With just 2,000 training steps, VTR matches the performance of the full-resolution model on OSWorld, CUA-World, and video game action prediction, while using 2.5-5.8x fewer visual tokens. These savings reduce inference cost by up to 3.3x and speed up prefill by up to 2.9x. VTR also outperforms lowering the image resolution and other baselines for dropping tokens, by up to 12.8 points on OSWorld. Overall, VTR enables computer-use agents to process only the visual tokens they need, allowing them to be used in long-horizon tasks and real-time domains at a fraction of the computational cost. Code and models are available at https://pranjal2041.github.io/vtr
bullets: Targets the computational bottleneck caused by thousands of visual tokens accumulating across long interaction histories.
Jointly trains a vision-language model with a lightweight spatio-temporal router that selects action-relevant, nonredundant image-region tokens.
Uses an adaptive loss to minimize token count while limiting performance degradation.
Matches the full-resolution model on OSWorld, CUA-World, and video-game action prediction using 2.5–5.8× fewer visual tokens.
Reduces inference cost by up to 3.3× and prefilling time by up to 2.9×; outperforms resolution reduction and other token-dropping baselines on OSWorld.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of Visual Token Routing (VTR). It drops the regions that did not change, and also drops the circled part of the video, which changed but is not relevant to the task.

papers.title: Visual Token Routing: Learning to keep tokens that matter
papers.tldr: Visual Token Routing sparsifies screenshot representations for computer-use agents, preserving action performance while substantially reducing visual-token and inference costs.

papers.abstract: Looped Transformers increase effective depth by re-executing shared layers, but three limitations hinder their adoption: memory grows with the loop count, compute can only be adjusted in whole-block steps, and the loop count is hard to change after training. We propose LooM (Loop-invariant Memory), which addresses each in turn. In a causal encoder-decoder (CED), LooM loops only the decoder layers after the first, which read a global memory written once per token, and each of them publishes the key-value (KV) entry for a token only on its first visit, so the cache does not grow with the loop count. These layers loop independently, providing every budget from 3 to 21 layer executions per token, and one model trained on randomly sampled budgets covers all of them without a router. With enough loops, LooM outperforms a single-pass baseline trained on the same data on language modeling, zero-shot accuracy and long-context perplexity, while using the same cache size. Our analysis further shows that the training budget distribution decides what extra depth buys. These results suggest that a CED is a natural place to loop: memory is written once, and depth becomes a budget chosen at deployment.
authors: Lele Yang, Muxi Diao, Zhonghao Yan, Jiankang Chen, Bin Wen, Tingting Gao, Wentao Zhang, Kongming Liang, Zhanyu Ma, Weiran Xu
bullets: Targets looped Transformer limitations: loop-dependent memory growth, coarse compute control, and fixed post-training loop counts.
Loops decoder layers after the first, using global memory written once per token and publishing each token’s KV entry only on its first visit.
Independent layer loops provide budgets from 3 to 21 layer executions per token; one model supports all budgets without a router.
With sufficient looping, LooM improves language modeling, zero-shot accuracy, and long-context perplexity over a same-data single-pass baseline while keeping cache size unchanged.
Training-budget distributions determine what additional depth provides; the approach supports deployment-time depth selection.

papers.selection_reason: Novel looped transformer architecture that keeps cache size constant, improving long-context perplexity and efficiency.
papers.title: LooM: Loop-Invariant Memory for Causal Encoder-Decoder Language Models
papers.tldr: LooM enables flexible, memory-efficient looping in causal encoder-decoder language models, allowing deployment-time depth adjustment without increasing cache size.

papers.abstract: Small language models offer a compact basis for shell simulation without executing submitted commands, but full-output decoding requires them to predict recurring utility structure alongside content that varies across executions. We introduce template gap reconstruction (TGR), which supplies reusable output literals interspersed with sentinels to be interleaved with autoregressively generated gaps. A template selector chooses which template to be reconstructed, with the empty template retaining full-output decoding. We construct a template bank from 18.7 million outputs collected across heterogeneous execution environments and train a template selector and five reconstruction models initialized from various small language model checkpoints on a target environment excluded from bank construction. Evaluation demonstrates that TGR improves output edit similarity (O-ES) over full-output decoding (FOD) when the optimal template covers more than 25\% of the template, while performing similarly for lower-coverage outputs. Additionally, TGR outperforms FOD for shorter gap sequences, with O-ES values of 0.964 and 0.812, respectively, while maintaining similar performance for longer sequences. TGR reduces the number of tokens generated by 26.3--38.3\% across used tokenizer families. These results support using a reusable output structure as a practical design choice for small shell simulators, improving response fidelity and shortening generation targets while keeping template selection and residual prediction central to response quality.
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of predicting recurring shell-output structure alongside execution-specific content without running commands.
Provides reusable output templates with sentinels; the model autoregressively generates only the missing gaps.
A template selector chooses a reconstruction template, while an empty template preserves full-output decoding.
Improves output edit similarity when templates cover more than 25% of the output and performs similarly at lower coverage.
Outperforms full-output decoding on shorter gap sequences, with O-ES of 0.964 versus 0.812, while maintaining similar performance on longer sequences.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models map camera observations and language instructions to robot actions. However, their large backbones and repeated action generation can make inference take longer than the robot's real-time requirements for its next action. To reduce the load of VLA computations, researchers have proposed multiple optimization approaches, including quantization and pruning. These optimizations can be combined with other general optimizations such as better kernel compilation or using CUDA graphs instead of the eager mode. However, most of these optimization results are usually reported on a single GPU type, typically for a few VLA models, with no analysis of what the real bottlenecks are for a model on a particular hardware or how these optimizations would generalize beyond the reported results. In this paper, we provide a comprehensive measurement study of seven families of inference optimization methods, from CUDA graphs and compilation to token pruning and quantization, on seven state-of-the-art VLAs evaluated on four GPU families ranging from a datacenter H100 to an embedded Jetson Thor. We analyse how CPU launch overhead, memory bandwidth, and kernel efficiency jointly shape optimization gains, and how applying one method changes the benefit of another. From this analysis, we derive VLA-Triage, guidelines for stacking optimizations under latency budgets. The guidelines identify which stages can provide the required savings and which combinations need testing in the deployed execution mode.
authors: Muhammad Danish Waseem, Ahmed Ali-Eldin Hassan
bullets: Evaluates seven inference-optimization families across seven VLAs and four GPU families, from H100 to Jetson Thor.
Analyzes the roles of CPU launch overhead, memory bandwidth, and kernel efficiency in determining optimization gains.
Shows that optimization benefits and interactions depend on the model, hardware, and deployed execution mode.
Introduces VLA-Triage, guidelines for selecting and stacking optimizations under latency budgets.

papers.selection_reason: Measurement study of VLA inference optimizations including token pruning and quantization across GPUs; fits efficient inference.
papers.title: Where Is VLA Inference Time Spent? Bottlenecks and Optimization Interactions Across GPUs
papers.tldr: A cross-GPU study identifies where VLA inference time is spent and provides guidelines for combining optimizations to meet robot latency requirements.

papers.abstract: Efficient video human pose estimation must balance localisation accuracy, motion quality, and energy cost. We present SpikePose, a lightweight video pose estimator that pairs a frame-reset, single-step spiking encoder with motion-aligned heatmap memory (MAM). The encoder supplies per-frame spatial evidence, while MAM estimates joint displacement, aligns historical heatmaps, and adaptively fuses them with current predictions. By confining temporal reasoning to a compact, lightweight module outside the spiking backbone, SpikePose helps bridge the gap between spiking and classical Artificial Neural Networks (ANN) on large-scale, non-event-driven video tasks. We evaluate spatial accuracy, motion errors, and estimated arithmetic energy on MPII and a fixed NTU60 Cross-Subject subset. Against the architecture-matched ANN with MAM, SpikePose cuts estimated arithmetic energy by 91.4% at a cost of just 1.12 points in head-bone-normalised PCK at 0.5 threshold (PCK_HB(0.5)). Within SpikePose, adding MAM reduces velocity and acceleration errors by 28.13% and 31.46% while slightly improving localisation, at a cost of only 0.003M parameters and 0.0023 analytical GFLOPs per frame. Code will be released on GitHub upon acceptance.
authors: Yunhao Huang, Kaushik Bhargav Sivangi, Tianyi Yu, Fani Deligianni
bullets: Targets the trade-off among pose localisation, temporal motion quality, and energy use in non-event-driven video.
Uses a frame-reset, single-step spiking encoder for spatial evidence and MAM to estimate joint motion, align past heatmaps, and fuse them adaptively with current predictions.
Evaluated on MPII and a fixed NTU60 Cross-Subject subset using localisation, motion-error, and estimated arithmetic-energy metrics.
Compared with an architecture-matched ANN using MAM, it reduces estimated arithmetic energy by 91.4% with a 1.12-point PCK_HB(0.5) decrease.
Adding MAM reduces velocity and acceleration errors by 28.13% and 31.46%, respectively, with minimal computational and parameter overhead.
