papers.abstract: Collaborative inference serves as a critical methodology in edge intelligence. Existing collaborative inference methods operate by splitting the deep neural network (DNN) model between edge devices and cloud servers. However, these methods need to load different models for multiple split points when the communication or device changes, thus resulting in long switching times and substantial storage overhead on the edge side. To address this issue, we propose a Dynamic Split Network (DS-Net), which not only enables efficient split point switching but also enhances the collaborative speed and accuracy across various scenarios. Specifically, we design a dynamic switching framework that enables flexible selection among multiple split points within a single model, thereby reducing storage, memory, and switching overhead. To mitigate the feature distribution shifts and task-relevant information loss caused by dynamic splitting and high-ratio compression, we further propose a hierarchical compensation mechanism. Local alignment calibrates the decoded feature distribution at each split point, while task-specific global compensation restores task-relevant information at the global level. In addition, we incorporate sample-adaptive global compensation selection into split-point selection based on sample complexity and runtime resource conditions. Experimental results demonstrate that DS-Net reduces memory overhead by 74.6% and achieves millisecond-level switching latency. Moreover, under a 10 Mbps bandwidth constraint on the Nano platform, DS-Net outperforms state-of-the-art collaborative methods by achieving 1.2% higher accuracy on the COCO dataset, reducing latency by 42.5%, and improving throughput by a factor of 1.8$\times$.
authors: Xinyun Zhang, Li Wang, Lei Jin, Lianming Xu, Zhu Han
bullets: Addresses storage and switching delays caused by maintaining separate models for different split points and changing communication or device conditions.
Uses a single dynamic model with flexible split-point selection, reducing edge memory overhead and enabling millisecond-level switching.
Applies local feature-distribution alignment and task-specific global compensation to recover information lost through dynamic splitting and compression.
Selects global compensation adaptively based on sample complexity and runtime resources.
On Nano under 10 Mbps bandwidth, reports 74.6% lower memory overhead, 42.5% lower latency, 1.8× higher throughput, and 1.2% higher COCO accuracy than prior collaborative methods.

papers.abstract: Pretraining scaling laws treat training data as a one-dimensional quantity: a token count. Agentic reinforcement learning (RL) inherits this scalar abstraction, but modern synthesis pipelines now generate \textit{tasks}, \textit{environments}, and \textit{trajectories} independently and at very different costs, turning data into a structured design space. This raises a question pretraining never had to answer: given a synthesis budget, \textit{which axis} should be scaled? We address this question end-to-end with three tightly coupled contributions. First, we decompose agentic data into three cardinality axes (task, environment, trajectory), plus a reward-density control variable, and fit per-axis scaling relations on different large language models (LLMs) across math+code, SWE, web, and UI/tool application domains. Across all model sizes, model families, domains, and RL algorithms (PPO and GRPO) we measured, the scaling exponents order as environment $>$ task $>$ trajectory. When environment diversity is decomposed into world and environment-structure diversity, its advantage is mainly driven by the former, while the latter is just comparable to the task diversity. Second, we use the fitted laws as a common ruler to price synthesis methods, capturing each method's efficiency as a per-axis discount factor and identifying critical synthetic-to-real ratios at which collapse begins; these ratios differ by an order of magnitude across axes. Third, we cast budget allocation as a constrained optimization under our laws and discounts, deriving a Chinchilla-style compute-optimal recipe and validating it at held-out scale. The empirical results demonstrate that following the recipe yields up to $1.7\times$ compute efficiency over the dominant ``scale-the-trajectories'' practice.
authors: Bowei He, Yankai Chen, Xiaokun Zhang, Changjiang Han, Ye Yuan, Chong Li, Xue Liu
bullets: The study models agentic data using task, environment, and trajectory cardinalities, plus reward density, under a synthesis budget.
Across tested LLMs, domains, and PPO/GRPO, scaling exponents rank environment > task > trajectory; world diversity chiefly drives the environment advantage.
Fitted scaling laws price synthesis strategies through per-axis discounts and identify axis-specific synthetic-to-real collapse thresholds.
A constrained, Chinchilla-style budget allocation recipe is derived and validated at held-out scale.
Following the recipe achieves up to 1.7× compute efficiency compared with primarily scaling trajectories.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Per-axis scaling laws under controlled sweeps. Each panel sweeps one axis with the other two held at saturation; symbols are mean±SE over 3 seeds, lines are weighted log-log fits. Across all three model sizes, environment scaling is the steepest, trajectory scaling the flattest. The exponent ordering αE > αT > ατ holds with non-overlapping 95% CIs at every model size.

Figure 3: Cross-axis interaction. Heatmap of held-out success on Qwen3-8B (math+code) over a (DE, DT) grid at fixed Dτ = 8. Iso-cost contours (dashed) reveal a Pareto ridge: at low DE, scaling DT has near-zero return. Environment diversity is a prerequisite for task diversity to matter.

Figure 4: Synthesis collapse, per axis. x-axis: synthetic-to-real ratio r = Ds/Dr (log scale). y-axis: agent success rate on a held-out evaluation, normalized to the r = 0 (real-only) value of the same seed group. papers.abstract: The size of the KV cache grows linearly with context length, making it a major memory bottleneck in LLM serving. Motivated by recent progress in identifying the functional roles of attention heads, a growing body of work compresses the KV cache non-uniformly across heads. Existing methods either fix the important heads via offline profiling or select them using attention signals from the prefill stage. In both cases, however, accuracy fluctuates substantially across workloads. While investigating the cause of this instability, we find that the active heads shift between the prefill and decode stages even within a single input. Along the decode path, by contrast, the activehead composition remains stable across content tokens once format tokens are filtered out. Based on this observation, we propose PeekKV. PeekKV observes a single content token immediately after prefill - a one-token peek - to jointly obtain head-group scores and token-importance scores. Guided by these scores, PeekKV allocates KV cache budgets to head groups in proportion to their group scores and retains only the top-scoring tokens within each budget. PeekKV requires no offline profiling or training and thus applies directly to unseen workloads and new models. Across four public benchmarks, PeekKV achieves the highest accuracy in more than half of the per-model comparisons against state-of-the-art methods, and stays closest to the full-cache accuracy on RULER and LongBench. On Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, PeekKV retains 95.7% of the full-cache accuracy at a 10% memory budget on RULER with 16K contexts and 95.9% at a 1.5% budget on LongBench.
bullets: KV-cache memory grows with context length, while existing non-uniform head compression methods can be unstable across workloads.
The method finds that active-head composition shifts between prefill and decode but remains stable across later content tokens after filtering format tokens.
PeekKV performs a one-token peek to jointly score head groups and token importance, then allocates cache budgets and retains the highest-scoring tokens.
It applies directly to unseen workloads and models because it requires neither offline profiling nor additional training.
Across four benchmarks, it is closest to full-cache accuracy on RULER and LongBench; reported retention reaches 95.7% and 95.9% of full-cache accuracy at low memory budgets on Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates large language model inference through parallel verification of tokens proposed by a drafter. Diffusion drafters further parallelize proposal generation, but greater proposal capacity or higher mean accepted tokens (MAT) need not yield higher throughput. Because verification accepts only a consecutive prefix, early rejections can render later correct predictions ineffective, limiting MAT gains, while even higher MAT may not improve throughput if per-round latency increases. We introduce DScout, which uses two complementary factorizations to guide diffusion drafter training and inference for higher throughput. For training, DScout factorizes position-wise loss into inclusion, weighting, and prediction loss. This guides the design and combination of mixed-horizon training, intra-block unmasking, and acceptance-weighted loss to align supervision with prefix acceptance and improve MAT. For inference, DScout factorizes throughput as the ratio of MAT to per-round latency, guiding target-conditioning depth, drafter depth, and inference block size selection to identify a high-throughput configuration for each workload. Across six benchmarks, DScout achieves $3.84\times$ and $4.14\times$ mean speedups over autoregressive decoding on Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B, respectively, improving mean speedup over the state-of-the-art baseline by 9.1% and 7.1%. Across models and concurrency settings, our inference configuration policy provides up to 9.75% additional mean speedup over DScout's fixed configuration.
authors: Jiakun Fan, Min Xiao, Qiang Wang, Neiwen Ling, Zhichao Liu, Zhihao Jia, Dimitrios S. Nikolopoulos, Zijun Wei
bullets: Diffusion drafters can achieve higher mean accepted tokens without improving throughput because early prefix rejections invalidate later predictions and larger proposals may increase latency.
Training factorizes position-wise loss into inclusion, weighting, and prediction components to combine mixed-horizon training, intra-block unmasking, and acceptance-weighted loss.
Inference factorizes throughput into mean accepted tokens divided by per-round latency, guiding target-conditioning depth, drafter depth, and block-size selection.
Across six benchmarks, DScout reaches mean speedups of 3.84× on Qwen3-4B and 4.14× on Qwen3-8B over autoregressive decoding.
Its workload-specific configuration policy adds up to 9.75% mean speedup over DScout’s fixed configuration.

papers.abstract: Vector quantization is widely used for large-scale data compression and approximate nearest neighbor search (ANNS). Multi-codebook quantization (MCQ) is a practical paradigm that represents database vectors with compact codes and supports efficient retrieval through asymmetric distance computation (ADC). However, existing shallow MCQs encode vectors independently within each inverted file (IVF) cluster, without exploiting local references. Therefore, we propose Spatio-Topological Linkage Quantization (STLQ), a topological shallow MCQ method that organizes each IVF cluster as a directed-forest with compact codes and scaling coefficients. Its basic encoding phase first quantizes vectors independently, while the linked encoding phase re-encodes relative residuals with respect to selected reconstructed parents, reusing local reconstruction information to obtain finer representations. The corresponding linked-ADC preserves linear scanning complexity. STLQ further compresses the scaling coefficients and directed-forest structure to control the additional topology overhead. Extensive experiments show that STLQ achieves higher recall than the evaluated shallow MCQs at comparable bit budgets, although at a higher offline construction cost. Meanwhile, it has a competitive recall-QPS tradeoff against deep MCQs. The code is available at https://github.com/ighxiy/STLQ.
authors: Kuizhi Liu, Junying Zhang, Xindi Ma, Xiangyu Wang, Qi Jiang, Sheng Gao, Chen Gong, Jianfeng Ma
bullets: Targets shallow multi-codebook quantization methods that encode vectors independently and miss local references.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models(VLMs)have advanced Visual Document Retrieval (VDR) by enabling OCR-free, multi-vector representations. However, these models generate excessive tokens to preserve dense visual details, which severely limits retrieval scalability. Existing compression methods mitigate this overhead but rely on isolated heuristics that fail to balance token importance, semantic redundancy, and coverage capacity. We propose a visual token compression framework formulated as an Unbalanced Optimal Transport (UOT) problem. Our approach unifies these three objectives into a single alternating optimization process. Furthermore, we theoretically show that minimizing the transport cost upper-bounds the MaxSim retrieval error, ensuring ranking stability. Extensive experiments on the ViDoRe V1 and V3 benchmarks demonstrate that our method preserves fine-grained document semantics and improves the efficiency-effectiveness trade-off over state-of-the-art base-lines. Code is available at https://github.com/shhhhhyy/Unbalanced-Optimal-Transport-for-EVDR.
authors: Hoyeon Shin, Jeongyeon Kim, Yeong Jun Koh, Yeoneung Kim, Hanul Kim
bullets: Addresses the scalability problem caused by excessive tokens in OCR-free, multi-vector VLM-based visual document retrieval.
Formulates token compression as an Unbalanced Optimal Transport problem balancing token importance, semantic redundancy, and coverage.
Uses alternating optimization to jointly optimize these compression objectives.
Provides a theoretical guarantee that lower transport cost bounds MaxSim retrieval error, supporting ranking stability.
Experiments on ViDoRe V1 and V3 show a better efficiency–effectiveness trade-off than existing baselines while retaining fine-grained semantics.

Our method establishes a superior Pareto frontier compared to recent stateof-the-art baselines [15,27].

papers.abstract: Native NVFP4 promises to accelerate reinforcement learning (RL) for large language models (LLMs), but achieving stable learning across separate training and sampling engines remains challenging. We show that matching model weights and numerical formats is insufficient to ensure consistent policy evaluation, highlighting the importance of cross-engine numerical execution. We introduce miniTE, a lightweight framework that combines execution diagnostics, cross-engine numerical alignment, and efficient native W4A4 (4-bit weights and activations) GEMM computation for LLM RL. It improves numerical execution consistency without modifying the RL objective, while reducing implementation overhead to realize the benefits of native low-bit computation. Long-horizon RL experiments on Qwen3-30B-A3B demonstrate stable training and benchmark performance close to BF16, outperforming naive Transformer Engine (TE) NVFP4 in evaluation quality. On single NVIDIA B300 GPU node, the optimized learner reaches 33,540 tokens/s, yielding 1.39x and 1.47x the throughput of BF16 and TE NVFP4, respectively, for complete learner updates. We released the framework, kernels, diagnostics, and training configurations to make native low-bit RL easier.
authors: Zhen Li, Mingfa Feng, Yiming Zhang, Yang Yu, Changhai Zhou, Pengxiang Li, Dongkuan Wu, Congkai Xie, Hongxia Yang
bullets: Matching weights and numerical formats alone does not guarantee consistent policy evaluation across engines.

Long-horizon experiments on Qwen3-30B-A3B achieve stable training and benchmark quality close to BF16, outperforming naive TE NVFP4 in evaluation quality.
On a single NVIDIA B300 node, the optimized learner reaches 33,540 tokens/s—1.39× BF16 and 1.47× TE NVFP4 throughput for complete learner updates.
The framework, kernels, diagnostics, and configurations are released; results focus on the reported model and hardware setup.

papers.abstract: Layer pruning reduces the size and inference cost of vision-language-action (VLA) models, but selecting a deployable configuration requires deciding both which layers to remove and how to recover task performance. These decisions depend on the model and task, and a failed trial can reflect either the deletion set or insufficient recovery. We present AutoPruner, an agent-driven framework that jointly searches pruning structures and recovery recipes through closed-loop experimentation. Offline layer interventions measure changes in action output to provide functional evidence. An LLM agent combines this evidence with evaluation history and retained diagnoses to propose deletion sets and recovery recipes within a search budget. Each proposal is executed and evaluated on the target tasks, and the resulting feedback guides the next experiment. Across OpenVLA-OFT, StarVLA, and FastWAM on four LIBERO suites, AutoPruner removes 16.7--87.5% of backbone layers while maintaining task success above 90%, with measured inference speedups of up to 2.50$\times$. Further analysis shows that functional probes identify action-sensitive layers despite high representation similarity, and that recovery can make previously failing structures viable.
authors: Tao Lin, Yikeng Chen, Qiwei Liang, Zinan Xie, Zhengtu Liang, Renjing Xu
bullets: Targets the joint problem of selecting layers to remove and choosing recovery procedures after pruning.

Across three VLA models and four LIBERO suites, removes 16.7–87.5% of backbone layers while maintaining over 90% task success.

papers.abstract: Adaptive VLM ensembles save computation by stopping early on easy images and escalating harder ones. Although a single conformal threshold can make the final predictor marginally valid, it can still fail severely along individual computational routes. We characterize this failure precisely: if a route has prevalence pi, marginal 1-alpha coverage allows its conditional coverage to fall to max{0, 1-alpha/pi}. To address this mismatch, we learn the router on development data, freeze all routing choices, and calibrate the returned score separately for early exits and escalated inputs. We call this pipeline SAGE-CP. Its calibration step applies Mondrian split conformal prediction to the operational groups created by the router. Under exchangeability, the resulting prediction sets achieve finite-sample coverage within each route. Across 10 benchmarks, 4 frozen VLMs, and 5 aligned splits, both global calibration and SAGE-CP achieve 0.900 marginal coverage at a 0.90 target, but their route behavior differs substantially. SAGE-CP raises mean worst-route coverage from 0.623 to 0.887 and reduces the mean route-coverage gap from 0.324 to 0.025, using the same routed scores and 1.177 source calls per image. The stronger guarantee increases the mean prediction-set size from 1.893 to 2.212; nevertheless, the sets remain smaller than those of the full ensemble (2.486) while requiring 70.6 percent fewer source calls. The route-level reliability persists across 6 fixed query fractions, while finer exit-depth groups demonstrate the need for additional calibration data on rare routes. Across 5 datasets, SAGE-CP also reduces measured batch-one latency by 58.8 to 63.4 percent and gross GPU energy by 55.7 to 57.5 percent relative to full inference. Thus, routing provides computational savings, while route-stratified calibration attaches coverage guarantees to the operational paths created by the router.
bullets: Problem: Marginal conformal coverage can conceal severe failures for rare early-exit or escalation routes.
Method: Freeze the learned router and apply Mondrian split conformal calibration separately to operational route groups.
Guarantee: Under exchangeability, prediction sets achieve finite-sample coverage within each route.
Results: At 0.90 target coverage, SAGE-CP raises mean worst-route coverage from 0.623 to 0.887 and shrinks the route-coverage gap from 0.324 to 0.025.
Trade-off and scope: Sets are larger than with global calibration but remain smaller than full-ensemble sets, with 70.6% fewer source calls; rare, finer-grained routes require more calibration data.

papers.abstract: Adaptive speculative decoding changes the active batch size B and draft length d from one decode step to the next, whereas a CUDA Graph replays a fixed launch configuration. The resulting verification width M = B d forces serving systems to pre-capture many shapes, capture new ones on the serving path, or pad every step to the largest draft. We present PolyGraph, a plan-buffer mechanism for custom Triton kernels that avoids this choice. PolyGraph captures one maximum-grid graph and writes the active shape to GPU memory before each replay. Kernels skip tiles beyond that shape, while graph topology, allocations, layouts, pointers, and launch grids remain fixed; the update transfers only 28 bytes. On one NVIDIA H800, a trace-driven prototype with Qwen2.5-3B dimensions replaces 64 shape-specific graphs with one, matches the warmed baseline in observed step latency (17.7 vs. 17.8 ms P50), and reduces measured pre-serving graph-build time from 3,915 to 93 ms. Fixed-draft controls show that the benefit comes from avoiding padded payload: the P99 difference from MaxPad is negligible at zero padding waste but reaches an 18.7% reduction at 100% waste. Our evidence establishes a bounded work-shape mechanism for custom kernels, not a production serving system, and is limited to synthetic traces on one GPU.
bullets: Addresses changing batch size and draft length, which otherwise require many graphs, runtime captures, or padding to the largest shape.
Uses a maximum-grid graph whose kernels skip inactive tiles based on a 28-byte shape update before replay.
Replaces 64 shape-specific graphs with one while matching warmed step latency: 17.7 vs. 17.8 ms P50.
Reduces measured pre-serving graph-build time from 3,915 to 93 ms.
Compared with MaxPad, reduces P99 latency by up to 18.7% at 100% padding waste; evaluation is limited to synthetic traces on one NVIDIA H800.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding has become a mainstream technique for accelerating large language model (LLM) inference by using a lightweight draft model to generate candidate tokens that are subsequently verified by the target model. However, agentic workloads introduce long and continuously evolving contexts and frequent multi-turn interactions. Under such workloads, we observe that existing draft models suffer from up to an 80% degradation in acceptance length, while maintaining their historical KV cache introduces substantial system overhead. In this paper, we identify the growing historical context as a common source of both problems and introduce DLite, a history-free speculative decoding framework for agentic AI. DLite directly reuses contextual hidden states from the target model and performs local speculative prediction without explicitly maintaining the historical context, transforming an increasingly complex modeling problem into local simple prediction problem. A lightweight sequential head further restores intra-block causal dependencies with low overhead. To effectively train this heterogeneous history-free architecture, we introduce a tailored two-stage training strategy. Experiments on general-purpose, long-context and agentic workloads show that DLite achieves 2-6 acceptance length and outperforms the state-of-the-art speculative decoding method, DSpark, up to 70%.

papers.abstract: Diffusion-based protein structure prediction models produce all-atom structures in about 200 denoising steps, and that cost has driven a number of few-step samplers. We present Blitz, a few-step distillation framework that uses a geometric noise schedule to distribute steps more evenly across noise scales, then learns those updates through multistep consistency training. Physical steering and target-free candidate selection help reduce the remaining geometric defects at inference. We apply Blitz to AlphaFold 3 and Boltz-2, reducing denoising from 200 steps to eight. Because published few-step results use different benchmarks and scoring procedures, we compare both distilled models with their teachers and other few-step methods under a common evaluation protocol covering structural accuracy, interface quality, ligand placement, and stereochemical validity. Blitz retains teacher-level structural accuracy, with AF3-Blitz outperforming all evaluated few-step baselines and exceeding its teacher on several accuracy metrics.
authors: Vinay Saji Mathew, Soundar Kumara, Gretta Kellogg, William K. M. Lai

papers.abstract: Dense assistance methods such as speculative decoding repeatedly verify draft tokens with a target model, keeping target computation coupled to generation. We study sparse collaborative decoding, where a draft model generates most tokens and a target model is invoked only for short corrective segments. The key problem is deciding when to call the target. We show that local uncertainty is a weak trigger: entropy, negative log-likelihood, logit margin, top-$k$ mass, and velocity features give near-chance failure prediction, with AUC 0.50-0.53. In contrast, aggregate trajectory-shape features over the draft confidence path reach AUC 0.86 using a lightweight logistic predictor trained only from draft correctness labels. This induces a trigger-timing tradeoff: early calls have more leverage but weaker evidence, while later calls have stronger evidence but less ability to redirect the trajectory. Used online, learned sparse collaborative decoding improves over the best open-loop schedule by +5.3 to +20.0 accuracy points across five GSM8K draft-target pairs. On MATH-500, it gains 7.0-13.5 points when early prediction and target competence align, but loses when either is weak. On StrategyQA, it improves over open-loop by 5.0-8.3 points, showing transfer beyond arithmetics.
authors: Amit Ranjan Trivedi, Sruthikesh Surineni, Kyong Ho Lee, Mohit Mittal, Steven Li, Rex Hill
bullets: Sparse decoding uses a draft model for most tokens and invokes the target only for short corrective segments.
Local uncertainty features are weak failure predictors (AUC 0.50–0.53), while aggregate confidence-trajectory features reach AUC 0.86.
A lightweight logistic predictor, trained only on draft correctness labels, learns when to trigger target-model intervention.
Online triggering improves over the best open-loop schedule by 5.3–20.0 accuracy points on five GSM8K pairs and transfers to MATH-500 and StrategyQA.
Performance depends on timing and alignment between early prediction quality and target-model competence; gains can disappear when either is weak.

Figure 3: Intervention leverage decreases with decoding position. We perturb the draft prefix at different token positions and measure whether the final decoded sequence changes. papers.abstract: Muon has emerged as a strong optimizer for neural network training and admits an interpretation as steepest descent under a spectral-norm geometry. Yet we find that Muon-trained Transformers can degrade sharply when their MLP hidden channels are pruned after training. To reconcile Muon's optimization performance with structured compressibility, we introduce Budget Muon (BMuon), which modifies Muon's spectral geometry so that hidden channels across blocks compete for a shared allocation budget. The resulting oracle is exactly normalized steepest descent under a family of norms that interpolate between Muon's geometry and structured sparse geometries. Our principal sparsity control is an interpretable global channel-allocation budget, rather than a setting-dependent sparsity-penalty coefficient. For linear factorization models, we show that Muon admits minimum-cost exact representations with redundant hidden width, whereas under the BMuon oracle geometry and a sufficiently scarce budget, every minimum-cost representation is width-minimal. For practical training, we derive a minorization-maximization surrogate for the exact allocation problem. On ImageNet-1K with ViT-S/16, BMuon improves over Muon under gradual structured MLP pruning, and its learned allocations provide a more effective pruning criterion than weight magnitude. On a 1B-parameter LLaMA-style model trained on FineWeb, BMuon improves over Muon under post-training MLP channel pruning.
authors: Rida Assalouh, Tom Jacobs, Rebekka Burkholz, Yani Ioannou, Umut \c{S}im\c{s}ekli
bullets: Muon-trained Transformers can degrade sharply when MLP hidden channels are pruned after training.
BMuon makes channels across blocks compete for a global, interpretable allocation budget instead of using a sparsity penalty coefficient.
Its oracle is normalized steepest descent under norms interpolating between Muon’s geometry and structured sparse geometries.
For linear factorization, scarce BMuon budgets force minimum-cost representations to use minimal width, unlike Muon.
BMuon outperforms Muon under structured MLP pruning on ViT-S/16 ImageNet-1K and a 1B-parameter LLaMA-style model trained on FineWeb; learned allocations beat weight magnitude for pruning decisions.

papers.abstract: LLMs and LVLMs are increasingly deployed across heterogeneous hardware, ranging from data-center GPUs to resource-constrained edge devices. Their fixed-size architectures limit the ability to reuse a single model across deployment settings with different compute, latency, and model-size targets. We introduce HydraLLM, an elastic MQA-based architecture. Its number of active attention heads determines the effective widths of the embeddings, attention projections, feed-forward layers, and the output head, forming a nested family of subnetworks within a single parameter set. We introduce a static-to-elastic conversion pipeline that, starting from a pre-trained model checkpoint, includes importance-driven weight reordering and stochastic subnetwork training with knowledge distillation. We extend this principle to multimodal inference through an elastic projection module whose output width follows the active text width. HydraLLM covers a wider range of active parameter configurations than FFN-only elastic architectures. With 75% of heads active, HydraLLM achieves 2.2 percentage points higher TriviaQA accuracy than a state-of-the-art nested baseline configuration which has 17.25% more parameters. With 50% of heads active, our multimodal model achieves a CLIPScore comparable to that of the 7$\times$ larger Gemma 3 4B model. With only 25% of heads active, HydraLLM increases token-generation throughput by 75.3% over the full-width configuration.
authors: Oscar Kemme, Janek Haberer, Ali Hojjat, Olaf Landsiedel
bullets: Uses the number of active attention heads to jointly control embedding, attention, feed-forward, and output widths.
Converts pretrained checkpoints into elastic models through importance-based weight reordering and stochastic subnetwork training with knowledge distillation.
Adds an elastic multimodal projection whose width matches the active text-model width.
Reports higher TriviaQA accuracy than a larger-parameter nested baseline at 75% active heads, comparable CLIPScore to a much larger Gemma 3 4B model at 50%, and 75.3% higher token throughput at 25%.

papers.abstract: Evaluating candidate changes (hypotheses) to recommendation models requires full-scale training runs consuming thousands of GPU-hours, severely limiting the hypothesis space engineers can feasibly explore. We introduce Predictable Scaling (PS), a systematic framework that exploits empirically verified regularity conditions to predict full-scale model performance from small-scale proxies. PS constructs scaled-down variants via composable scaling functions along distinct resource axes, and projects metrics to the target scale via curve fitting with calibrated uncertainty estimates. We compare three prediction strategies of increasing expressiveness: even the simplest (raw proxy) achieves prediction error within the empirical noise floor of repeated-run variance; the most expressive (Gaussian Process) provides an indicative 15% relative MAE improvement and calibrated uncertainty. Evaluation on two ranking models of increasing complexity---a task-specific model and a foundation model---demonstrates that PS correctly ranks actionable hypotheses across diverse hypothesis types at 79-88% compute reductions.

papers.abstract: Resampling is the standard remedy for weight degeneracy in particle filters, but in high dimensions it distorts the spectrum of the ensemble covariance in a way that is computable from the importance weights. This paper studies the inverse problem: recovering the pre-resampling spectrum from the observed weights and the empirical spectrum alone, and using it without biasing the filter. We first show that the forward spectral law extends to random importance weights once one conditions on the weights together with the realized offspring counts, rather than on the weights alone. We then construct a regularized free-deconvolution estimator, prove its consistency with an explicit error budget at a fixed resolution scale, and certify model mismatch through a computable forward residual. The repaired spectrum enters the filter only as the preconditioner of a Metropolis-adjusted rejuvenation move, so that spectral error affects mixing efficiency but not the invariant target. For the full filtering cycle, we derive a geometrically summable error recursion under stable scalar dynamics and an explicit law for the cost of abstaining from repair. Pre-registered simulations show that the inversion reduces the spectral error by an order of magnitude, that the corrected preconditioner recovers about 90% of the oracle's sampling efficiency in an anisotropic regime, and that the cost of abstention depends on when abstentions occur rather than on how many. The repair recovers eigenvalue laws, not eigenvectors, and is certified only within an explicitly stated exogenous-weight regime.
authors: Deming Song, Chi-Kin Lam, Kefeng Li, Hui Yu, Xilin Li, Huagang Lin
bullets: Resampling distorts ensemble-covariance eigenvalue distributions, motivating recovery of the pre-resampling spectrum from weights and observed spectra.
The method conditions on importance weights and realized offspring counts, then applies regularized free deconvolution with consistency guarantees and a computable model-mismatch residual.
The repaired spectrum is used only to precondition a Metropolis-adjusted rejuvenation step, so spectral errors affect mixing efficiency but not target invariance.
Simulations report an order-of-magnitude reduction in spectral error and roughly 90% of oracle sampling efficiency in an anisotropic setting.
The approach recovers eigenvalue laws rather than eigenvectors and is certified only for an explicitly stated exogenous-weight regime.

papers.abstract: Federated Learning (FL) enables collaborative training of complex models across large-scale networks of edge devices while keeping data localized. However, data heterogeneity and high communication overhead remain fundamental bottlenecks. Recently, the spectral optimizer Muon has demonstrated remarkable advantages over Adam-like methods in centralized training. While recent efforts have attempted to transition Muon to FL, naive integrations into traditional architectures fail short. Crucially, existing approaches do not support the the communication compression and local steps --- the two foundational techniques of efficient FL. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel spectral FL method that utilizes both local updates and compression. We establish rigorous convergence guarantees under mild assumptions, notably eliminating the restrictive bounded heterogeneity condition. Empirical evaluation on standard image classification benchmarks validates the efficiency and robustness of our approach.
authors: Dmitriy Bystrov, George Chirkov, Daniil Medyakov, Dmitry Bylinkin, Aleksandr Beznosikov
bullets: Targets data heterogeneity and communication overhead in federated learning.
Addresses the incompatibility of prior Muon-based FL methods with local steps and compressed communication.
Introduces a spectral FL approach supporting both efficient communication and local updates.
Proves convergence under mild assumptions while removing the restrictive bounded heterogeneity condition.
Experiments on standard image-classification benchmarks demonstrate efficiency and robustness.

papers.abstract: The recurrent neural network transducer (RNN-T) remains a practical choice for streaming speech recognition, but training requires large intermediate tensors. We present Flash RNN-T, a joint and loss implementation combining specialized kernels with optional tiled recomputation over the full alignment space and vocabulary. Tiled and untiled Flash form the entire measured throughput-memory frontier on medium and long workloads. On H100, untiled Flash achieves 24-39% higher throughput with 26-56% less memory than the fastest baseline on these workloads wherever it fits. Tiling reduces memory further through recomputation. On medium, tiled Flash uses ninefold less memory than that baseline at 16% lower throughput when both use one backward call per batch. On long, it fits where all tested alternatives with that backward schedule run out of memory with 80 GB. These comparisons use each implementation's lowest-memory configuration reaching at least 95% of its peak throughput.
bullets: Addresses the large intermediate tensors required to train streaming RNN-T models.
Uses specialized joint-network and transducer-loss kernels across the full alignment space and vocabulary.
Untiled Flash delivers 24–39% higher throughput with 26–56% less memory than the fastest baseline on supported H100 workloads.
Tiled Flash further reduces memory through recomputation, using ninefold less memory on medium workloads at a 16% throughput cost.

papers.abstract: Modern deep learning systems increasingly rely on high-dimensional vector operations, in which large input and parameter vectors are repeatedly stored, transferred, and processed. Although substantial research has focused on reducing neural-network model size through pruning, quantization, knowledge distillation, and efficient architectures, the storage, memory-traffic, and communication costs associated with repeatedly presented high-dimensional input vectors remain important practical considerations, particularly in distributed and edge-computing environments. This paper proposes the SETAREH (Sorting-assisted Energy-concentrating Transform for Approximate Representation using Haar wavelets) transform, a Haar-wavelet-based sparsification approach for approximating the inner product between a fixed high-dimensional coefficient vector and successive input vectors. By applying the same sequence of permutations and Haar transforms to both vectors, SETAREH preserves the exact inner product before truncation. It then retains only a subset of the transformed coefficient-input pairs, reducing their representation cost while introducing a controllable approximation error. To evaluate SETAREH, we consider two complementary experimental settings: a synthetic Gaussian-vector baseline and a real apparent-age estimation task using a convolutional neural network on the APPA-REAL dataset. The results show that SETAREH can approximate the evaluated inner products using substantially fewer transformed coefficient-input pairs than the original vector dimension. The findings support its use as a potential structured data-representation method for repeated inner products with fixed weights, while the practical benefit depends on approximation accuracy and the cost of storing or transmitting permutation metadata.
bullets: Targets storage, memory-traffic, and communication overhead for repeatedly presented high-dimensional inputs with fixed weights.
Applies identical permutations and Haar transforms to the coefficient and input vectors, preserving their exact inner product before truncation.
Keeps only selected transformed coefficient–input pairs to reduce representation size while introducing approximation error.
Evaluated on synthetic Gaussian vectors and an apparent-age estimation task using a CNN on APPA-REAL.
Practical gains depend on the accuracy required and the cost of storing or transmitting permutation metadata.

papers.abstract: Real-time inference on small devices needs low activation memory without extra latency, which makes operator order the most valuable memory lever: it is free in time. We show that the usual way of deploying a better order, handing it back to the compiler and regenerating code, is unreliable. In PyTorch Inductor the regenerated program misses its predicted peak in 22 of 54 CPU configurations. It is worse than the stock program in 9 of them and in 19 of 50 on a GPU, and on the GPU it also changes numerical results. We instead profile the generated program, model its memory exactly from its own statements and their read/write effects, and permute those statements. We prove that this realizes the modeled peak whenever allocation does not depend on history. It does so to the byte, with bitwise-identical results, in all our CPU runs. On the GPU we characterize why the caching allocator breaks the condition. To know when to stop, we give forward and reverse "trap" lower bounds, each computable with $O(n^2)$ minimum cuts. They certify the found order optimal for 94% of held-out wrapper graphs and all 16 microcontroller-class models we study, in under a second. So most inference graphs are already scheduled optimally. Branching networks are the exception, where reordering is free and pays, e.g. 10.0% on DeepLabV3. In compiled training we save up to 7.6%. Beyond the certified optimum we study selective recomputation with per-operator caps. It is strongly NP-hard for every fixed cap even at treewidth two, encodes knapsack exactly on series-parallel graphs, and is solvable exactly on bounded treewidth. It is useless on public tiny models whose peak is a single layer, but on architectures that hold a cheap value for a late reuse it pays: on the public ReDimNet speaker networks, whose order is already optimal, it lowers the peak by 5.2-6.1% at under 0.4% extra MACs, with bitwise-identical outputs.
authors: Ivan Fomin, Ivan Koryabkin, Boris Sheludko
bullets: Compiler regeneration often fails to realize predicted memory savings and can worsen memory use or alter GPU results.
Profiling generated code and reordering its statements exactly matches modeled peak memory and preserves bitwise-identical outputs on CPU.
Forward and reverse minimum-cut bounds certify optimal schedules for most tested graphs, including all studied microcontroller-class models.
Branching networks benefit most from reordering; compiled training saves up to 7.6%, while DeepLabV3 improves by 10.0%.
Selective recomputation is strongly NP-hard under fixed caps, but reduces peak memory by 5.2–6.1% on ReDimNet with under 0.4% extra MACs.

papers.selection_reason: Exact peak-memory scheduling and recomputation limits for inference directly target memory-efficient AI.
papers.title: Peak-Memory Schedules You Can Trust: Exact Realization, Certified Optimality, and the Limits of Recomputation for Inference
papers.tldr: The paper presents a reliable, certifiably optimal operator-ordering approach for reducing inference peak memory, while showing when recomputation is useful or computationally hard.

papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) repeatedly process hundreds of visual tokens across decoder layers, incurring substantial computation and memory costs. Existing inference-time visual token pruning methods often irreversibly remove low-ranked tokens, although the set of visual tokens receiving high query-conditioned attention can change across decoder depth. Recoverable routing preserves skipped tokens for later reconsideration, but re-admits them with stale representations after bypassing intermediate transformations. We further find that replacing stale re-admitted states with their current-depth oracle states from a full-token reference trajectory substantially improves grounding performance. We therefore propose CatchUp, a training-free framework for depth-aware visual-token re-admission. CatchUp repeatedly re-evaluates query-conditioned visual relevance, processes only selected visual tokens through each decoder interval, and preserves deferred tokens for later re-admission. Upon re-admission, CatchUp approximates missed representation evolution using reference-to-current transition signals from semantically and spatially related visual tokens. Across three referring-expression grounding datasets and six multimodal benchmarks, CatchUp achieves the highest average relative retention in both benchmark groups at 64-, 128-, and 192-token budgets. At a 64-token budget with 88.9% fewer active visual tokens, CatchUp retains 92.17% of the full model's performance on average across six multimodal benchmarks while reducing end-to-end latency by 8.0%. Code is available at https://github.com/pej0918/CatchUp
bullets: Problem: Irreversible visual-token pruning can discard tokens that become relevant later, while recoverable routing may re-admit them with stale representations.
Method: Re-evaluates query-conditioned token relevance at each decoder interval, processes only selected tokens, and preserves deferred tokens for later re-admission.
Key idea: Uses transition signals from semantically and spatially related tokens to approximate the representation evolution missed by skipped tokens.
Results: Across three grounding datasets and six multimodal benchmarks, CatchUp achieves the highest average relative retention at 64-, 128-, and 192-token budgets.
At 64 tokens, it uses 88.9% fewer active visual tokens, retains 92.17% of full-model performance on average, and reduces end-to-end latency by 8.0%.

papers.title: CatchUp: Depth-Aware Re-Admission of Visual Tokens for Efficient Large Vision-Language Models

papers.abstract: A common way to make language models and agents more accurate is to spend more compute at inference time: generate many candidate solutions and submit the one a verifier prefers. Success then requires that some candidate is correct and that the verifier picks it. The first grows predictably with the number of samples; the second does not, because real verifiers (unit tests, majority votes, LLM judges, reward models) accept wrong answers, reject right ones, and make correlated mistakes. With a fixed budget, a practitioner must decide how many samples to draw, which models to draw them from, and how much to spend on verification, and today these choices are made by rules of thumb. We introduce SPLIT, which makes them from a small labelled pilot. It rests on an exact formula for the probability of submitting a correct answer under accept/reject and top-score selection that accounts for varying task difficulty, blind spots shared across models, and correlated repeated verifier calls. SPLIT fits the formula by empirical Bayes and uses it to plan budgets on unseen tasks. Across seven benchmarks spanning math, science QA, code and software-engineering agents, 26 models, 175 agent systems and six kinds of real verifiers, all from public releases, SPLIT lands within 0.02-0.8 percentage points of the best allocation in hindsight, while every fixed rule we test loses at least 2.5 points in some setting. Regret depends only on how well SPLIT ranks configurations, and it stays near-optimal under compute, price and latency costs and online. The formula also explains when asking more LLM judges lowers precision. As a forecaster far beyond the pilot, SPLIT beats power-law fitting when the verifier caps success, and we report where it loses.
bullets: Test-time accuracy depends on both generating a correct candidate and having the verifier select it; real verifiers can make correlated false accepts and rejects.
SPLIT fits an exact success-probability formula with empirical Bayes, modeling task difficulty, shared model blind spots, and repeated-verifier correlations.
It plans sample counts, model mixtures, and verification effort for unseen tasks under compute, price, latency, and online constraints.
Across seven benchmarks, SPLIT came within 0.02–0.8 percentage points of the hindsight-best allocation; fixed rules lost at least 2.5 points in some settings.
The analysis identifies when additional LLM judging reduces precision and when SPLIT loses as a long-range forecaster.

papers.abstract: Small-to-large language model routing can reduce inference cost by escalating difficult inputs while retaining easier ones on a smaller model. Its success, however, depends on identifying examples that benefit from escalation, and the reliability of confidence across multilingual tasks remains unclear. We present a systematic evaluation of confidence-based routing across three model families, four languages, and three task types, covering 72 model, dataset, language, and scale configurations and 42,288 predictions. We compare global confidence routing with random routing, equal-quota confidence routing, and an oracle upper bound. Confidence identifies beneficial escalations on the Belebele reading comprehension and SIB-200 topic classification datasets, with mean correction-detection AUCs of 0.612 and 0.705. At 50% escalation, it improves over random routing by 1.40--4.67 percentage points on Belebele and 2.54--5.63 points on SIB-200. In contrast, the mean AUC on the MMLU-ProX-Lite knowledge and reasoning dataset is only 0.510, and routing provides no consistent improvement over random selection because small models often remain highly confident while incorrect. Global confidence routing also creates language escalation gaps up to 30.33 percentage points, whereas equal-quota routing removes this disparity with little aggregate accuracy cost. These results show that confidence routing is task-dependent and can allocate computation unevenly across languages. Code is available at https://github.com/sabbir5622r/multilingual-llm-routing
authors: Md Sabbir Hossen, Anichur Rahman, Pabon Shaha, Airin Afroj Aishi, Andrew H. Sung, Md Shohel Rana
bullets: Evaluates routing across three model families, four languages, and three task types, covering 72 configurations and 42,288 predictions.

papers.abstract: Detecting faithfulness hallucinations in large language models (LLMs) is crucial for their safe deployment in high-stakes domains. Recent approaches address this by contrasting contextual against parametric knowledge utilization, yet measuring context reliance typically demands noticeable overhead, such as materializing attention maps, running additional forward passes, or training auxiliary probes. In this work, we show that context reliance can be estimated by projecting hidden states onto the dark space - directions that compose weakly with the unembedding matrix. Beyond its recognized function as an initial-token attention sink, we show that this subspace actively mediates context processing, and that its share of hidden-state norm - termed the Dark Matter Ratio (DMR) - provides a direct score of context utilization. Pairing DMR with a parametric knowledge score yields DarkLens, a lightweight faithfulness detector operating strictly within a single forward pass. Evaluated across three QA and summarization benchmarks on six open-weight LLMs (4B-13B parameters), DarkLens matches or outperforms a wide range of baselines without requiring extra forward passes or probe training.
authors: Alexandra Kuleshova, Andrey Volodichev, Daria Kotova, Alexey Zaytsev
bullets: Context reliance is estimated from the hidden-state norm in weakly unembedded directions, called the Dark Matter Ratio (DMR).
The dark space is shown to mediate context processing, beyond its known role as an initial-token attention sink.
Combining DMR with a parametric knowledge score yields the lightweight DarkLens detector.
Across three QA and summarization benchmarks and six open-weight LLMs, DarkLens matches or outperforms many baselines without extra passes or probe training.

papers.abstract: Recent speech brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) increasingly rely on large models and complex multi-stage pipelines for neural decoding. However, in speech BCI, where training data are scarce, noisy, and expensive to collect, the benefits of model scaling remain unclear. This work revisits a fundamental question: are large models truly necessary for accurate neural decoding? We propose BEST (Brain-Encoding-Speech-Text), a two-stage framework for efficient neural-to-text decoding. Instead of relying on large generative models or phoneme-centric pipelines, BEST introduces hierarchical intermediate representations and a compact speech-oriented decoder that directly maps neural activity to text. This design preserves essential structure while significantly reducing computational cost, enabling robust generalization in low-resource settings and practical deployment under constrained resources. On the Brain-to-Text '24 and '25 benchmarks, BEST achieves word error rates (WERs) of 6.19% and 1.62%, respectively, using only 3.85% of the parameters required by comparable methods. Beyond these results, we provide three key insights: (1) decoder scaling yields non-monotonic gains; (2) cross-modal alignment is more critical than model size; and (3) overfitting degards sequence-level performance. Representation analysis further reveals a consistent neural-audio-text alignment pathway.
authors: Zehui Feng, Weichuan Wang, Xiaohan Chen, Cuntai Guan, Ting Han
bullets: Speech BCI data are scarce, noisy, and costly, making the value of model scaling uncertain.
BEST uses two stages with hierarchical intermediate representations and a compact speech-oriented decoder that maps neural activity to text.
It reports 6.19% and 1.62% WER on the Brain-to-Text ’24 and ’25 benchmarks, respectively, using 3.85% of the parameters of comparable methods.
The study finds that decoder scaling has non-monotonic benefits, cross-modal alignment matters more than model size, and overfitting harms sequence-level performance.
Representation analysis indicates a consistent neural–audio–text alignment pathway, supporting efficient deployment in low-resource settings.

papers.tldr: BEST shows that compact, hierarchically structured decoders can achieve strong speech BCI neural-to-text performance without relying on large models.

papers.abstract: On AWS Trainium2, every component of a diffusion model runs as a program compiled ahead of time for fixed shapes, while pipelines differ across models, prompt lengths across requests, and caching decisions across denoising steps. We present Difflet, a serving engine in which five model pipelines share one compilation backend, joint attention is split across cores by attention head, and a host controller decides at each denoising step whether to run the denoiser or reuse its earlier output. A small probe program computes the caching signal on the device and returns one number per step, and a resident model process keeps every program loaded across requests. Across five image and video model families, fused attention accelerates denoiser steps by 1.2-4.3x over the same framework using PyTorch/XLA attention, and at 32.8k visual tokens it is the only attention that compiles. On four of the five models, resident serving is 1.5-3.4x faster than standalone runs that reload weights from a warm file cache for each generation.
authors: Bin Ma, Min Yu, Vijay Kodamalla, Jialin Liu, Dong Li
bullets: Addresses fixed-shape compilation constraints across varying pipelines, prompt lengths, and denoising-time caching decisions.
Uses one compilation backend for five pipelines, splits joint attention across cores by head, and fuses attention computation.
A host controller selectively reuses denoiser outputs, guided by a device-side probe that produces one caching signal per step.
Fused attention is 1.2–4.3× faster than PyTorch/XLA attention and is the only attention variant compiling at 32.8k visual tokens.
Resident serving is 1.5–3.4× faster than reloading weights for each generation on four of five models.

papers.abstract: On neuromorphic chips, spiking neural networks (SNNs) consume far less energy than artificial neural networks (ANNs), but the limited memory of these chips requires low-bit synaptic weights and membrane potentials. Existing post-training quantization (PTQ) methods provide them without retraining and, like those for ANNs, minimize numerical errors such as the mean squared error (MSE). In an SNN, however, a quantization error reaches later layers only through the spikes it flips. We find that errors of equal MSE can cause very different accuracy losses, whereas errors that flip the same fraction of spikes cause the same loss. We therefore propose SpikeQ, a spike-guided PTQ framework. For weights, we select the level of each weight by simulating the downstream neurons and minimizing their spike errors. For membrane potentials, most existing methods quantize the state after the reset, whereas neuromorphic chips compare the threshold with the membrane potential stored at a fixed bit width. We target this pre-fire quantization and build a reset-aware grid that places the threshold on a rounding boundary, so rounding never flips the spike at the current time step. We evaluate SpikeQ on seven benchmarks of image classification, semantic segmentation, and object detection. With 2-bit pre-fire membrane potentials, every existing grid collapses, whereas SpikeQ retains most of the full-precision accuracy. With both at 4 bits, the models stay within 2.59 points of full precision, shrink their memory footprint 7.8--7.9 times, and use 6.4--6.9 times less energy.
authors: Kai Sun, Peibo Duan, Zhanglu Yan, Guowei Zhang, Yongsheng Huang, Levin Kuhlmann
bullets: SNN quantization errors matter primarily when they flip downstream spikes, not when they increase MSE.
For weights, SpikeQ simulates downstream neurons and selects quantization levels that minimize spike errors.
For membrane potentials, it quantizes the pre-fire state with a reset-aware grid that prevents current-step spike flips.
Across seven image classification, segmentation, and detection benchmarks, SpikeQ retains most full-precision accuracy with 2-bit membrane potentials.
At 4-bit weights and membrane potentials, models remain within 2.59 percentage points of full precision while reducing memory 7.8–7.9× and energy use 6.4–6.9×.

papers.selection_reason: Spike-guided post-training quantization for SNNs reduces memory and energy use, fitting efficient AI.
papers.title: SpikeQ: Spike-Guided Post-Training Quantization for Spiking Neural Networks
papers.tldr: SpikeQ improves post-training quantization for SNNs by minimizing spike flips rather than numerical error, preserving accuracy at very low precision while reducing memory and energy use.

papers.abstract: Mainstream point cloud completion methods are unanimously based on deep learning architectures. On one hand, these methods tend to repetitively stacking attention modules to enhance network performance, which drifts away from the neat design of unified and interpret-able networks; on the other hand, nearly all existing architectures rely solely on feed-forward connections to propagate information, neglecting feedback from deeper layers. The recurrent neural architecture, formed by feedforward-feedback loops, have shown its ability to generate Illusory Contours (ICs) in the V1 brain region of mammals; and ICs are essentially a completion mechanism of the brain for visual information. Motivated by this, we design a Brain-inspired Recurrent Illusory Contour Encoder (BRICE) to "imagine" what is missing in the incomplete 3D point clouds. Building upon the foundation model of Predictive Coding (PC), the plug-and-play nature enables BRICE to be seamlessly integrated into mainstream point cloud completion baselines. Experimental results show that BRICE can enhance various completion baselines on different 3D datasets such as MVP2K, PCN, and PlantPCom. Our code: Https://github.com/wangyunlei-wyl/BRICE.
authors: Yunlei Wang, Dawei Li, Xue-song Tang
bullets: Addresses the reliance on stacked attention and purely feed-forward information propagation in existing completion networks.
Models illusory-contour formation in the visual cortex through feedforward-feedback recurrent connections.
Provides a plug-and-play encoder that can be integrated with mainstream point-cloud completion baselines.
Enhances multiple baselines across the MVP2K, PCN, and PlantPCom datasets.
The abstract does not report specific quantitative gains or limitations.

papers.abstract: Minimizing the wall-clock time required to reach a target accuracy is crucial in federated learning (FL), where many applications require frequent model updates as data distributions evolve over time. Nevertheless, in heterogeneous environments, slow clients with limited computational and communication capabilities can delay global synchronization, forcing faster clients to wait and increasing the overall training time. To mitigate this straggler effect, recent studies have introduced per-round time constraints and adapted client workloads within the available time. However, these approaches primarily focus on local computation, whereas communication can become a major bottleneck in communication-limited environments, motivating the joint optimization of training workload and communication compression. Although previous studies have explored such joint optimization, determining an effective training--communication balance under a fixed per-round time budget remains challenging, as the resulting model performance depends on both training progress and compression-induced degradation. We therefore propose TALLOP, which jointly optimizes the local training workload and communication compression under per-round time constraints. TALLOP predicts the training loss achievable under different computation budgets from the early-stage mini-batch loss trajectory (LENS), and estimates the degradation caused by communication compression using a compression-error model (CLEN). TALLOP combines these predictions to select the training-communication allocation that minimizes the post-compression loss under the given round time constraint. Experiments in heterogeneous FL environments show that TALLOP generally achieves competitive or improved time-to-accuracy compared with approaches that optimize only local training or neither, although the benefit over training-only adaptation depends on the setting.
authors: Honoka Anada, Yafei Ou, Shinya Takamaeda-Yamazaki
bullets: Addresses stragglers and communication bottlenecks in heterogeneous federated learning.
Uses LENS to predict training loss for different computation budgets from early mini-batch loss trajectories.
Uses CLEN to estimate loss degradation caused by communication compression.
Selects the computation–compression balance minimizing predicted post-compression loss within each round’s time budget.
Generally matches or improves time-to-accuracy over training-only or non-adaptive approaches, though gains depend on the setting.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Test accuracy as a function of wall-clock time for MobileNetV2 on CIFAR-10 under the two system configurations.
Figure 2: Overview of TALLOP. TALLOP predicts the post-compression loss by combining LENS and CLEN, and determines the optimal time allocation factor ρ by minimizing the predicted loss.
Figure 3: Actual and predicted losses of sparsified models for various non-zero ratios p. The proposed CLEN accurately estimates the loss after compression.

Figure 1: Given a fixed per-round time budget T , the time allocated to local training and communication determines the local training steps s and the communication compression ratio p. While the optimal training-communication time allocation is unknown in advance, TALLOP predicts the post-compression model loss for different allocations and selects the one expected to achieve the best training outcome.

papers.selection_reason: Jointly optimizes local training and communication compression to reduce wall-clock time in federated learning, fitting efficient AI.
papers.title: TALLOP: Joint Optimization of Local Training and Communication Compression for Time-Constrained Federated Learning
papers.tldr: TALLOP jointly allocates local computation and communication compression under per-round time limits to reduce federated learning time-to-accuracy.

papers.abstract: Long-context decoding in large language models (LLMs) is increasingly bottlenecked by the memory and computation required to attend over an ever-growing Key-Value (KV) cache at each autoregressive step. Although token-level sparse attention reduces this burden by restricting computation to a small subset of relevant past tokens, its practical gains are often offset by repeatedly recomputing layer-wise sparse indices as the context grows. A common remedy is to share sparse indices across layers by computing them only at designated anchor layers, but such static reuse ignores the layer-wise evolution of attention patterns, causing the reused indices to progressively deviate from the layer-specific optima and incur substantial attention loss. By revisiting cross-layer sparsity from the perspective of attention dynamics, we find that inter-layer salient token shift is highly localized: although the exact top-$\kappa$ indices differ across layers, the core high-attention tokens remain stable, with changes concentrated near the expanded boundary of previously selected regions. Motivated by this, we propose Prism Attention, a proposal-refined sparse attention framework. It replaces rigid cross-layer index reuse with a coarse-to-fine strategy, preserving layer-wise adaptability while retaining the efficiency benefits of cross-layer sharing. Extensive experiments show that Prism Attention achieves state-of-the-art performance among mainstream sparse attention methods on both reasoning and long-context benchmarks, while attaining a $3.4\times$ end-to-end decoding speedup over FlashAttention at 128K context length.
authors: Zhenxu Tian, Kebin Liu, Zhengwu Yang, Yi Su, Qingqing Dang, Yanlin Sha, Kaipeng Deng, Dianhai Yu, Yanjun Ma, Juntao Li, Min Zhang
bullets: Long-context decoding is bottlenecked by repeated attention over the growing KV cache.
Static cross-layer index sharing is efficient but can lose accuracy as attention patterns evolve across layers.
The method observes that salient-token changes are localized near the boundaries of previously selected regions.
Its coarse-to-fine proposal-refinement strategy preserves layer adaptability while reducing index recomputation.
It reports state-of-the-art performance among mainstream sparse-attention methods and a 3.4× decoding speedup over FlashAttention at 128K context.

papers.abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) have become a common backbone for high-quality text-to-image and text-to-video generation, but repeated dense self-attention remains a major inference bottleneck as token sequences grow and the same operator is invoked across many denoising steps. Our study suggests that dense attention in pretrained DiTs contains reusable layer/head-specific high-mass structure that can be identified from a small offline calibration set and reused across future generations. This leads to Sink-Sparse Hybrid Attention, a train-free attention replacement that reuses static sink masks and supplements them with a lightweight pooled-KV branch, while leaving model weights and sampling schedules unchanged. On Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B, the method attains 1.54$\times$ end-to-end speedup while maintaining generation quality. On Z-Image-Turbo, it attains 1.57$\times$ end-to-end speedup with competitive GenEval2 performance. These results indicate that reusable importance-aware sparse support can provide an effective train-free acceleration path for both T2V and T2I DiTs.
authors: Bingxin Xing, Yu Zhang, Jiatong Ding, Lei Lu, Ping Wang
bullets: Targets the inference cost of repeated dense self-attention in DiTs with long token sequences and many denoising steps.
Uses small offline calibration to identify reusable, layer/head-specific high-mass attention structure.
Combines static sink masks with a lightweight pooled-KV branch as a train-free attention replacement.
Achieves 1.54× end-to-end speedup on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B while maintaining generation quality.
Achieves 1.57× end-to-end speedup on Z-Image-Turbo with competitive GenEval2 performance; scope covers T2V and T2I DiTs.

Online inference reuses these masks at every denoising step: a static sparse sink branch preserves recurrently important interactions, a pooled-KV compensation branch supplies coarse omitted context using full-resolution queries and pooled keys/values, and the two branches are fused into the final attention output.

papers.title: Sink-Sparse Hybrid Attention for Efficient Inference in T2I/T2V Diffusion Transformers
papers.tldr: Sink-Sparse Hybrid Attention accelerates pretrained text-to-image and text-to-video diffusion Transformers by reusing calibrated sparse attention structure without retraining or changing sampling schedules.

papers.abstract: Visual information worth extracting from an image and the token budget it warrants depend on the text query. Yet modern vision and vision-language models largely encode images independently of the query and allocate a fixed visual token budget to every input. We introduce the Query-Adaptive Recurrent Tokenizer (QART), a backbone-agnostic module that makes visual representations both query-steerable and budget-adaptive. QART steers the visual representation toward query-relevant evidence while adapting its token budget to the amount of information required. Its key principle is simple. Additional tokens are allocated until the visual features relevant to the query are represented with sufficient fidelity. Starting from frozen encoder features, QART recurrently constructs a compact representation and uses reconstruction quality over the query-relevant visual support to control token allocation. On Visual7W and VQAv2, QART achieves 81.96% and 76.37% accuracy using only about 29 visual tokens, reducing token counts by 20-25x relative to dense VLM inputs. It further reaches 92.0% P@1 on CORE and 36.3% PR-AUC on PODS, outperforming SteerViT on PODS by 8.4%. Together, these results show that visual representations need not be fixed in either content or capacity and can instead adapt to what each query requires.
authors: Bavesh Balaji, Pranav Gopinath, Pouya Sadeghi, Sirisha Rambhatla
bullets: Addresses fixed, query-independent visual representations and token budgets in vision-language models.
Uses frozen encoder features and recurrently builds a compact representation steered toward query-relevant evidence.
Controls token allocation through reconstruction quality over the query-relevant visual support.
Achieves 81.96% on Visual7W and 76.37% on VQAv2 with 20–25× fewer tokens than dense inputs.
Also reaches 92.0% P@1 on CORE and 36.3% PR-AUC on PODS, outperforming SteerViT on PODS by 8.4%.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of QART. Given an image and a text query, frozen encoders provide visual and linguistic features V and T respectively. A relevance module Hϕ selects query-relevant patches VA; QART then recurrently refines a small set of query-conditioned slots S by passing them along with VA and T to the shared transformer Fθ. After each round r, a shared decoder Dψ reconstructs the visual features, and reconstruction quality determines whether more slots are added or recurrence halts. Only slot states propagate across rounds.

Figure 1: QART combines query steerability with budget adaptivity. Fixed patch tokenizers use the same representation and token budget for every query. Adaptive tokenizers change how many tokens are allocated, while steerable methods change what visual information is emphasized. QART does both, steering the representation toward the query while adapting its capacity to the required visual evidence. The clear regions represent the tokenizers’ focus.

Figure 4: Recurrent refinement and inference efficiency. (a) QART’s recurrence refines representations even upon disabling token growth. (b–c) The compact visual sequence increasingly improves throughput and language-model prefill as batch size grows.

Figure 3: QART steers visual representations while preserving transferable visual information. (a) On CORE, QART redirects visual representations toward queried content. (b) The same representation transfers zero-shot to natural images on GeneCIS without dataset-specific tuning. (d) On PODS, coarse conditioning preserves fine-grained instance information beyond the prompt.

The support progressively shifts toward the query-relevant region, including the foreground backpack, the person in plaid, and jersey number 13.

Figure 7: QART adapts its token budget across image–query pairs. Representative examples span the allocation range from K = 2 to K = 32. Localized queries can be represented with only a few active tokens, while broader or more spatially distributed visual evidence receives a larger representation.

papers.title: Query-adaptive Recurrent Tokenization
papers.tldr: QART makes visual tokenization query-aware and dynamically allocates only as many tokens as each query requires, achieving strong performance with about 29 tokens.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown strong promise for generalist robotic manipulation, but their inference cost remains a major bottleneck for real-time control. This limitation is especially pronounced in flow-matching VLAs such as $\pi_{0.5}$, where the action expert is evaluated repeatedly during iterative denoising. We introduce MambaAct, an efficient Mamba action expert for flow-matching VLA policies. MambaAct retains the pretrained visual-language prefix encoder of $\pi_{0.5}$, while replacing its transformer-based action expert with a compact Mamba-based action expert. Within this expert, Mamba serves as the action mixer that models dependencies across the noisy continuous-action sequence. To preserve visual-language conditioning without repeated token-level cross-attention, MambaAct uses a lightweight Context Compressor to map Vision-language model (VLM) prefix tokens into a compact conditioning signal that gates and modulates each Mamba action block. MambaAct uses a $10\times$ smaller action expert and reduces flow-matching denoising latency by $64.8\%$ on LIBERO and $58.8\%$ in real-world deployment, while improving mean LIBERO success by $1.08$ percentage points across three independent fine-tuning seeds and maintaining gains on LIBERO-Plus and real-world benchmarks. Our code and model weights are publicly available at https://github.com/giakhuyendihoc/MambaAct.
authors: Khuyen Pham, Tran Nguyen Le, Edoardo Fazzari, Cesare Stefanini
bullets: Targets the repeated action-expert evaluations that make flow-matching VLAs costly for real-time robotic control.
Retains π₀.₅’s pretrained vision-language encoder and uses Mamba to model dependencies across noisy continuous-action sequences.
Compresses vision-language prefix tokens into a conditioning signal that gates and modulates Mamba blocks without repeated token-level cross-attention.
Uses a 10× smaller action expert and reduces denoising latency by 64.8% on LIBERO and 58.8% in real-world deployment.
Improves mean LIBERO success by 1.08 percentage points across three seeds, with gains also reported on LIBERO-Plus and real-world benchmarks.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: MambaAct architecture. MambaAct retains and jointly fine-tunes the pretrained π0.5 visual-language backbone while replacing its Transformer action expert with a compact Mamba-3 expert. The VLM prefix is compressed into visual, language, and learned-query global context tokens C and pooled into z, which block-specific FiLM MLPs map to scale, shift, and residual-gate parameters. The noisy action chunk Xt is projected into the initial action-token sequence H(0), while the embedded flow time ct is injected through block-specific projections. The L = 4 gated Mamba-3 blocks transform the full action-token sequence into H(L), and a final RMSNorm-linear head predicts the flow velocity V̂θ. Repeated Euler updates use this velocity to obtain the denoised action chunk X0.

papers.title: MambaAct: Efficient Mamba Action Experts for Flow-Matching Vision-Language-Action Models

papers.abstract: The Levenberg-Marquardt (LMA) algorithm is a widely used nonlinear least-squares solver known for its rapid convergence. For small-scale neural networks, LMA provides better convergence and architectural robustness than first-order optimizers like Adam. However, LMA imposes prohibitive memory and computational costs. These costs are primarily from the Jacobian matrix, whose dimensions scale with both the number of samples and parameters. This bottleneck prevents its use in large-scale neural networks. Recent efforts scale LMA using preconditioned conjugate gradient (PCG) solvers to avoid materializing the Jacobian. However, PCG only approximates the solution, requiring many network propagations and a task-specific preconditioner. Other studies optimize LMA to reduce costs, but they restrict their methods to specific tasks or network architectures. As a result, LMA remains impractical for training general large-scale neural networks. In this paper, we propose LeMA, a distributed LMA algorithm for large-scale neural network training on multi-GPU platforms. Our contributions are twofold: First, an exact dual formulation of LMA removes the memory dependence on the parameter dimension. Second, a Jacobian sharding strategy computes Jacobian shards on the fly and in parallel to avoid materializing the full Jacobian. For large-scale neural networks, LeMA reduces the memory footprint of LMA from quadratic in the number of parameters to quadratic in the batch size. This makes exact LMA steps feasible for billion-parameter models without approximate PCG solves. Furthermore, for a convolutional neural network with 1,000,022,632 parameters on an 8-GPU node, LeMA achieves a 7.97x speedup over a single GPU, corresponding to a 99.7% strong scaling efficiency.
authors: Xianghao Wang, Johan Barth\'elemy, John Taylor
bullets: LMA can converge rapidly but is normally impractical at scale because storing and processing its Jacobian is prohibitively expensive.
LeMA uses an exact dual formulation to eliminate memory dependence on the number of parameters.
It computes Jacobian shards on the fly and in parallel, avoiding materialization of the full Jacobian and approximate PCG solves.
The resulting memory footprint scales quadratically with batch size rather than parameter count.
On an 8-GPU node, LeMA achieves 7.97× speedup and 99.7% strong-scaling efficiency for a 1-billion-parameter CNN.
