papers.abstract: Context: Organizations increasingly delegate code review to multi-agent large language model (LLM) pipelines billed per token. Low code quality raises human maintenance effort, but its effect on agent review cost has not been measured. Objective: We test whether baseline CodeHealth predicts the token cost of agentic review and fix beyond pull request (PR) footprint. Method: In a pre-registered observational study, we sampled 465 agent-authored PRs from 246 repositories in AIDev, jointly stratified by CodeHealth and footprint under repository caps. A frozen five-agent review-and-fix pipeline processed every PR with three different LLMs. Per LLM, we fitted a mixed model of log tokens on CodeHealth and log PR footprint, with a repository random intercept. Results: For all three LLMs the CodeHealth coefficient was negative, with 95% CI excluding zero; each CodeHealth point was associated with 3.5% to 6.1% lower token cost. CodeHealth was unrelated to PR footprint, so PR size does not explain the association. Two of three registered smells predicted fix cost; batch fixing left median CodeHealth unchanged. Exploratory analyses located the association in the review stage, where agents iterated more on unhealthy code without writing more comments. Adjusting for the size of the scored files absorbed the association, which we interpret as mediation by file size. Conclusions: A quality metric calibrated against human maintainability also predicts the inference cost of multi-agent review and fix. The effect is modest per point and not carried by PR size, so the refactoring case extends to agent-reviewed code when it changes structure and file size, not only the score. Data Availability: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22127920
authors: Lo Gullstrand Heander, Markus Borg, Emma S\"oderberg, Christofer Rydenf\"alt
bullets: CodeHealth negatively predicted agentic review-and-fix token cost across all three tested LLMs, independent of PR footprint.
Each additional CodeHealth point corresponded to 3.5%–6.1% lower token cost.
The association appeared during review, where agents iterated more on unhealthy code without producing more comments.
Adjusting for scored-file size removed the association, suggesting file size mediates the relationship.
Two registered code smells predicted fix cost, while batch fixing did not change median CodeHealth.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the study procedure in four phases, with its milestones on a timeline. Takeaway: Hypotheses and sampling were locked after pilot 3, and the pre-registration was finalized after the review agents had started but before the fix agent ran, so no complete row existed at filing (Section 3.12).

Figure 3: Associational path diagram of the registered model, log(tokens total) ∼ health + log(footprint) + language + (1|repo). Takeaway: Change footprint is treated as a mediator candidate sitting on the path from CodeHealth to cost, not as a nuisance covariate to be removed, so RQ1 concerns the direct path c′ that survives conditioning on footprint and RQ2 concerns the decomposition of a, b, and c′; the arrows denote regression paths in an observational design and do not imply causality.

Figure 4: One PR from each CodeHealth tier traced through the measurement instrument, all three from the medium footprint tercile and all three measured with sonnet-5. A pass is one invocation of an agent over its whole input; the iteration counts in each cell are the agent turns taken inside that single pass, so a batch fix pass with no retry can still run many iterations. Each is the PR whose total token cost lies closest to its own tier’s median among PRs with 95 to 125 changed lines, so none is an extreme case. Takeaway: At a nearly identical PR footprint, total cost rises as baseline CH falls, and the rise is not explained by the number of review comments, which are unrelated to CH across the whole sample (ρ = −.03, p = .56). Agent iterations, in contrast, are correlated with CH (ρ = −.16, p < .001). Three PRs illustrate the measurement path and are not evidence for it; the estimates are in Section 4.

Figure 1: The registered answers to RQ1 and RQ2, fitted separately per LLM. Takeaway: Token cost falls with CH for all three LLMs, and CH does not predict footprint, so larger PR footprints do not account for the extra cost of unhealthy code.

Table 12: The registered model form refitted on each pipeline stage separately, one fit per LLM per outcome, on the same PRs as Table 8. Fix-stage fits drop the PRs with zero review comments: n reports the rows that remain. Takeaway: The CodeHealth effect survives removing the fix stage from the outcome entirely, and in fact strengthens for every LLM, so the association lies with the review stage and not with the fix stage that follows it.

Table 13: Decomposition of the review-stage effect, same model form and same rows as Table 12. Because log(review tokens) = log(iterations) + log(tokens per iteration), the first two coefficients in each block sum to that LLM’s review-token coefficient by construction. Comment counts, and the per-comment ratio, are modeled on the PRs with at least one comment. The last row of each block corresponds to the review-token row of Table 12 minus the sixth row of this block, but it is fitted independently on the ratio, on the smaller sample that having at least one comment requires. Takeaway: Lower CodeHealth is associated with more agent turns and more tokens within each turn, and it shows most consistently on the input side, yet it does not correlate with additional review comments, so the additional spend buys no additional output and the cost per review finding rises accordingly.

Table 9: RQ2 three-path decomposition, every path estimated in the registered mixed-model family with a repository random intercept, fitted separately per LLM. Path (a) is log(footprint) ∼ health + language + (1|repo); paths (b) and (c) are the log(footprint) and health coefficients of the primary fit in Table 8. Takeaway: CodeHealth is not associated with PR footprint for any LLM, footprint is the strongest driver of cost for every LLM, and the CH effect on cost persists with footprint held constant, so the effect is direct with respect to PR footprint; Section 4.6.4 examines file size.

Table 1: The three pilot exercises and the main collection. Takeaway: Pilots 1 and 2 failed for sampling reasons rather than pipeline reasons, and each failure influenced the final design; pilot 3 is the main collection at one tenth of the scale, run with the same three LLMs, prompts, and workflow, with small harness updates in between.

Table 10: RQ3 confirmatory test on the main collection: partial Spearman correlation with log1p fix-agent tokens, controlling for log changed lines, Holm-corrected within each LLM’s three-hypothesis family. Takeaway: Complex Method and Complex Conditional are confirmed for all three LLMs; Code Duplication is confirmed for none of them, and its sign even reverses for sonnet-5, so only two of the three pre-registered smell hypotheses are supported.

Table 14: Exploratory refit of the comment-count outcome with both the CodeHealth score and the smell count as predictors on the same rows, controlling for log changed lines, log scored-file lines, log changed files, language, and a repo random intercept. Comment counts are modeled on the PRs with at least one comment, as in Table 13. Takeaway: The number of findings the agents report tracks how many smells CodeScene counted, while remaining unrelated to the CH score those smells produce, so the null in Table 13 reflects the predictor and is not evidence that the agents attend to unrelated properties of the code.

Table 15: The registered model refitted with log total lines of the scored files added, one fit per LLM on the same rows as Table 8. The size coefficient is the change in log tokens per unit of log file lines; it is reported as an estimate and is not part of the corrected family. Takeaway: Adjusting for file size absorbs the CodeHealth association for all three LLMs, which in this sample cannot be separated from the size of the files it is computed over.

Table 2: Achieved cell fill on the 3× 3 CodeHealth by footprint grid, against a target of 56 PRs per cell. Takeaway: Seven of nine cells filled completely. The two short cells are in the unhealthy tier at medium and large footprint, reflecting a real scarcity of low-CH PRs in the AIDev pool.

Table 4: The three LLMs, their serving stacks, versions, and cached input shares. The cached input share is computed as the share of all input tokens served from the prefix cache across the 465-PR collection, pooled over review and fix agents. Takeaway: The three instruments differ simultaneously in provider, quantization, serving stack, and prefix-cache regime, which is why the analysis fits them separately and never compares them inferentially.

Table 3: The four review agents and their primary ISO/IEC 25010 quality characteristics (ISO/IEC 2023). Takeaway: The agent set partitions review concerns along an externally defined taxonomy, which makes the choice of roles auditable; the mapping is approximate only for DesignReviewer, which spans two characteristics.

Table 6: Agent-session termination categories and their treatment. Takeaway: A guard-stopped review session is kept because it is instrument behavior and part of the cost being measured; a guard-stopped fix session leaves no completed fix record or post-fix score, so that PR is excluded for that LLM. Infrastructure failures and unexpected errors are retried until success.

Table 5: The three code smells registered as confirmatory hypotheses for RQ3, selected from pilot data by the pre-specified rule. Takeaway: The rule retained the three smells present in enough pilot PRs, with a sign agreed by all three LLMs and the largest mean adjusted correlations; each was then registered with a mechanism of its own.

Table 7: Pilot 3 per-LLM CodeHealth-to-cost slope and the resulting power characteristics at the achieved main-collection design (n = 465, 246 repositories). Takeaway: All three pilot slopes are negative and similar in magnitude, but every LLM’s own required sample size exceeds the achieved 465, which is why no single LLM is designated primary and why the confirmatory claim is a direction-consistency criterion across all three.

Table 16: Run-to-run variance decomposition on the 27-PR replication subsample (three runs per PR per LLM). λ is the run-to-run variance divided by the between-PR variance; ICC(k = 1) is the implied reliability of a single run. Takeaway: qwen3-6’s run-to-run noise is about an order of magnitude larger, relative to its stable PR signal, than either of the other two LLMs, while deepseek-v4-flash and sonnet-5 are both highly reliable at a single run.

papers.selection_reason: Studies the token cost of agentic code review, providing empirical insights into the efficiency of LLM inference pipelines.
papers.title: CodeHealth Predicts the Token Cost of Agentic Code Review: A Pre-Registered Study of 465 Agent-Authored Pull Requests
papers.tldr: In a pre-registered study of 465 agent-authored PRs, healthier code consistently required modestly fewer tokens for multi-agent review and fixing, largely because it involved smaller scored files.

papers.abstract: Grid foundation models (GridFMs) are graph transformers pretrained on a masked power-flow objective, and evaluate power flow orders of magnitude faster than an iterative solver. Their size, however, targets data-centre inference, whereas low-inertia operation increasingly asks for inference at the edge, next to the measurement, at batch size one and within a single synchrophasor (PMU) reporting frame. We distil a 20.1M-parameter, 12-layer GridFM teacher into a 0.62M-parameter, 6-layer student, a $32.5\times$ parameter reduction at half the message-passing depth, using an objective that combines the masked power-flow loss with output, physics-residual, latent-state and attention transfer. The physics-residual term, which matches the teacher's power-residual profile, has not previously been applied to typed power-grid graphs. We evaluate on a renewable variant of the IEEE 118-bus benchmark grid in which 26 of the conventional (synchronous) generators are replaced by inverter-based renewables with battery flexibility and standardised reactive-power limits (IEEE 1547), giving $97\,529$ physically valid (AC-OPF-feasible) operating scenarios, and we ablate all eight combinations of the transfer terms, reporting accuracy against ground truth and fidelity to the teacher separately. Distillation lowers student error on all four predicted quantities, by up to $48\%$ on active-power dispatch, and every distilled student is more accurate than its teacher on reactive-power dispatch. The gain is largely carried by the output matching term. The physics-residual term, in the layer-aggregated form used here, is consistently harmful, which we attribute to the spatial averaging it applies to a bus-level residual field. The resulting student is $32.5\times$ smaller in parameter count and has half the message-passing depth, making it a candidate for subsequent edge-device benchmarking.
authors: Vlad Alexandru S\u{a}nduleac, Shahariya Rasheed Rayamarakkarveettil Puthanpurayil, Noman Khan, Remus Teodorescu
bullets: Targets real-time, batch-size-one grid inference at the edge within a single PMU reporting frame.
Distils a 20.1M-parameter, 12-layer teacher into a 0.62M-parameter, 6-layer student using output, latent, attention, masked power-flow, and physics-residual transfer losses.
Evaluated on a renewable IEEE 118-bus variant with 97,529 AC-OPF-feasible operating scenarios and separate accuracy and teacher-fidelity analyses.
Student error decreases for all four predicted quantities, with up to 48% lower active-power dispatch error; all distilled students outperform the teacher on reactive-power dispatch.
Output matching provides most of the benefit, while layer-aggregated physics-residual matching is consistently harmful, likely due to spatial averaging of bus-level residuals.

papers.selection_reason: Distillation of a grid foundation model for real-time edge inference directly targets computation and latency reduction.
papers.title: Physics-Aware Distillation of a Grid Foundation Model for Real-Time Edge Inference
papers.tldr: Physics-aware distillation compresses a large GridFM into a 32.5× smaller student that improves power-flow prediction accuracy, though the tested physics-residual transfer term hurts performance.

papers.abstract: Aggressive quantization of neural networks can expose activation functions as bottlenecks for efficient hardware acceleration. Implementing quantized activations as multi-threshold operations has been shown to be a promising optimization, allowing for efficient hardware implementation of few-bit activations. However, current implementations are limited to monotonically increasing functions, quantization schemes with one-dimensional (per-channel) granularity and a small set of predefined activation-quantizer combinations. We formalize the multi-threshold representation to extend it to non-monotonic functions and fine-granular parameters, i.e., multi-dimensional thresholds. For automated conversion of quantized function compositions into threshold representation, we propose a systematic approach via algebraic rules integrated into the ONNX-based compiler infrastructure. We experimentally validate our solution on a selection of monotonic and non-monotonic functions by extending the binary search based multi-threshold operator that is integrated into the FINN framework for end-to-end synthesis of custom-tailored FPGA accelerators. The cost of hardware support for non-monotonicity and fine-granularity is characterized in comparison to an alternative approach utilizing existing operators via graph-level decomposition. We compare our method to prior work as well as the approach taken by the hls4ml framework. As an outlook, we demonstrate the prospects of using the multi-threshold representation during the training of a neural network as a form of quantization aware training.
authors: Christoph Berganski, Felix Jentzsch, Marco Platzner
bullets: Addresses hardware bottlenecks caused by aggressively quantized activation functions.
Formalizes multi-threshold representations for non-monotonic functions and multidimensional thresholds.
Introduces algebraic compiler rules in an ONNX-based infrastructure to automatically convert quantized function compositions.
Validates the approach on monotonic and non-monotonic functions using FINN’s binary-search multi-threshold operator and end-to-end FPGA synthesis.
Characterizes hardware costs against graph-level decomposition, prior work, and hls4ml; also explores multi-threshold representations for quantization-aware training.

papers.selection_reason: Compiling quantized activations into multi-threshold operators for custom DNN accelerators directly targets efficient AI inference on hardware.
papers.title: Compiling Multi-Threshold Operators for Quantized Non-Monotonic and Fine-Granular Activations in Custom-Tailored DNN Accelerators

papers.abstract: Conditional memory expands language-model capacity through selective lookup, but the full embedding table must remain available for every possible input. We introduce Conditional Program (CP), a compressed representation that reconstructs only the rows an input requests. CP represents each row by a short code and a local scale, with a reconstruction program shared across the table. We instantiate this representation with a Gaussian trellis, norm restoration and independently decodable row records. CP's two-bit code lowers output KL by 41--63\% relative to 2-bit round-to-nearest. Analysis across three trained n-gram memory families shows that Gaussian-like coordinate statistics coexist with learned relationships among rows; at matched storage budgets, the shared trellis outperforms the fitted codebooks and low-rank residual variants we test. For DeepSeek, it reduces table storage from 203GB to 51GB, leaving room for larger workloads when the table is kept on GPU.
authors: Donghoon Han, Minseop Jung, Dong Woo Kwak, SeungJae Lee, Junhoo Lee
bullets: Targets conditional memories whose full embedding table must remain available for lookup.
Encodes each row with a short code and local scale, using a shared Gaussian-trellis reconstruction program.
Adds norm restoration and independently decodable row records for practical access.
Reduces output KL by 41–63% versus 2-bit round-to-nearest quantization.
Cuts DeepSeek table storage from 203GB to 51GB, enabling larger GPU-resident workloads.

papers.title: N-Gram Memories at Two Bits: Quantizing Lookup Tables in Large Language Models

papers.abstract: Weight quantization below four bits shrinks memory and bandwidth at a perplexity that looks acceptable, but often at the cost of factual knowledge and task accuracy. Ternary weights have mostly been obtained by training from scratch or long fine-tuning. We introduce RoleQ, a quantization framework that places scales by the functional roles of Transformer units rather than by the layout of the weight matrix, as conventional formats do. Vectors that read from the residual stream take one scale per output unit; those that write to it, one per input unit. The rule is structural, needs no search, calibration or stored state, and holds on integer and ternary grids. In a rotated basis it matches a per-layer axis search at half the solver work, and at ternary it cuts perplexity by up to half against layout-based placement in two families at every size from 0.6B to 14B, where per-row scales leave MMLU at chance. Our lightweight post-training pipeline converts an existing checkpoint to 1.59 bits per weight in a few GPU-hours, a fraction of the cost of learned ternarization, and leads every post-training ternary method at matched or lower memory-resident bits on perplexity, zero-shot accuracy and MMLU, most widely on knowledge. A sparse second ternary plane placed by a per-unit Fisher saliency keeps the matmul multiplication-free and recovers what ternary loses first: at 8B, a fraction of a bit returns about half the MMLU that conversion costs, well ahead of random or Hessian-based placement at equal bits.
authors: Johannes Knittel, Alec Helbling, Hanspeter Pfister
bullets: Targets sub-four-bit quantization, where memory savings often degrade factual knowledge and task accuracy.
Assigns scales by Transformer unit function: residual-stream readers use per-output-unit scales, while writers use per-input-unit scales.
Requires no search, calibration, or stored state, and converts existing checkpoints to 1.59 bits per weight in a few GPU-hours.
In two model families from 0.6B to 14B parameters, ternary RoleQ reduces perplexity by up to half versus layout-based scaling; per-row scaling leaves MMLU near chance.
A sparse second ternary plane selected by Fisher saliency recovers about half of the lost 8B MMLU performance with a fraction of a bit.

papers.title: RoleQ: Role-Aligned Scales for Converting Language Models to Ternary

papers.abstract: Multi-modal semantic segmentation benefits from complementary sensors, but this benefit is fragile when some modalities are degraded or missing at test time. Many existing methods rely on dedicated fusion modules or multi-branch cross-modal encoders, and the fusion often becomes unreliable when modalities are absent, leading to substantial performance drops. We propose \textbf{FuseAdapt}, a parameter-efficient framework that performs fusion within the adaptation space of a frozen vision foundation model (VFM), exploring whether VFM priors can serve as an effective shared backbone for multi-modal segmentation. Instead of attaching a standalone fusion network, FuseAdapt assigns each modality a lightweight adaptation branch and performs \emph{adaptation-space fusion} by keeping Q/V low-rank adaptation private to each modality and routing only FFN low-rank residual activations across modalities inside the frozen backbone. The pretrained VFM remains fixed while modality-specific corrections and explicit cross-modal interaction are learned through the adaptation paths. To handle missing modalities, we further introduce \textbf{Predictive Modality Modeling (PMM)}, a direct representation-level objective for cross-modal redundancy. During training, PMM masks a target modality and predicts its embedding from the visible ones, supervised by a teacher target computed under full-modality input. PMM is used only during training and adds no inference-time overhead. Across three multi-modal segmentation benchmarks (MCubeS, DELIVER, MUSES), FuseAdapt consistently improves both modality-complete and modality-incomplete segmentation with a small trainable budget, yielding up to +3.01 mIoU under full modalities and +12.56 mIoU under missing modalities over prior state-of-the-art. Project page: https://devinxzhang.github.io/FuseAdapt-Page/.
bullets: Addresses performance degradation when modalities are absent or corrupted at test time.
Uses modality-specific low-rank adaptation branches inside a frozen vision foundation model.
Fuses modalities by routing only FFN adaptation residuals across modalities while keeping Q/V adaptations private.
Introduces Predictive Modality Modeling to reconstruct masked modality embeddings during training without inference overhead.
Improves complete- and incomplete-modality segmentation across three benchmarks, with gains of up to 3.01 and 12.56 mIoU, respectively.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of our FuseAdapt framework. (a) Adaptation-Space Fusion: Multi-modal inputs (e.g., RGB, depth, event, LiDAR) share a frozen VFM backbone. Each modality attaches a lightweight adaptation branch inside the transformer blocks, and a receiver-conditioned router mixes only FFN low-rank residual activations. Fusion is thus performed inside the adaptation path while keeping the backbone frozen, and the fused features are sent to a shared segmentation head. For clarity, we show the routing for one modality; the others follow the same design. (b) PMM: To handle missing modalities, an EMA teacher provides the target embedding for a selected modality. A student and a Perceiver-style predictor use the visible modalities to predict this embedding via learnable queries. PMM is trained with a distance loss D(ẑ, z).

Figure 2: Comparison of designs for robustness under missing modalities (MISS). (a) Semanticanchor methods align modality features to text embeddings, but text anchors can be coarse for pixel-level segmentation. (b) Semantic-consistency methods enforce agreement across different modality subsets, but such constraints can be affected by cross-modal mismatch. (c) Predictive Modality Modeling (PMM) casts MISS training as conditional representation prediction. Learnable query tokens aggregate cues from visible modalities to predict a missing-modality embedding, improving MISS performance on DELIVER and MUSES.

papers.abstract: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) offer a compelling pathway toward energy-efficient artificial intelligence, fundamentally anchored in presynaptic input-driven sparsity. However, a substantial yet chronically overlooked source of computational overhead persists: the continuous subthreshold dynamics of postsynaptic neurons. Quantitative analysis reveals that up to 44% of neurons in an ImageNet-trained ResNet-18 model reside in a deeply inhibited state, imposing a persistent computational burden despite having a negligible probability of firing. To address this inefficiency, the Dormant Spiking Neuron (DSN) model is introduced. By incorporating a state-driven dynamic gate, the DSN allows a neuron to enter a dormant state when its membrane potential falls below a predefined negative threshold, dynamically pruning redundant computations at the instance level. Crucially, this dormancy mechanism is directly integrated into the neuronal dynamics and trained end-to-end via backpropagation through time using surrogate gradients, enabling the network to actively learn a robust dormancy policy that adaptively preserves critical information flow. Extensive experiments across static and neuromorphic datasets demonstrate that the DSN framework consistently reduces computational energy by 40% to over 70%. Notably, on the large-scale ImageNet dataset, the DSN outperforms state-of-the-art static pruning techniques at comparable reported cost reductions and simultaneously improves the corresponding baseline SNN accuracy by 1.34%. By establishing a trainable, state-driven sparsity paradigm orthogonal to conventional input-driven methods, the DSN unlocks synergistic efficiency gains, presenting an effective approach for advancing neuromorphic computing.
authors: Ruichen Ma, Yicai Chen, Pujun Zhou, Yue Zuo, Chongyang Li, Shuang Liu, Shaogang Hu, Guanchao Qiao
bullets: SNNs incur substantial overhead from continuously updating postsynaptic neurons unlikely to fire; up to 44% are deeply inhibited in an ImageNet-trained ResNet-18.
DSN adds a state-driven gate that places neurons below a negative membrane-potential threshold into a dormant state.
The mechanism is integrated into neuron dynamics and trained end-to-end with backpropagation through time and surrogate gradients.
Experiments on static and neuromorphic datasets report 40%–over 70% lower computational energy.
On ImageNet, DSN exceeds static-pruning performance at comparable reported cost reductions and improves baseline SNN accuracy by 1.34%.

papers.abstract: Echo State Networks (ESNs), as lightweight implementations of reservoir computing, provide efficient solutions for temporal data processing in resource-constrained environments. While standard ESNs offer computational efficiency, their dense readout layers inflate the stored model and the per-sample inference cost. This paper introduces a Smooth-L1 regularized ESN (SL1ESN) that promotes sparsity in the readout layer while preserving differentiability for gradient-based optimization. The method employs a twice-differentiable Smooth-L1 approximation compatible with Newton's method, which we exploit both for centralized training and for a second-order (Newton-step) federated aggregation scheme. Under a single fixed shrinkage threshold shared by every dataset and both settings, experiments on seven time-series classification benchmarks show that SL1ESN learns readouts that are $77$--$95\%$ sparse in the centralized setting and $75$--$95\%$ sparse in the federated one, while staying within $0.7$ accuracy points of the strongest dense baseline on five of the seven benchmarks in the centralized setting and within $1.6$ points on the same five in the federated one, and the second-order federated update converges in only a few rounds. The resulting sparsity compresses the stored model, the per-sample inference cost, and the server-to-client broadcast by a comparable factor. These results demonstrate the practical value of sparse readouts for edge computing and IoT deployments.
authors: Gengcheng Lyu, Manuel R\"oder, Frank-Michael Schleif
bullets: Targets the storage, inference, and communication costs of dense ESN readout layers in resource-constrained edge and IoT settings.
Uses a twice-differentiable Smooth-L1 regularizer to promote sparsity while enabling Newton-based centralized training and federated aggregation.
With one fixed shrinkage threshold across datasets and settings, readouts reach 77–95% sparsity centrally and 75–95% federated.
On seven benchmarks, accuracy remains within 0.7 points of the strongest dense baseline centrally and 1.6 points federated on five benchmarks.
The sparse readouts provide comparable reductions in model storage, per-sample inference cost, and server-to-client broadcasts; federated training converges in a few rounds.

figures.caption: Figure 1: FedSL1ESN training pipeline. The server broadcasts the fixed global reservoir once and a sparse global readout each round (CSR, minimal payload); clients evaluate the local gradient and Gauss-Newton Hessian of their Smooth-L1 loss on private data and return this curvature information for the server’s Newton-step aggregation.

Figure 4: Federated setting; the counterpart of Figure 2. As in the centralized case, accuracy stays essentially flat out to 75–95% sparsity on most datasets, and collapses only once the readout is driven to near-total sparsity.

Figure 3: FedSL1ESN convergence over communication rounds for each dataset (five clients, IID split, 50 rounds, mean over ten seeds; shaded bands are ±1 std). (a) Test accuracy reaches near-peak within a few rounds on most datasets and is stable thereafter (Strawberry is the slowest, climbing until round ∼ 20). The bands in (b) are wide at early rounds, where seeds sit at different points on the steep part of the curve, and narrow by round 50, which is why the round-50 sparsity is reproducible across seeds.

papers.abstract: Fixed-function CNN accelerators make edge inference fast and energy-efficient, but they execute only networks that obey a precise numerical contract. On the MAX7800x family, this contract requires power-of-two, per-tensor, symmetric scales, 8-bit activations and biases, integer-only arithmetic, and one statically configured shift per layer. We present ShiftQAT, the quantization-aware training (QAT) flow we developed for this family, which produces networks satisfying the contract by construction. It is the default training path of ai8x-training, the family's open-source training toolchain. ShiftQAT resolves residual, concatenation, and weight-sharing dependencies so that activation scales propagate statically and each layer's requantization reduces to one offline-configured shift. It also trains weights and biases on a joint power-of-two grid that fits the 8-bit bias budget. Among the compared methods, only ShiftQAT satisfies all of the contract's scaling constraints, including signed 8-bit activation storage. Even so, on ImageNet it matches the W8A8 accuracy drop of less constrained QAT methods and stays within 2.9 percentage points of FP32 at W4A8. On MAX78002 silicon, ShiftQAT-trained MobileNetV2 and ResNet-18 classify ImageNet images in 14.6 and 8.4 ms at 5.1 and 2.8 mJ per inference.
authors: Oguzhan Buyuksolak, Osman Erman Okman, Mehmet Gorkem Ulkar
bullets: Targets fixed-function MAX7800x accelerators requiring per-tensor symmetric power-of-two scales, signed 8-bit activations and biases, integer arithmetic, and one shift per layer.
Statically propagates activation scales through residuals, concatenations, and weight sharing, reducing requantization to offline-configured shifts.
Trains weights and biases on a joint power-of-two grid within the 8-bit bias budget.

It is the only compared method satisfying all stated scaling constraints, while matching the accuracy drop of less constrained W8A8 QAT and remaining within 2.9 percentage points of FP32 at W4A8 on ImageNet.
On MAX78002 silicon, MobileNetV2 and ResNet-18 classify ImageNet images in 14.6 ms/5.1 mJ and 8.4 ms/2.8 mJ per inference, respectively.

(b) For a concatenation, the inputs adopt the largest scale among them. Figure 2. The ShiftQAT flow. FP32 training is followed by offline initialization, which consists of BN folding, activation-scale proposal, and activation-scale refinement (dependency resolution and propagation). QAT then runs with per-iteration weight/bias scale determination.

Figure 4. Static scale propagation on a two-layer network. On the left, each layer’s output carries its real-valued scale. papers.abstract: Biomedical research articles are mainly written for experts and often contain terms that are difficult for the general public to understand. Automated lay summarization has become a solution to make biomedical knowledge easier for patients and the public to understand. However, generating lay summaries from full-text articles requires more computing power because the articles are long and costly to process. Fine-tuning large language models for this task also requires substantial resources. This study asks two questions: (1) whether abstracts contain enough information to produce lay summaries as good as those based on full-text articles, and (2) whether few-shot learning performs as well as task-specific fine-tuning. The study used two public biomedical lay summarization datasets and two recent models, evaluated for readability, factual consistency, semantic similarity, and runtime efficiency. Results show that abstract-based summarization performs better overall. Across both datasets and models, abstract fine-tuning is 4.70 times faster, while abstract zero- and few-shot prompting is 5.31 times faster than full-text methods. These results show that abstract-based prompting reduces runtime cost while maintaining lay summary quality.

papers.abstract: Vision Transformer architectures have showcased impressive performance on semantic segmentation, yet their quadratic attention complexity hinders practical applications. Recent works have focused on merging tokens to reduce sequence length and thus improve transformer efficiency. However, existing token merging methods primarily rely on feature similarity to identify similar tokens, overlooking spatial consistency, which may introduce segmentation errors in semantic segmentation. In this work, we propose SCMerge, a training-free token merging method that jointly considers feature similarity and spatial consistency in pairing similar tokens. The pairwise tokens are then merged within the encoder, and the resulting token sequences are reconstructed onto the original patch grid after decoding. The proposed method is flexible and can be plugged into existing vision Transformer-based semantic segmentation pipelines. Extensive experiments on the benchmark datasets ADE20K, Pascal Context, and Cityscapes show that SCMerge consistently achieves a better trade-off between segmentation accuracy and efficiency than baseline methods.
authors: Junfeng Ren (Southern University of Science and Technology), Yi Gong (Southern University of Science and Technology), Yuan Zeng (Shenzhen Technology University)
bullets: Addresses the quadratic attention cost of Vision Transformers in semantic segmentation.
Pairs tokens using both feature similarity and spatial consistency to reduce segmentation errors from spatially inconsistent merges.
Merges tokens in the encoder and reconstructs the decoded sequences onto the original patch grid.
Plug-and-play with existing Vision Transformer semantic segmentation pipelines.
Experiments on ADE20K, Pascal Context, and Cityscapes show a better accuracy–efficiency trade-off than baseline methods.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has been a critical paradigm for improving large language model (LLM) reasoning and agentic capabilities, but its efficiency remains a major bottleneck. Existing RL systems commonly rely on asynchronous execution to overlap rollout generation with policy optimization for enhanced efficiency. However, this approach faces inherent limitations: mild policy staleness offers only limited training efficiency gains, whereas aggressive asynchrony can degrade model quality and yields diminishing efficiency gains. The dynamic nature of LLM RL and multi-turn agentic workloads further challenges RL system design, as resource demands shift over time, making static resource allocation and generation strategy inefficient. This paper presents ReFlow, a system-algorithm co-designed RL framework for efficient LLM post-training. Its key insight is that, unlike existing RL frameworks which consume each trajectory only once, experience replay of recent trajectories enables effective sample reuse, thereby amortizing the high cost of rollout generation without incurring excessive policy staleness. To fully exploit this opportunity, ReFlow adopts a decoupled and adaptive architecture with three key designs: a dual replay data cycle supports efficient experience reuse while balancing training throughput and optimization stability; an elastic resource pool enables dynamic resource placement to accommodate evolving RL workloads; an adaptive scheduler coordinates generation strategies and resource allocation to improve resource utilization and boost generation throughput. Experiments across representative single-turn reasoning and multi-turn agentic RL tasks show that ReFlow improves training throughput by up to $2.06\times$ over state-of-the-art synchronous and asynchronous RL systems, while maintaining comparable or better model performance.
authors: Yukun Tian, Junwei Su, Haofeng Xu, Lansong Diao, Zhengping Qian, Weibo Zhao, Wenchao Zhou, Ruiting Zhou, Chuan Wu
bullets: Addresses rollout-generation overhead, policy staleness, and inefficient static resource allocation in LLM RL.
Uses experience replay to reuse recent trajectories and amortize rollout costs.

Evaluations on single-turn reasoning and multi-turn agentic tasks report up to 2.06× higher training throughput with comparable or better performance.

papers.abstract: Recent feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) methods have enabled effective multi-view 3D reconstruction by predicting Gaussian primitives in a single forward pass. However, existing approaches predominantly adopt a pixel-aligned paradigm that predicts one Gaussian per input pixel, coupling the Gaussian count to the input resolution and number of views. This also leads to redundant primitives in textureless regions and insufficient coverage in geometrically complex areas. We present Anchor3DGS, a pose-free feed-forward 3DGS framework that replaces pixel-aligned prediction with a compact anchor-based representation. Guided by information entropy, our method places a set of 3D anchors in the scene, concentrating them in regions of higher visual complexity while maintaining broad spatial coverage. Each anchor performs occlusion-aware aggregation of multi-view image features, exchanges information with other anchors, and is decoded into a set of local Gaussians. A lightweight feature enhancement module further refines the coarse RGB output from Gaussian splatting and improves rendering fidelity. Extensive experiments on diverse benchmark datasets demonstrate that our Anchor3DGS achieves state-of-the-art novel view synthesis quality while only using an order of magnitude fewer Gaussian primitives.
authors: Sheng Ye, Jiangke Lin, Fudong Wang, Yi Yuan, Zhen-Hui Dong, Yong-Jin Liu
bullets: Addresses redundant Gaussians in textureless regions and insufficient coverage in geometrically complex areas.
Uses entropy-guided 3D anchors to concentrate representation where visual complexity is higher while preserving scene coverage.
Anchors aggregate multi-view features with occlusion awareness, exchange information, and decode into local Gaussian sets.
A lightweight enhancement module refines Gaussian-splatting RGB outputs for improved rendering fidelity.
Experiments on diverse benchmarks report state-of-the-art novel-view synthesis quality with an order of magnitude fewer Gaussian primitives.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of Anchor3DGS. Given uncalibrated multi-view images, (1) a VGGT-based [28] geometry backbone first predicts the scene’s geometric scaffold. (2) A fixed budget of 3D anchors is then sampled from the scaffold, combining uniform sampling with entropy-guided sampling. (3) Each anchor is projected back into all input views to gather features via occlusion-aware aggregation, and then interacts with other anchors through self-attention. (4) Finally, each anchor is decoded into a set of local Gaussians, which are rasterized and refined to yield the final RGB output.
Figure 4: Qualitative comparison of novel view synthesis. Our method recovers sharper textures and finer details while mitigating artifacts in poorly observed regions.
Figure 5: Rendering metrics under varying anchor count N and decoded Gaussians K (left), and qualitative comparisons of removing the enhancement module and entropy-guided sampling (right).

papers.abstract: Looped Transformers improve parameter efficiency by repeatedly applying the same Transformer layers. However, generating each token still involves sequential computation and repeated access to model weights, leading to high decoding latency. Recent pipelined self-speculative decoding methods reduce this delay by drafting tokens from early-loop predictions and asynchronously advancing tokens at different recurrent depths in the same batch, but they do not fully exploit early-loop features for longer lookahead and still spend computation verifying incorrect speculative branches. We introduce \method, a speculative decoding framework for looped transformers that enables earlier drafting of future tokens and assigns complementary roles to different recurrent depths. A lightweight lookahead drafter (LAD) predicts multiple future tokens with early-loop states, and deeper-loop feedback helps decide which draft branches to continue and which to pause, while the full-depth model makes the final token decisions. LoopAhead achieves up to 7.82x decoding speedup over autoregressive decoding while preserving the target model's output distribution.
authors: Zixuan Liu, Nan Xue, Rui Bao, Yuhang Xu, Xiaofeng Cao, Jiangchao Yao, Zhiyong Chen
bullets: Addresses decoding latency from sequential token generation and repeated weight access in looped language models.
Uses a lightweight lookahead drafter to predict several future tokens from early-loop features.
Employs deeper-loop feedback to continue promising draft branches and pause likely incorrect ones.

papers.abstract: Real-world video denoising for communication systems must handle mixed degradations such as sensor noise, compression artifacts, and motion-induced inconsistency while remaining deployable under tight latency budgets. Purely deep models often achieve high accuracy but come with significant computational cost, whereas classical filters are robust and efficient but insufficiently adaptive. We present FilterFusion, a prior-guided multi-frame denoising framework that combines temporally-aware learned features with an interpretable bank of denoising branches. The model predicts a low-cost guidance signal and uses it to adaptively mix a compact set of denoising responses at the original resolution. The lightweight design uses only 109K parameters and explicitly injects temporal variance and spatial variance cues into the low-resolution controller. On CRVD (real sensor noise), it reaches 34.72 dB PSNR and 0.9330 SSIM with only 0.18 GFLOPs (network-only). Because the filter-bank operations are simple and regular (Gaussian blur, median, weighted sum), a straightforward compiled C implementation of the synthesis path achieves 17.9ms per frame (55.9 FPS) on a single CPU thread at 1080p---exceeding real-time and 122--252 times faster than lightweight CNN baselines that require over 2 seconds per frame. The results demonstrate a strong quality-efficiency-speed trade-off and a practical route to real-time denoising through low-resolution control and explicit filter-based synthesis.
authors: Wenlong Yang, Weihang Yuan, Canran Jin, Jiahao Li, Henrik Turbell, Lifeng Sun
bullets: Targets mixed real-world degradations, including sensor noise, compression artifacts, and motion inconsistency, under tight latency constraints.

Injects temporal and spatial variance cues into a low-resolution controller that predicts adaptive filter mixing.
Uses 109K parameters and 0.18 GFLOPs; on CRVD, achieves 34.72 dB PSNR and 0.9330 SSIM.

papers.abstract: Reusing the attention KV cache across requests is a standard way to cut prefill cost in long-context LLM serving, and production systems increasingly back the per-engine cache with a remote tier shared by every engine. We study such a tier in a disaggregated deployment of GLM-5.3, an FP8 mixture-of-experts model with multi-head latent attention (MLA), on 8xB300 nodes running prefill context parallelism (PCP8). Enabling the remote tier (LMCache with a Valkey store) left median time-to-first-token unchanged but raised the 16k-token p99 from 3.96 s to 17.3 s. Replaying a production request stream on an isolated engine, we find that a remote hit took 0.88 s against 0.31 s to recompute the prompt, and that synchronous loading turned a hit-heavy stream into an unstable queue: p99 83.32 s with the GPUs 7% busy. A two-term cost model explains both: a hit pays off only if the tier delivers more than B* = sR (2.53 GB/s for this model and GPU), and a fixed per-hit engine cost (T0 ~ 0.33 s) means that hits on prompts shorter than about 17k tokens cannot beat recompute at any bandwidth. Guided by the model, we (i) shard the MLA KV store across PCP ranks, with a proof that the existing minimum-over-ranks lookup returns the longest cached prefix and a load protocol that can never desynchronize collectives; (ii) partition the remote tier by rank, one server instance per rank with no coordination, which raises GET bandwidth 6.3x to 10.76 GB/s; (iii) add asynchronous loading to the sharded store; and (iv) fix three client bugs that caused unbounded stalls. On the hit-heavy stream, with 98.5% of prompt tokens served from the remote tier, p99 falls from 83.32 s to 0.67 s. The sharded store raises prefill throughput by 14%, and by 34% together with an upstream kernel fix. All changes are submitted upstream to LMCache.
bullets: A remote LMCache/Valkey tier increased 16k-token p99 latency from 3.96 s to 17.3 s, despite unchanged median time-to-first-token.
Remote hits initially took 0.88 s versus 0.31 s for prompt recomputation; synchronous loading caused severe queueing and 83.32 s p99 latency.
A cost model shows caching helps only above 2.53 GB/s and for prompts longer than roughly 17k tokens.
The proposed design shards MLA KV state and the remote tier across PCP ranks, adds asynchronous loading, and fixes three stalling client bugs.
The optimized system reduced hit-heavy p99 latency to 0.67 s, increased prefill throughput by 14%, and by 34% with an upstream kernel fix.

papers.abstract: Large language models can produce fluent answers that the supplied context does not support. A compact frozen proxy model can detect such answers by reading the context and another model's response, even from a proprietary generator. Attention-based detectors use summary statistics of the proxy's attention weights, but standard pipelines materialize the attention matrix, whose memory grows quadratically with sequence length. We compute these statistics without materializing attention, by accumulation in the FlashAttention pass, sparse lookups after it, or a second tiled pass over the scores, and classify them by this path into nearly free and costlier ones. On an H100, the statistics of five published detectors add 16% to the latency of a Qwen3-8B forward at 2K tokens, falling to 1.4% at 35K, and store 22.5 KiB per response token. On three benchmarks, probes trained on frozen Qwen3 proxies of 0.6B to 8B parameters prove strong detectors: a 4B proxy outperforms the strongest of nine zero-shot 4-9B LLM judges in F1 on two of the three, the proxies match or outperform specialized grounding checkers of up to 7B parameters, probing each proxy beats prompting it as a judge, and adding attention features significantly improves F1 in half of the 12 benchmark-proxy pairs, never significantly lowering it.
authors: Andrei Volodichev, Maksim Savichev, Nikita Sviridov, Artem Yuliy, Dmitry Simakov, Alexey Zaytsev
bullets: Targets unsupported but fluent LLM answers, including responses from proprietary generators.

Across three benchmarks, frozen Qwen3 probes are strong detectors; a 4B proxy beats nine zero-shot LLM judges on two benchmarks and matches or exceeds specialized checkers.
Attention features significantly improve F1 in 6 of 12 benchmark–proxy pairs and never significantly reduce it.

papers.abstract: Device-cloud speculative decoding reduces server computation, but growing a deep draft tree with a small language model (SLM) requires repeated passes on a mobile neural processing unit (NPU). We present HyCo, which assigns depth to the server model's native multi-token prediction (MTP) head, executed on the device, and alternative branches to one SLM pass. The server returns the hidden state, input embedding, and key-value entries needed by the head instead of executing its sequential steps. Quantization, a restricted vocabulary, and a 1K-token window fit both drafters to the NPU. An {\epsilon}-threshold rule additionally relaxes exact preservation of the verifier's sampling distribution. In single-client runs with a Galaxy S26 Ultra over LTE/5G, HyCo reduces server GPU time per output token relative to server-side MTP self-speculation by 38.6% on Spec-Bench and 29.2% on 32K-token summarization. With the same acceptance rule, three Spec-Bench runs per system show 9.0 percentage points more saving and 1.9x delivery speed than an SLM-only drafter. HyCo differs from Cloud+MTP by +0.2 judge-score points (paired 95% CI: -0.9 to +1.3); exploratory translation favors SpecEdge-{\epsilon}. Without relaxation, HyCo exact saves 27.7% and 11.9% on the two datasets.
authors: Hanbin Bae, Heejin Choi, Joohyung Lee, Byoung Jin Choi, Sangjun Park, Hoon-Young Cho

On a Galaxy S26 Ultra over LTE/5G, reduces server GPU time per output token by 38.6% on Spec-Bench and 29.2% on 32K-token summarization versus server-side MTP self-speculation.
With the same acceptance rule, saves 9.0 percentage points more and delivers 1.9× higher speed than an SLM-only drafter; exact mode still saves 27.7% and 11.9%.

papers.abstract: Diffusion models achieve high-quality image generation but remain computationally expensive due to iterative denoising across many timesteps. Existing acceleration methods mainly reduce per-sample latency, but gains along this axis are becoming saturated. We instead explore an orthogonal throughput-oriented direction by processing multiple samples within a single denoising evaluation. To this end, we propose ManiFusion, a backbone-agnostic framework for multi-sample generation through fused-space computation. ManiFusion jointly processes multiple samples by fusing them before the denoising backbone and separating them afterward through unfusion. We provide a geometric perspective on how multiple samples can share a fused representation while retaining the information needed to guide their individual generation trajectories. To better align fusion allocation with denoising stages, ManiFusion uses Trajectory-Fusion Scheduling (TFS), which dynamically adjusts fusion factors throughout sampling. ManiFusion generalizes across diffusion families, including both U-Net and transformer backbones in pixel and latent spaces. We further show that ManiFusion composes with existing acceleration methods and reaches throughput regimes unattainable by prior approaches with minimal quality degradation.
authors: Minkyu Kim, Baekseung Kim, Junhoo Lee, Jangho Kim, Nojun Kwak
bullets: Targets throughput rather than only reducing latency for individual samples.
Fuses multiple samples before the denoising backbone and separates them afterward.
Uses Trajectory-Fusion Scheduling to adapt fusion factors across denoising stages.
Works across U-Net and transformer diffusion models in pixel and latent spaces.
Composes with existing acceleration methods and enables higher-throughput regimes.

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents now fix software, operate computers and serve customers, but their harnesses, the programs that run them, call a large LLM at every step, which makes long tasks slow and costly. Most of these calls end in a multiple-choice decision, such as which tool to call next. Decision models such as Jev answer these questions directly, at a fraction of an LLM call's time and price. We ask how a harness can delegate these decisions to a decision model with little loss of success. To evaluate decision models in agentic tasks, we build AgentDecisionBench, which tests them from isolated questions up to control of a running agent, on public benchmarks and our DecisionGym environment. The decision model most accurate on isolated questions solved only 69.5% of agent tasks, and without a fitted confidence threshold, delegating tool choices lowered success by 19.0 points. Building on these findings, we then design JevAgentHarness, which fits this threshold for each choice on the agent's own trajectories and lets the LLM decide below it. Because existing decision models never see the states an agent reaches after its own mistakes, we train AgentDecision-4B, an open 4B model, on such states with Jev's answers as labels. On tasks unlike its training data, the agent solved 91.5% of them with AgentDecision-4B and 82.0% with Jev. On tasks like their training data, 4B models trained this way made agents 81.1-89.0% cheaper and up to 2.5 times faster, without losing 3 or more points of task success. The models, data, and harness will be released at https://github.com/JevAgentHarness/JevAgentHarness.

bullets: AgentDecisionBench evaluates decision models from isolated choices to controlling running agents across public benchmarks and DecisionGym.

papers.title: JevAgentHarness: Benchmarking, Deploying and Training Decision Models That Share Control with LLMs
papers.tldr: JevAgentHarness enables agents to delegate many tool-choice decisions from LLMs to faster, cheaper decision models while preserving task success through confidence calibration and trajectory-based training.

papers.abstract: Multi-agent LLM systems rely on generative models for expert execution, workflow planning, and artifact review. Yet many coordination operations require only bounded decisions, such as selecting the next expert or judging artifact quality. Profiling three representative MAS frameworks, we find that routing and review account for 31.7-43.5% of generative-LLM tokens. However, replacing these operations with low-cost decision models introduces two interface gaps: generative planners produce execution plans and handoff instructions (planning gap), while reviewers provide actionable feedback for repairing flawed artifacts (review gap), which bounded decisions alone cannot provide. We introduce Jev-LiteMAS, a multi-agent framework that bridges both gaps by combining a lightweight decision model (Jev) with generative execution and feedback. To address the planning gap, Jev selects experts dynamically from the task and prior expert outputs, using accumulated context to ground subsequent execution without a pre-generated trajectory. To address the review gap, Jev screens intermediate artifacts against task criteria: passing artifacts proceed directly, whereas flagged ones undergo LLM re-review for acceptance or corrective feedback. Across four benchmarks and two backbones, Jev-LiteMAS reduces generative-LLM tokens by 12.7-54.6% over LAS, maintaining accuracy within 1.34 percentage points and lowering latency in seven of eight settings. Grounding routing in substantive expert outputs prevents up to 18.0 points in accuracy loss.

bullets: Routing and review consume 31.7–43.5% of generative-LLM tokens in profiled multi-agent systems.

Jev screens artifacts; only flagged results receive full LLM re-review and corrective feedback.
Across four benchmarks and two backbones, it cuts generative-LLM tokens by 12.7–54.6%, keeps accuracy within 1.34 points, and lowers latency in seven of eight settings.

papers.abstract: Multi-agent large language model (LLM) systems are increasingly deployed at the edge to support complex tasks that require collaboration and information exchange among multiple agents. However, when task contexts are passed across agents, shared context that has already been processed by upstream agents often needs to be prefilled again, resulting in substantial redundant computation. Reusing an already prefilled key--value (KV) cache can avoid this recomputation, but requires the reusable KV state to be transferred across the network before the receiving agent can begin generation. Under strict time-to-first-token (TTFT) deadlines and unreliable edge links, delivering the complete KV cache may be infeasible, making it necessary to prioritize and protect the most valuable KV information within a limited transmission budget. This paper proposes PriorityFEC, a utility-aware KV-cache handoff scheme that jointly exploits model-side KV importance and transport-side reliability. PriorityFEC first constructs a utility-aware source stream by placing high-utility KV blocks at earlier transmission positions. It then protects the ordered stream using a feedback-adaptive Streaming Forward Erasure Correction (FEC) mechanism, which schedules repair packets according to receiver feedback before the TTFT deadline. We implement PriorityFEC on a distributed edge LLM serving prototype and evaluate it with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct across multiple datasets. Results show that PriorityFEC achieves superior task quality over the compared transport schemes, with its advantages becoming particularly pronounced under stringent deadline constraints. These results demonstrate the importance of jointly optimizing KV-cache utility and deadline-aware transport reliability when reusable LLM state must be handed off across unreliable edge networks.
authors: Han Shen, Qifu Tyler Sun, Fanyang Meng, Ye Wang, Yongsheng Liang
bullets: Addresses redundant prefill computation when shared context moves between agents.
Orders KV blocks by model-side utility so the most valuable information is transmitted first.
Uses feedback-adaptive streaming FEC to schedule repairs before the receiver’s TTFT deadline.
Evaluations on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct across multiple datasets show better task quality than compared transport schemes, especially under tight deadlines.
Scope: effectiveness depends on KV-utility estimation, link reliability, and available transmission time.

papers.title: PriorityFEC: Deadline-Aware Streaming FEC for KV-Cache Handoff in Edge Multi-Agent Systems

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies commonly place a multi-billion-parameter model inside the feedback loop, repeatedly recomputing task context whenever they predict a new action chunk. Yet task understanding changes far more slowly than the robot state. We introduce Fast-VLA, which invokes a frozen 4B VLM once per episode to contextualize the instruction and initial views as fixed, multi-layer key-value task memory. During execution, a lightweight online actor fuses learned time- and arm-indexed queries with current visual and proprioceptive feedback to form action queries. These queries retrieve task context from the fixed memory and predict action chunks without re-running the foundation model. Fast-VLA achieves 92.46% and 92.40% success on RoboTwin 2.0 Clean and Randomized, and 95.95% and 79.11% on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus evaluation. Against three continually conditioned baselines on the same hardware, it reduces RoboTwin amortized policy inference time by 10.9-17.1x and requires 1.22 GiB of post-prefill online resident memory. Task-memory swaps further show that the actor relies on episode-matched task memory. These results show that task context can be established once while closed-loop control remains responsive throughout execution. Project page: https://garfield-kh.github.io/FastVLA
authors: Kehong Gong, Guanli Hou, Xiaoxu Zheng, Qi Wang, Mingxi Xu, Anbang Zhai, Xiaoyu He, Mingyuan Zhang, Michael Bi Mi
bullets: Addresses the high inference cost of repeatedly recomputing task context in VLA policies.
Stores instruction and initial-view context as fixed, multi-layer key-value task memory.
A lightweight actor combines current visual/proprioceptive feedback with learned time- and arm-indexed queries to predict action chunks.
Reports strong success across RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus, with 10.9–17.1× lower amortized RoboTwin inference time than continually conditioned baselines.
Task-memory swaps indicate that performance depends on episode-matched task context.

Figure 2: Memory-conditioned online control in Fast-VLA. A frozen VLM constructs layer-wise KV task memory from the instruction and initial views once per episode. In the online actor, query fusion combines learned queries with arm state and wrist-view CLS tokens to form action queries. The action decoder reads visual tokens from current and historical views and retrieves task context from the fixed memory. The action head predicts a 50-step bimanual action chunk.

As control passes from the left arm to the right, headcamera attention shifts from the red block to the green block. papers.abstract: Block Influence (BI) ranks Transformer blocks for depth pruning from their input-output cosine change, but the ranking depends on the calibration distribution. We study whether English calibration transfers to Indian languages in Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, Llama-3.2-1B, and Gemma-2-2B. English, Hindi, Marathi, and Tamil use disjoint Wikipedia articles for calibration and evaluation; every selector receives the same 150-chunk budget, and Tamil is excluded from multilingual aggregation to test cross-script transfer. Across all three models, late-block BI is 20.7-55.5% higher for the three Indian languages than for English, and every predeclared late-minus-middle contrast has a 95% bootstrap interval above zero. This mismatch changes the low-BI blocks selected for removal despite high global rank correlations. Averaging BI over equal English, Hindi, and Marathi budgets mitigates the resulting perplexity damage for Qwen at six removed blocks and for Gemma at all tested depths, including held-out Tamil. The mitigation is not universal: on Llama, balancing improves Hindi and Marathi at two removed blocks but severely harms Tamil, while larger pruning budgets select the same blocks and collapse perplexity regardless of calibration. Rank-mean and minimax-rank aggregators do not dominate the raw mean. These results support a diagnostic claim rather than a universal pruning rule: English-only BI systematically misses late-layer activity for Indian-language text, but multilingual calibration must still be validated per architecture and pruning budget.
bullets: BI rankings depend strongly on calibration language, despite high overall rank correlations.
Across Qwen2.5, Llama-3.2, and Gemma-2, Indian-language calibration produces higher late-block influence than English.
This shifts which low-influence blocks are selected for removal.
Equal-budget English–Hindi–Marathi averaging mitigates perplexity damage for Qwen and Gemma, including held-out Tamil in some settings.
The benefit is not universal: effects vary by architecture and pruning depth, and larger budgets can cause perplexity collapse.

papers.tldr: English-only calibration systematically underestimates late-block influence for Indian languages, while multilingual calibration can reduce pruning damage but is architecture- and budget-dependent.

papers.abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models reduce computation by routing each token to a small set of experts, but each selected expert is still used at a fixed precision. We present DPA-MoE, a runtime precision control framework that makes routed experts any-precision. DPA-MoE encodes expert feed-forward weights as prefix-decodable chunks using SharedScale AnyBCQ, profiles per-expert reconstruction residuals offline, and allocates chunks at inference time using live router gate scores. This post-routing allocation lets a single encoded MoE checkpoint operate at multiple effective weight budgets without retraining or re-encoding. Experiments on Qwen3-30B-A3B and DeepSeekMoE-16B show that DPA-MoE improves KL divergence and downstream accuracy over uniform chunk allocation at matched budgets, with modest steady-state throughput overhead in our prototype.
authors: Jaeyun Kim, Hoonki Lee, Susie Shin, Hyunmin Kim, Dahyun Lee, Sangyeob Kim
bullets: Addresses the fixed-precision limitation of routed MoE experts.
Encodes expert FFN weights into prefix-decodable SharedScale AnyBCQ chunks and profiles reconstruction residuals offline.
Allocates precision at inference time using live router gate scores and per-expert residual profiles.
Outperforms uniform chunk allocation on KL divergence and downstream accuracy at matched weight budgets.
Evaluated on Qwen3-30B-A3B and DeepSeekMoE-16B, with modest steady-state throughput overhead in the prototype.

papers.abstract: Test-time adaptation (TTA) mitigates the performance degradation of source-pretrained models on unlabeled test data under distribution shifts. Recent backpropagation-free token-purging methods address 3D point cloud distribution shifts by filtering unreliable tokens. However, their reliance on predefined purge-size candidates requires multiple forward passes per sample and increases inference cost. We propose SATOR (Sample-Adaptive TOken Routing), a source-free and backpropagation-free 3D TTA framework that eliminates this search by deriving both the partitioning threshold and routing decision directly from each sample. SATOR computes token abnormality scores from complementary attention and geometric relation graphs. It then derives a sample-specific partition into retained and pruned tokens via Otsu-based separability, without evaluating candidate sizes. Keep-ratio-calibrated routing then selects the pruned prediction only when its entropy, penalized by the keep ratio, is lower than that of the original prediction. Experiments on ModelNet40-C, ScanObjectNN-C, and ShapeNet-C demonstrate that SATOR achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on three 3D corruption benchmarks.
authors: Inseok Kong, Geunyoung Jung, Jiyoung Jung
bullets: Addresses distribution shifts in 3D point clouds without source data or backpropagation.
Computes token abnormality from attention and geometric relation graphs.
Uses Otsu-based separability to derive each sample’s retained/pruned token partition.
Routes to the pruned prediction only when keep-ratio-penalized entropy favors it.
Achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on ModelNet40-C, ScanObjectNN-C, and ShapeNet-C.

A keep-ratio-calibrated routing mechanism selects between the original and pruned token sequence predictions, accounting for the keep ratio in the routing criterion.

papers.title: SATOR: Backpropagation-Free 3D Test-Time Adaptation via Sample-Adaptive Token Routing
papers.tldr: SATOR enables efficient backpropagation-free 3D test-time adaptation by routing tokens using sample-specific decisions instead of costly purge-size searches.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) effectively transfers capabilities from a teacher to a student through feedback on student-generated rollouts. However, generating complete student rollouts and computing teacher feedback for every token make OPD computationally expensive. We introduce Stochastic Truncated On-Policy Distillation (STOPD), which accelerates OPD by randomly truncating student rollouts and correcting the resulting sampling bias with blockwise inverse-probability weighting (IPW). At each training step, we sample a stopping position for each rollout before generation and let the student generate until that position or natural termination. We obtain teacher feedback on every generated token and use blockwise IPW to compensate for the lower probability of retaining later tokens while controlling the weights. We prove that this weighting preserves Vanilla OPD's gradient sum in expectation and derive one-step update-error bounds for SGD, Adam, and Muon. We evaluate STOPD across multiple teacher-student model pairs, task domains, and optimizers. STOPD reduces generated tokens by 25-48% while maintaining accuracy comparable to Vanilla OPD, achieving 1.3-2.2x training speedups.
authors: Zhengxin Zhang, Maosen Tang, Ning Wang, Changhao Li, Jingren Zhou, Bo Dai, Sainyam Galhotra, Alex Townsend, Claire Cardie
bullets: OPD is costly because it completes student rollouts and obtains teacher feedback for every token.
STOPD samples a stopping position before generation and truncates each rollout at that point or at natural termination.
Blockwise inverse-probability weighting compensates for the reduced chance of retaining later tokens while controlling weight magnitude.
The method preserves Vanilla OPD’s gradient sum in expectation, with update-error bounds derived for SGD, Adam, and Muon.
Across multiple model pairs, domains, and optimizers, STOPD achieves 1.3–2.2× training speedups.

papers.abstract: Exact $k$-nearest-neighbor (kNN) search over image descriptors and embeddings underlies visual retrieval, near-duplicate detection, the evaluation of learned representations, and increasingly the memory of LLM agents. However, exhaustive search computes every distance at full precision, whereas approximate indexes return recall below one. We observe that exact search only needs a proof that each excluded vector cannot be a neighbor. Because such a proof only has to be conservative, it can be checked in low precision, much as the retina examines the whole scene at low resolution. We call this principle certified exclusion and realize it in an exact kNN method for GPUs, which we call \certex. Specifically, \certex\ stores a lower-bounding projection of each vector in half precision and folds a rounding certificate into the same tensor-core dot product, so that only the few vectors that the test keeps need exact distances. We prove that \certex\ returns the exact kNN of every query. On sixteen datasets with up to 100M vectors, \certex\ is exact for every query at 7.1$\times$ to 18.0$\times$ the throughput of the fastest cuVS search on one H100 and outperforms quantized and graph indexes whenever every query must be exact.
bullets: Targets exact visual retrieval, where exhaustive search is costly and approximate indexes may miss neighbors.
Stores conservative lower-bounding projections in half precision and incorporates rounding certificates into tensor-core dot products.
Computes exact distances only for vectors that pass the exclusion test.
Proves that every returned result is the exact kNN set.
Across 16 datasets with up to 100M vectors, reaches 7.1×–18.0× the throughput of the fastest cuVS search on one H100 when exactness is required.

papers.abstract: Although Graph Neural Networks are widely used in various domains, they remained mostly unexplored in computer vision. Convolutional Neural Networks and Vision Transformers were leading the field, until the quite recent introduction of Vision Graphs (ViG) that treat images as a set of nodes and apply graph convolution on their k-NN graphs. ViGs show impressive accuracy on image classification but their computational cost remains relatively high. Inspired by optimization methods for GNNs, we present CoViG, a novel approach combining graph coarsening and ViGs. Our method introduces an additional MinCUT pooling step within the Grapher component of intermediate ViG blocks. By simplifying the intermediate graphs and thus decreasing the number of nodes of specific blocks, our approach considerably reduces the computational cost of ViG during inference. We evaluated our approach on ImageNet with several ViG architectures, and we obtained accuracies equivalent to the original ViG models with only about 51\% of FLOPs.
authors: Martial Guidez, Stefan Duffner, Christophe Garcia
bullets: Vision Graphs model images as nodes connected through k-NN graphs, but their computational cost is relatively high.
CoViG adds a MinCUT pooling step within the Grapher component of intermediate ViG blocks.
Graph coarsening reduces the number of nodes processed in selected blocks.
On ImageNet across several ViG architectures, CoViG achieves comparable accuracy using about 51% of the original FLOPs.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) demand efficient inference, where the multiply-accumulate (MAC) operations in linear projections dominate compute and energy cost. Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces this cost by mapping weights and activations to low-bit integers. Power-of-Two (PoT) weight quantization promises efficient multiplier-free LLM inference via shift-add logic, but suffers significant accuracy degradation at low bitwidths due to its coarse base-2 quantization grid. We introduce Fractional PoT (FPoT), a base-$\sqrt{2}$ (half-octave) fractional PoT grid that achieves practical 4-bit weight quantization while preserving a fully integer shift-add datapath. The method combines (i) the base-$\sqrt{2}$ weight grid with uniform integer activations, (ii) a calibration-time grid-alignment refinement absorbed into the static per-channel scale, and (iii) a lightweight 1-adder $\sqrt{2}$ approximation whose error is absorbed during weight calibration via approximate-grid quantization, yielding a processing element (PE) with significantly fewer gates than a 4-bit integer multiplier. On Llama-3-8B with 4-bit weight and activation quantization, FPoT improves zero-shot commonsense reasoning performance by 8.72% relative to the PoT baseline, while maintaining performance close to the uniform integer baseline, with only a negligible 0.4%p degradation. These results hold across various configurations spanning seven models and three bit-widths. Furthermore, FPoT can be integrated with state-of-the-art LLM PTQ methods, demonstrating framework-agnostic applicability.
authors: Sunghyun Wee, Geunjae Choi, Hyeonjin Kim, Suyoung Kim, Nojun Kwak
bullets: Addresses the coarse base-2 grid of Power-of-Two quantization, which causes severe low-bit accuracy degradation.
Uses a base-√2 weight grid, uniform integer activations, calibration-based grid alignment, and approximate-grid quantization.
Implements √2 with a lightweight one-adder approximation, producing a processing element with fewer gates than a 4-bit multiplier.
On Llama-3-8B, improves zero-shot commonsense reasoning by 8.72% relative to PoT and remains within 0.4 percentage points of the uniform integer baseline.
Generalizes across seven models, three bit-widths, and existing LLM post-training quantization frameworks.

papers.abstract: Point-cloud streams are central to autonomous driving and robotics, yet existing segmentation networks process every frame from scratch, although consecutive frames largely overlap. We observe that the intermediate features of point-cloud transformers remain semantically consistent across frames for the same spatial region, especially in deep stages. Building on this, we present SpaceCache, a training-free feature cache that reuses these features across frames. Tokens of previously observed regions skip a sequence of transformer blocks and take their cached features, only the remaining tokens are computed, and the full token layout is restored for dense prediction. Lightweight cache management keeps reused features reliable by limiting each entry's age and evicting low-confidence entries. Unlike token merging, SpaceCache selects tokens at negligible cost and runs its cache operations once per encoder stage. On both outdoor and indoor benchmarks, such as nuScenes, Waymo, and ScanNet, with two transformer backbones of Utonia and LitePT-B, SpaceCache achieves up to 1.65x speedup with less than 1-point mIoU drop and consistently outperforms token-merging methods.
authors: Dongheon Yang, Beomseok Kang, Jae-Joon Kim
bullets: Addresses redundant frame-by-frame processing caused by substantial overlap in consecutive point-cloud streams.
Uses a training-free cache to let previously observed tokens skip transformer blocks while computing only new or changed tokens.
Maintains reliability by limiting cache-entry age and evicting low-confidence features; cache operations run once per encoder stage.
Evaluated on nuScenes, Waymo, and ScanNet with Utonia and LitePT-B backbones.
Achieves up to 1.65× speedup with less than a 1-point mIoU drop and consistently outperforms token-merging methods.
