papers.abstract: Synchronous data-parallel training usually assigns every rank the same number of records, even when record costs vary by orders of magnitude. For variable-length models, this converts input variation into idle time because each step waits for its most expensive rank-local batch. We present Batch Cost Lookahead (BCL), a coordination-free data-loading policy that buffers a bounded rank-local window and repartitions it into fixed-cardinality packs with balanced estimated cost. BCL preserves the trainer's record-count contract and requires neither cross-rank metadata exchange nor runtime modification. In simulation over public workload distributions, enabling BCL reduces per-rank estimated batch-cost variability by up to 82.8%. Across 13 NeMo-RL SFT corpora on eight H200 GPUs, rank-local BCL runs 1.050 to 1.167 times faster than pooled MFFD. Compiled H200 measurements on an internal sequence workload show speedups of 1.197 to 1.343 times over packed execution from one to four nodes. We also identify a memory-feasibility boundary: a p99 cap for high-variance or OOM-prone data bounds outliers before BCL balances the rest. These results show that substantial variable-cost imbalance can be removed at the data-loader boundary, while clarifying when data preparation or broader coordination is still necessary.
authors: Tao Huang, Chen Zhu, Antonio Alonso, Daming Li, Adarsh Goura, Jaideep Ray, Yitong Zhou
bullets: Variable-length records can leave ranks idle because each step waits for the most expensive local batch.
BCL buffers a bounded local window and repartitions it into fixed-size packs with balanced estimated cost.
It preserves record-count requirements and operates entirely at the data-loader boundary.
Simulations reduce estimated per-rank batch-cost variability by up to 82.8%; experiments report faster execution across public and internal workloads.
A p99 memory cap is needed for extreme or OOM-prone outliers, and some cases still require data preparation or broader coordination.

papers.abstract: Dual-system vision-language-action (VLA) models pair a high-frequency fast policy with a slow, expensive module, and published trigger mechanisms for invoking it lack a shared objective, measured costs, and any standard separating schedule quality from module quality. We provide the missing account: invocation is formalized as a calibrated decision problem whose fixed-ratio, fixed-budget, and history-gated schedules are degenerate cases of one quantity, the Value of Intervention (VoI); a renewal baseline proves the optimal schedule periodic under state-independent collapse, with adaptive gains governed by the cost ratio $\rho$ and the dispersion of collapse. Measured systems span three orders of magnitude in $\rho$ (FiS-VLA $0.95$; RoboICL about $10^3$), and a direct test confirms the low-$\rho$ prediction: calibrated gains vanish under homogeneous collapse and grow with heterogeneity. Fourteen closed-loop arms on LIBERO test the contested middle of the continuum ($\rho=1.53$): the adaptive trigger allocates its queries exactly as the threshold rule predicts, yet the language-rewrite channel cannot convert them into success on either suite, and a revert actuator that undoes a failed rewrite is the only intervention with zero net downside on both LIBERO-Spatial and LIBERO-Goal, where the rewrite deficit deepens from thirteen to forty-two points. A four-measure leak-free protocol cuts apparent early-warning AUC from $0.93$ to $0.62$ on $929$ deployment traces, a detection-limited frontier theorem converts detection quality into a schedulability statement, and a compilation loop turns measured value functions into per-task refresh periods within $2.4\%$ of the closed-loop oracle. Together these results turn slow-module invocation from a design opinion into a measured decision.
authors: Shilin Zhang (North China University of Technology)
bullets: Unifies fixed-ratio, fixed-budget, and history-gated triggers as special cases of Value of Intervention; periodic scheduling is optimal when collapse is state-independent.
Adaptive scheduling benefits depend on intervention cost relative to fast-policy operation and on heterogeneity in policy collapse.
At intermediate cost (ρ=1.53), the adaptive trigger follows its predicted threshold, but language rewrites fail to improve either LIBERO suite; only reverting failed rewrites avoids net downside.
A leak-free evaluation protocol reduces apparent early-warning AUC from 0.93 to 0.62 across 929 deployment traces.
A detection-limited theorem and compilation loop connect measured intervention value to schedulability and produce refresh periods within 2.4% of a closed-loop oracle.

(c) The standard: a four-measure leak-free protocol and a distillation loop that compiles the measured staleness value function into per-task refresh periods.

papers.abstract: Spoken Dialogue Models (SDMs) typically share a speech-token space for generation and synthesis, leading to long autoregressive sequences and costly inference. Lower-rate speech tokenizers shorten sequences but may introduce compression-quality trade-offs and costly replacement without breaking this coupling. To address this limitation, we propose CoSTA, a compatibility-preserving post-hoc framework that decouples generation and synthesis token spaces while retaining the original speech tokenizer and decoder. CoSTA extends the generation token space with compressed representations via mean-initialized vocabulary extension, pronunciation adaptation, and dialogue adaptation, followed by deterministic expansion back to the original speech-token space before synthesis. On bilingual speech-dialogue benchmarks, CoSTA achieves approximately $1.7\times$ expanded speech-token generation speed, lower full-response latency, and higher throughput while preserving response quality. Analyses show more sustained interaction under limited budgets and a practical trade-off among compression, decoding efficiency, and quality. Further experiments demonstrate cross-architecture transfer and complementarity to low-rate tokenization.
authors: Yingzhuo Deng, Chong Li, Bingxin Liu, Yi Shu, Tianyu Peng, Can Xie, Siyao Song, Shuo Ren, Jiajun Zhang
bullets: Addresses long autoregressive sequences and costly inference caused by tightly coupled generation and synthesis token spaces.
Decouples the token spaces while retaining the original speech tokenizer and decoder.
Uses vocabulary extension, pronunciation adaptation, and dialogue adaptation, then deterministically expands compressed tokens before synthesis.
Reports approximately 1.7× faster expanded speech-token generation, lower full-response latency, and higher throughput on bilingual benchmarks.
Supports sustained interaction under limited budgets, transfers across architectures, and complements low-rate tokenization.

It also outperforms matched Vanilla-FT at every tested setting, with at most 0.68 GiB additional peak memory. These workload-level results show that CoSTA’s modelside efficiency gains translate into system-level improvements in latency and throughput with minimal memory overhead.

papers.abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) dominate video generation but suffer from high inference cost due to the quadratic complexity of self-attention. Sparse attention mitigates this by skipping unnecessary computation in the attention matrix, but existing methods apply a fixed sparsity ratio throughout denoising and struggle to accurately determine which computations to skip. To address these limitations, we analyze attention dynamics through attention entropy and mean attention distance, and find that attention becomes increasingly concentrated across denoising steps. We further observe that blocks selected early continue to capture a large fraction of the total attention weight at later steps. These findings suggest two acceleration opportunities: the sparsity ratio should grow as denoising progresses, and earlier search results can be reused to reduce the search space. Based on these findings, we propose Growing Sparsity and Reduced Search (GSRS), a training-free framework that retains more computation early and progressively reduces it later, while restricting subsequent searches to an early candidate set to reduce search overhead. GSRS adopts Top-p selection for adaptive sparsity control, supported by a precise evaluation scheme that computes exact attention weights within the FlashAttention computation at negligible overhead. Experiments on HunyuanVideo and Wan 2.1 validate that GSRS achieves 1.55$\times$--2.21$\times$ speedup while maintaining generation quality comparable to full attention.
authors: Yun Dai, Yuyun Chen, Jiarui Wen, Huiping Zhuang, Cen Chen, Ziqian Zeng
bullets: Video DiTs are slowed by quadratic self-attention, while fixed-sparsity methods poorly reflect changing attention patterns during denoising.
Attention becomes increasingly concentrated over denoising steps, and early-selected blocks retain much of the later attention weight.
GSRS is training-free: it keeps more computation early, reduces it progressively, and restricts later searches to an early candidate set.
Top-p selection provides adaptive sparsity, with exact attention-weight evaluation integrated into FlashAttention at negligible overhead.
Validated on HunyuanVideo and Wan 2.1, GSRS delivers 1.55×–2.21× speedup while maintaining quality comparable to full attention.

papers.abstract: Sparse KV compression reduces long-context inference costs by retaining selected historical states, yet these states typically keep their coordinates from the full history. Under Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE), gaps left by evicted tokens continue to affect query-key matching, potentially limiting the use of retained evidence. We study post-selection positional geometry on a fixed selector-produced cache, examining how positional organization affects the use of retained information and which coordinate and continuation rules improve answer quality. To reorganize this geometry, we propose RoPERelay, which assigns compact, order-preserving RoPE coordinates, relocates cached key phases through inverse rotation and re-rotation, and synchronizes the current query and subsequent generation. It reuses existing K/V without renewed selection, historical re-prefill, or additional cache budget. Across 36 comparisons spanning two models, six sparse selectors, and three long-term memory tasks, RoPERelay improves answer quality in 32 cases. For Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct with BM25 on LongMemEval-S, accuracy increases from 23.6% to 35.4%. Measured complete-request time overhead is approximately 1%-3% in the evaluated configurations. These findings establish positional organization as a distinct optimization dimension for sparse KV caches after content selection.
bullets: Sparse KV caches retain selected states, but gaps from evicted tokens can distort RoPE query–key matching.
The method assigns compact, order-preserving coordinates and relocates cached key phases while synchronizing queries and generation.
It operates on a fixed selector-produced cache without renewed selection or historical re-prefill.
Across 36 comparisons, answer quality improved in 32 cases; one reported result rose from 23.6% to 35.4%.
Measured complete-request overhead was approximately 1%–3% in the evaluated configurations.

papers.abstract: Peer review is under strain from the growth of submissions, and review comments written by humans or AI can misstate what a paper says. We introduce ReviewFact, a benchmark that labels such factual errors in review comments under one definition across NLP, machine learning, and the natural sciences, and that measures cost and latency alongside accuracy. A frontier LLM checks comments well but must read the whole paper for each check, while cheap decision models, which score whether a statement holds in a text, fall far short on whole comments that mix several implicit assertions. PremiseCheck is a framework that combines the two. An LLM rewrites each comment as explicit premises without reading the paper, and a decision model checks each premise against the paper. When each comment is checked on its own, PremiseCheck reaches accuracy comparable to GPT-5.5 across all three fields at about half its cost, and on NLP reviews at a quarter of its cost and less than half its latency.
authors: Dingjie Song, Zhiling Yan, Ziqian Zhang, Yuxuan Zhang, Lichao Sun
bullets: ReviewFact benchmarks factual errors in peer-review comments across NLP, machine learning, and natural sciences, while measuring accuracy, cost, and latency.
Whole-comment checking by cheap decision models performs poorly because comments may contain multiple implicit assertions.
PremiseCheck uses an LLM to extract explicit premises without reading the paper, then applies a decision model to verify each premise against the paper.
It achieves accuracy comparable to GPT-5.5 across three fields at roughly half the cost; for NLP reviews, it uses about one-quarter the cost and less than half the latency.
The framework is evaluated on comments checked independently; its scope beyond this setting is not established by the abstract.

papers.abstract: Reasoning-conditioned embeddings can improve retrieval by progressively refining semantic constraints. However, additional reasoning may introduce over-generalized or semantically noisy abstractions that weaken retrieval specificity. Existing methods largely supervise reasoning through final retrieval outcomes, providing limited guidance over the refinement process itself. We propose AURA, a framework that directly supervises intermediate reasoning states according to how well they separate relevant documents from hard distractors. AURA further trains a lightweight utility estimator over prefix-conditioned embeddings to adapt reasoning depth at inference time. On the reasoning-intensive BRIGHT benchmark, AURA-4B achieves 34.7 average nDCG@10 while using 2.8 reasoning steps and 96 generated tokens per query. Under matched deployment conditions, adaptive stopping reduces latency from 4.6 to 0.76 seconds relative to full-trajectory reasoning. Results on MS MARCO further suggest that this specialization need not substantially degrade conventional in-domain retrieval.
authors: Yingtao Luo, Kangyi Zhao, Shiyi Du, Yubo Li
bullets: Reasoning-conditioned embeddings can sharpen retrieval but may become noisy or overly general with additional steps.
AURA supervises intermediate reasoning states by their ability to distinguish relevant documents from hard distractors.
A lightweight utility estimator selects reasoning depth at inference time using prefix-conditioned embeddings.
On BRIGHT, AURA-4B reaches 34.7 average nDCG@10 with 2.8 reasoning steps and 96 generated tokens per query.
Adaptive stopping reduces latency from 4.6 to 0.76 seconds versus full-trajectory reasoning; MS MARCO results suggest limited impact on conventional retrieval.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of AURA. Training: A warm-up stage first establishes a retrieval-oriented embedding space. Specificity labels are then constructed from the warmed-up model, the utility estimator is trained on frozen embeddings, and utility-aware weighting is enabled for subsequent joint optimization. Inference: The utility estimator evaluates each state online and terminates reasoning according to the predicted utility, returning the selected embedding for retrieval.

Figure 2: Motivation behind AURA. Existing methods supervise only the final retrieval outcome, while AURA identifies the peak-utility reasoning state before overreasoning weakens retrieval specificity.

Figure 4: Inference-time scaling of AURA on BRIGHT. Greedy selects the best continuation at each step using utility estimator; best-of-k samples k full trajectories and selects the one with highest estimated utility.

papers.abstract: Data selection reallocates training support across visual concepts, including objects, attributes, color, texture, and backgrounds. Different allocation strategies may produce varied downstream model behavior, especially for tail concepts supported by only a few samples. Discarding them can hurt test-time robustness, while overemphasizing samples lying on category boundaries may introduce unstable training signals. This work explicitly investigates this relationship across fine-grained, spurious-correlation, and general image classification, as well as multimodal pretraining. Specifically, we use sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to extract concept activations from individual images. During selection, we accumulate the dataset-level concept support for each added sample. Applying diminishing returns to this distribution down-weights well-represented concepts and shifts the focus to the distribution tail. We then incorporate local support to find samples that reliably strengthen under-supported concepts. Empirical results show consistent improvements over strong data selection baselines across all benchmarks. We also reveal the connection between concepts our method enhances and the induced behavioral changes, including improved robustness against out-of-distribution and spurious contexts. This work establishes concept support, beyond individual sample importance, as a useful principle for data-efficient and robust learning.
authors: Ziheng Zhang, Neha Hulkund, Colin Lee, Zheda Mai, Hui Shen, Ying Ding, Tanya Berger-Wolf, Sara Beery, Wei-Lun Chao, Jianyang Gu
bullets: Data selection can neglect tail concepts or overemphasize category-boundary samples, harming robustness and training stability.
Sparse autoencoders extract visual concept activations from individual images.
A diminishing-returns objective down-weights well-supported concepts and shifts selection toward the concept-support tail.
Local support helps identify samples that reliably strengthen under-supported concepts.
The method consistently outperforms strong selection baselines across classification and multimodal pretraining benchmarks, with improved robustness to out-of-distribution and spurious contexts.

We then use local support to locate samples that contribute to filling the distributional gap together with their neighbors. The resulting objective favors candidates representing under-supported evidence with local support over redundant head concepts or isolated rare regions.

papers.abstract: Diffusion models are notoriously expensive to train, requiring large-scale datasets to learn how to gradually reverse the noise from images over multiple small denoising steps. Current approaches focus on distilling the number of diffusion steps, neglecting potential redundancies of the training data. In this paper, we explore the potential of harnessing eigensamples to train diffusion models on significantly smaller datasets, while preserving model performance. To mitigate the sensitivity to affine transformations of eigenimages, we harness the latent space of a pre-trained CLIP model. We next compute latent eigenvectors by performing principal component analysis (PCA) in CLIP space. Further, we employ eigenvectors as reference points to guide the selection of a representative training set comprising comprising both exemplars (images whose embeddings are closest to eigenvectors) and diverse images. Our comprehensive experiments with different diffusion models applied on multiple datasets indicate that our approach (EigDiff) can reduce training data by up to 14x and accelerate subset selection by up to 1607x, with marginal performance differences.
authors: Andrei Jarca, Vlad Hondru, Florinel-Alin Croitoru, Radu Tudor Ionescu
bullets: Targets redundancy in diffusion-model training data, complementing methods that reduce denoising steps.
Computes PCA eigenvectors in the latent space of a pretrained CLIP model to identify representative samples.
Builds subsets from exemplars closest to eigenvectors plus additional diverse images.
Experiments across multiple diffusion models and datasets reduce training data by up to 14× and accelerate subset selection by up to 1607×.
Reports only marginal performance differences, though results are scoped to the evaluated models and datasets.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of EigDiff (eigen-guided data selection). Preference image pairs are CLIP-encoded into embeddings, on which PCA yields the principal (eigen) components. The figure illustrates the near to far spread. Stage 2 stratifies the full remaining score range via diversity quantiles. Best viewed in color.

papers.selection_reason: Data-efficient diffusion training via CLIP-space eigensample subset selection; directly targets reducing training cost and subset-selection overhead.
papers.title: EigDiff: Eigensample Diffusion - or how to significantly reduce training dataset size with marginal performance variation?

papers.abstract: Compiler transformations interact, making GPU kernel optimization a search for combinations that preserve the computation while improving performance. We introduce HOW TO TRAIN YOUR LITTLE DRAGON, a training method that teaches a small language model both to construct complete optimization scripts and to improve existing ones. Instead of ranking candidates or generating kernel code, our model generates optimization scripts. We devise a compact, lossless representation whose deterministic decoding reconstructs the exact compiler trace, preserving its transformation parameters and dependencies. We use a compiler framework TVM MetaSchedule to build training data on 54,116 distinct workloads, and construct 108,594 examples in two training sets: 60,236 teach the model to generate an optimized script from an unoptimized kernel, while 48,358 teach it to produce a better script given the kernel and a somewhat optimized script. Supervised fine-tuning teaches the model to construct and improve optimization scripts from these search-derived examples. We then add reinforcement learning with a shaped reward that combines correctness with measured performance, awarding a latency-based bonus only to numerically correct kernels. We apply this training method to a model with 8 billion parameters. After supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, the model achieves per-attempt correctness of 91.27% for construction and 92.01% for refinement, while reinforcement learning produces faster kernels than supervised training on 88 of 102 construction tasks and 145 of 170 refinement prompts. With only 8B parameters, our LITTLE DRAGON achieves higher per-attempt correctness and better kernel performance than six frontier LLMs: GPT-6 Astra, Opus 5, Kimi-K3, and GLM-5.3 among them, each with hundreds of billions to trillions of parameters, for which task-specific training is unavailable or expensive.
authors: Annabelle Sujun Tang, Wei Tang, Songyao Jiang, Tianhui Li, Shengzhe Xu, Jiin Woo, Kaan Ozkara, Youngsuk Park, Zhen Jia, Hadi Esmaeilzadeh
bullets: Targets compiler-transformation search by generating optimization scripts rather than kernel code or candidate rankings.
Uses a compact lossless representation that deterministically reconstructs exact compiler traces, including parameters and dependencies.
Trains on 108,594 search-derived examples from 54,116 workloads using TVM MetaSchedule.
Combines supervised fine-tuning with correctness-aware, latency-based reinforcement learning.

Reinforcement learning improves kernel speed over supervised training on most evaluated construction and refinement tasks; the 8B model outperforms six much larger frontier LLMs in reported correctness and kernel performance.

Static and round-trip checks admit construction and refinement labels. papers.abstract: Occupancy predictors rely on large persistent banks of Gaussians or learned queries whose size is fixed by hand. Common pruning proxies, such as opacity, activation frequency, or parameter magnitude, do not measure whether removing a row changes the model's voxel decisions. We introduce Decision-FLIP, a budget-free compilation framework whose scoring and structure selection need only unlabeled calibration inputs. Exact Mean-FLIP scores each persistent row by the number of voxel argmax decisions that change when the row is removed from the readout; a guarded Otsu split of the log-score distribution selects the survivor count without a target and abstains when the split is unsupported; and the survivors are physically compiled into a smaller checkpoint, so camera sampling, attention, and aggregation shrink with the bank. For streaming banks, scores are integrated over each row's lifecycle through warp, death, and refill. Across four Gaussian-bank model-dataset settings and one persistent-query transfer, the automatically selected cuts remove 12-79% of eligible rows and cut bank/query-dependent latency by 7-45% across settings with component profiles, with whole-model savings of up to 8.0% on the primary endpoints bounded by fixed-cost image, voxel, and sensor modules and peak-memory savings of up to 16.6%. Under matched one-epoch recovery controls, semantic mIoU changes by at most 0.18 point. Same-$K$ controls show that the ranking, not only the bank size, matters: random removal collapses GaussianFormer-1 and OccFormer, while label-free Mean-FLIP matches or outperforms supervised Taylor ranking on all five settings where that control was run. The method applies when removable primitives keep a stable checkpoint-row identity; it is budget-free in survivor count, not parameter-free.
authors: Jingxing Li, Anurag Paul, Subhasis Das, Cindy Xu
bullets: Scores each persistent row by how many voxel argmax decisions change when it is removed, rather than using opacity, activation, or parameter magnitude.
A guarded Otsu split selects survivors automatically and abstains when the score distribution does not support a reliable split.
Across five model–dataset settings, it removes 12–79% of eligible rows, reducing bank/query-dependent latency by 7–45% and peak memory by up to 16.6%.
With matched one-epoch recovery, semantic mIoU changes by at most 0.18 point; ranking quality matters, as random removal can collapse models.
Applies to removable primitives with stable checkpoint-row identities; it is budget-free in survivor count, not parameter-free.

papers.abstract: Speculative decoding pairs a cheap drafter with parallel verification against the target. At ultra-long context it stops paying, because a drafter that attends over the full prefix inherits the target's context-dependent cost, so the speedup it was meant to provide first erodes and then reverses. The standard response is to build a long-context drafter, by training or fine-tuning one, or by using a multi-token-prediction head shipped inside the target checkpoint. We argue this is unnecessary, because the drafters in use are target-conditioned, reading hidden states the target computed over the entire prefix, so distant context already reaches them without their own attention, and verification corrects what they miss. We therefore freeze released short-context drafters and run them far past their training length under two inference-time mechanisms, one bounding the attention cache they see, which fixes their cost, and one re-basing their rotary position indices into the trained range. No weight is touched and the only tunable saturates early, so one vLLM-side configuration spans 4k to two million tokens, costing at most 0.16x of speedup at short length. We prove when a common index shift leaves the drafter's computation exactly unchanged, and decompose acceptance into two measurable gaps with sharp bounds. Whatever speedup a frozen drafter delivers at short context, it retains out to two million tokens, across three target-drafter pairs and five corpora. The claim concerns the flatness rather than the multiple, and removing either mechanism eliminates it. The gain is conditional on the speculative cost per emitted token staying below the matched target-only cost.
authors: Aref Jafari, Vansh Bhatia, Matt Qin, Subhajit Dutta Chowdhury, Ben Lee, Vikram Appia, Ali Ghodsi, Mehdi Rezagholizadeh
bullets: Long-context drafting becomes uneconomical when the drafter attends over the full prefix.
The approach freezes existing drafters and uses bounded attention-cache visibility plus rotary-position re-basing, with no weight updates.
A single vLLM-side configuration covers 4k–2M-token contexts; tuning saturates early and costs at most 0.16× short-context speedup.
Across three target–drafter pairs and five corpora, the drafter retains its short-context speedup up to two million tokens.
The result concerns stable speedup rather than its absolute magnitude and depends on speculative decoding remaining cheaper per emitted token than target-only decoding.

papers.title: Long-Context Drafting Does Not Require Long-Context Drafters
papers.tldr: Frozen short-context drafters can support speculative decoding at up to two-million-token contexts when inference-time cache and position handling prevent their cost from growing with context length.

papers.abstract: We investigate whether per-layer, per-task-phase (prompt/reasoning/response) expert-routing statistics in a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language model can guide layer-wise mixed-precision quantization of routed-expert FFN tensors (down/gate and up). To attain layerwise routing statistics, we build a routing-capture and profiling pipeline for Qwen-3.6-35B-A3B in ik_llama.cpp, derive a composite sensitivity score from routing entropy/decisiveness, coefficient of variation (CV), Jaccard/phase-fragility, and top-1 expert strength, and use coordinate descent to tune a layer allocation that respects a fixed average bits-per-weight budget. Notably, the profiling pipeline is applicable to standard top-k MoE architectures. Across independent experimental conditions (about 4.0 bpw flat, about 2.7 bpw steep, and about 2.7 bpw random allocation as a control), reallocation fails to outperform the uniform baseline within each quality tier. In the flat regime, reallocation is statistically neutral (z about 0.9). For the steep tier, the random reallocation performs within 1 SE of the routing-guided reallocation at the same tier, indicating a structural loss at this quality rung caused by mandatory downgrades and Kullback-Leibler Divergence (KLD) tail injection. This aggressive-budget condition shows a decisive loss (z greater than 4 SE) replicated across three independent weight vectors. We argue that the deeper issue is that routing-behavior statistics are an unvalidated proxy for true per-layer quantization cost.
bullets: The study tests whether routing entropy, decisiveness, variability, phase fragility, and top-1 expert strength can guide layer-wise bit allocation.
A routing-capture pipeline profiles Qwen-3.6-35B-A3B in ik_llama.cpp and uses coordinate descent under fixed average bit budgets.
Routing-guided reallocation does not outperform uniform allocation in the tested quality tiers; at the flatter budget it is statistically neutral.
At the aggressive budget, mandatory downgrades and KLD-tail injection cause a replicated quality loss, while random reallocation performs similarly to routing-guided allocation.
The results suggest routing behavior is an unvalidated proxy for true per-layer quantization cost.

papers.selection_reason: Quantization sensitivity analysis for efficient MoE LLM inference.
papers.title: Task-Phase-Conditioned Expert Routing Is Not a Reliable Proxy for Quantization Sensitivity in MoE FFN Tensors
papers.tldr: Routing statistics by task phase do not reliably identify which MoE expert FFN layers are most sensitive to mixed-precision quantization.

papers.abstract: Automating organizational work means answering many small typed questions about one piece of state (does this email need a reply, how urgent is it, who owns it) with probabilities good enough to act on without a human. The open typed-decision model we compare against, like a standard cross-encoder, answers each question with a separate pass over the input. We present Verdict-MQ, an open encoder that reads a case once and answers all of its questions: given identical retained state tokens after truncation (verified on every reported case), a structured attention mask makes the state encoding independent of the questions, keeps questions from influencing each other, and makes option order irrelevant by construction. On the typed-decisions benchmark, a 395M Verdict-MQ matches the soft gold labels significantly better than the released 421M Laya specialist on all five fresh seeds (KL 0.080 vs 0.117, Brier 0.045 vs 0.061), an advantage that survives per-system temperature scaling; its higher accuracy (0.801 vs 0.767) lies past the benchmark's own saturation point, so we read that margin as closer agreement with the benchmark's labelling teacher. On RACE, BoolQ and MultiRC, against a matched fine-tuned baseline it wins on MultiRC and loses on RACE and on BoolQ, where its training is unstable; we measure zero-shot references ourselves, including a closed general system (Jev) that beats every fine-tuned encoder. A controlled comparison measures what the shared state costs: giving each question its own question-aware copy of the state gains 0.9-3.5 points on RACE and MultiRC at 1.4-2.5x the per-case latency, and nothing measurable on typed decisions, with the invariance guarantees unchanged.
bullets: Structured attention makes state encoding independent of questions, prevents question interaction, and makes option order irrelevant.
On the typed-decisions benchmark, the 395M model beats the released 421M specialist on soft-label agreement and accuracy across five seeds.
Against a matched fine-tuned baseline, it wins on MultiRC but loses on RACE and BoolQ, where training is unstable.
Question-specific state copies improve RACE and MultiRC by 0.9–3.5 points at 1.4–2.5× latency, but show no measurable benefit on typed decisions.
The study also reports zero-shot references, including a closed general system that outperforms all fine-tuned encoders.

papers.selection_reason: Structured attention mask enables shared state encoding across many questions, reducing per-case latency.
papers.title: Verdict: Encode Once, Decide Many
papers.tldr: Verdict-MQ encodes each case once to answer many typed questions, improving typed-decision calibration and accuracy while trading some performance for lower repeated-processing cost on standard QA tasks.

papers.abstract: Calibrating a conformal prediction set at each early exit does not preserve coverage once a data-dependent exit is selected. We construct one terminal path score from prefix maxima, calibrate a single split-conformal quantile, and return nested prefix sets that all contain the valid terminal set. The guarantee is selection-safe without an alpha/L correction and holds simultaneously for every post-calibration label-free stopping policy that preserves terminal-set containment. We also bound the efficiency cost of the path maximum by the empirical tail of the early-over-terminal score excess. Across eight encoder task-backbone cells, pathwise selection attains macro coverage 0.901 versus 0.814 for naive layerwise selection, with average set size 1.41 and latency fraction 0.71. On CIFAR-100 with a 24-exit ViT-L/16 (n_cal=500), first-eligible stopping at budget b=4 attains coverage 0.902, set size 2.76, and latency fraction 0.57, and the same calibration supports deployment-time budget changes without refitting. In a joint exit-count/calibration-size sweep at n=100, pathwise set size moves only from 3.02 to 3.11 as exits increase from 4 to 24, while Bonferroni degenerates to the full label space for 12 or more exits. Paired comparison against MinSE valid selection at (n,L)=(100,24) gives a set-size difference of 0.80 [0.47, 1.13]. Full-vocabulary decoder experiments remain a negative boundary, with sets of 7,162-9,620 tokens. Pathwise calibration is most useful when candidate exits are many relative to calibration size, when budgets change after calibration, and when shallow heads return actionable sets.
authors: Adria Binte Habib, Ibne Farabi Shihab
bullets: Naive layerwise calibration loses coverage after data-dependent exit selection; pathwise calibration attains macro coverage 0.901 versus 0.814.
One split-conformal quantile yields nested prefix sets that contain the valid terminal set, supporting any post-calibration label-free stopping policy preserving containment.
Across eight task-backbone cells, average set size was 1.41 with latency fraction 0.71; on CIFAR-100, budget-4 stopping achieved coverage 0.902, set size 2.76, and latency fraction 0.57.
Pathwise calibration remained stable as exits increased from 4 to 24, while Bonferroni became degenerate at 12 or more exits; deployment budgets can change without refitting.
The approach is less effective for full-vocabulary decoding, producing sets of 7,162–9,620 tokens, and is most useful with many exits, limited calibration data, or actionable shallow-head sets.

papers.selection_reason: Conformal early-exit calibration for latency-efficient inference.
papers.title: Selection-Safe Conformal Early Exit: Distribution-Free Coverage under Adaptive Depth
papers.tldr: A prefix-max pathwise conformal score preserves distribution-free coverage under adaptive early-exit selection without alpha/L correction, while keeping prediction sets efficient across changing budgets.

papers.abstract: Multi-head latent attention (MLA) compresses the content of a key-value cache into a shared latent per token, making low-bit storage attractive for long-context inference. At two bits, errors in this representation perturb both attention matching and value readout, with effects that depend on error direction and reconstruction scale. We introduce RoLaQ (Rotation-calibrated Latent Quantization), an offline method for joint rotation and range calibration. RoLaQ refines a shared rotation within subspaces defined by the frozen key and value projections, and jointly learns quantization ranges whose thresholds and reconstruction gains are coupled to control the shared signal's response. Prediction matching and attention-output supervision guide calibration with model weights frozen. Across three MLA models and six benchmarks, RoLaQ achieves the highest average accuracy among the compared 2-bit methods both without and with token protection. On DeepSeek-V2-Lite, an SGLang implementation provides 3.96 times the BF16 KV capacity under the same memory budget and 2.51 times its decode throughput with 256K input tokens.
authors: Shiyu Ji, Peng Ling, Chen Lin, Shupeng Li, Yixuan Wang, Qingfu Zhu, Wanxiang Che
bullets: Targets errors in 2-bit MLA KV caches that affect both attention matching and value reconstruction.
Uses offline calibration with a learned shared rotation and coupled quantization thresholds and reconstruction gains.
Supervises calibration through prediction matching and attention-output matching while keeping model weights frozen.
Achieves the highest average accuracy among compared 2-bit methods across three MLA models and six benchmarks.
On DeepSeek-V2-Lite, delivers 3.96× BF16 KV capacity and 2.51× decode throughput at 256K-token inputs in SGLang.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces rotation and range calibration for 2-bit KV cache quantization in MLA, directly targeting memory-efficient long-context inference.
papers.title: RoLaQ: Joint Rotation and Range Calibration for 2-Bit KV Caches in Multi-Head Latent Attention
papers.tldr: RoLaQ improves 2-bit KV-cache quantization for multi-head latent attention by jointly calibrating rotations and quantization ranges, enabling higher accuracy and greater long-context capacity.

papers.abstract: We expand the exponential kernel of attention into a truncated Taylor series of $n$ terms and factorize each term into a tensor-power inner product, which collapses the causal history into exactly $n$ recurrent states, each updated by one rank-one outer product per token and independent of context length $N$. The recursion is lossless with respect to the truncated kernel ($2.2 \times 10^{-16}$ in float64), and the states are additive across chunks ($5.7 \times 10^{-14}$), so prefill admits a parallel scan. Measured exponents are $t \propto N^{2.28}$ for softmax against $N^{0.91}$ for states, with a crossover at $N \approx 728$ and $20.8\times$ at $N = 8192$; per-token decoding latency is constant at $7.3\,\mu$s against $N^{1.04}$ for softmax, giving $76.0\times$ at $N = 65536$. Accuracy improves exponentially in $n$ while cost grows combinatorially, since the $m$-th state is $\binom{d+m-1}{m}$ wide---a bound confirmed by SVD---so the optimum is second order, $n = 3$, at $6.5 \times 10^{-4}$ error and $9{,}945$ elements per head. Query and key normalization is a prerequisite: without it the argument exceeds the convergence radius and adding terms stops helping.
bullets: Approximates the exponential attention kernel with n Taylor terms and tensor-power factorization.
Maintains exactly n recurrent states using one rank-one outer-product update per token, independent of context length.
States combine additively across chunks, enabling parallel-scan prefill and constant per-token decoding latency.
The method scales more favorably than softmax attention for long contexts, with reported speedups up to 20.8× in prefill and 76.0× in decoding.
State width grows combinatorially with order; second order (n = 3) is identified as optimal, while query/key normalization is required for convergence.

papers.selection_reason: Linear-time attention via Taylor expansion with fixed recurrent states.
papers.title: Expanding Attention: A Taylor-Series Route to Linear-Time Transformers with a Fixed Number of Recurrent States
papers.tldr: A truncated Taylor expansion replaces softmax attention with a fixed number of recurrent states, enabling linear-time sequence processing while exposing a cost–accuracy trade-off.

papers.abstract: Sampling from continuous flow-based generators such as flow matching models requires numerical ODE or SDE integration, making inference cost depend on the number of function evaluations (NFEs). In practice, the sampling budget is inherited from prior work or selected through expensive FID-versus-NFE sweeps, using FID to assess image-generation quality, requiring sample generation and evaluation at multiple budgets. This makes sampling-budget selection dependent on repeated empirical evaluation. We therefore ask a complementary question to solver design and timestep allocation: for a fixed pretrained model and solver, what numerical resolution is sufficient? We introduce FLOWBUDGET, a training-free estimator of solver-relative sampling complexity. Using simulation-free interpolation probes of the learned dynamics, FLOWBUDGET normalizes the leading one-step discretization error by the motion, estimates its coefficient from interpolation probes, and maps a numerical tolerance to a step budget using the solver order. We derive estimators for numerical solvers in flow~matching sampling, namely Euler and Heun for ODE sampling and additive-noise Euler--Maruyama for SDE sampling, and connect the ODE coefficients to terminal integration error. Experiments on SiT, FlowDCN and Rectified Flow models, spanning flow-model architectures and formulations, test whether FLOWBUDGET can estimate the NFE budget without generating samples at multiple budgets or performing an FID-versus-NFE sweep. The code is available at https://github.com/Yasaman-dt/FlowBudget
authors: Zahra Dehghani, Pablo Piantanida, Mohammadhadi Shateri
bullets: Addresses the costly, empirical selection of numerical resolution for pretrained flow-based generators.
Uses training-free, simulation-free interpolation probes of learned dynamics to estimate normalized one-step discretization error.
Derives budget estimators for Euler and Heun ODE solvers and additive-noise Euler–Maruyama SDE sampling.
Maps a target numerical tolerance to an NFE budget using solver order and relates ODE estimates to terminal integration error.
Evaluated across SiT, FlowDCN, and Rectified Flow models and formulations.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Analysis of FLOWBUDGET budget estimation.

Table 1: FLOWBUDGET-predicted budgets and corresponding FID, reported as mean ± std over three seeds. Reference FID uses NFE = 250 for SiT-XL/2, FlowDCN-XL/2, and RF-UNet, and NFE = 1 for 1-RF, 2-RF, and 3-RF.

papers.selection_reason: Addresses efficiency in generative models by estimating sampling budgets for flow matching, a technique relevant to both video generation and efficient inference.
papers.title: FlowBudget: Training-Free Sampling-Budget Estimation for Flow Matching Models
papers.tldr: FLOWBUDGET estimates the sampling NFE budget needed by flow-matching models without repeated sample generation or FID-versus-NFE sweeps.

papers.abstract: Injecting skills into a frozen language model currently costs a million parameters and a reinforcement-learning pipeline. We introduce DecSteer, a System-1 decision operator trained by behavior cloning that lowers this cost by roughly two orders of magnitude. The default operator uses 330K parameters to match a 1.33M-parameter operator trained with reinforcement learning, exceeds or achieve comparable performance, while collapsing 3,685-token deliberation into a 6-token decision with no loss in accuracy. A rank-4 variant with 23K parameters, 1/58 of the strongest published skill operator, suffices for SearchQA and near-suffices for LiveMath, where higher rank still helps; the same recipe transfers across five tasks and three backbones, with out-of-distribution gains persisting on LiveMath problems released months after training. The gap to prior work is trainability, and it is set jointly by initialization and architecture. The initialization of prior operators zeroes the gradient of both large factor matrices at the first optimization step, whereas our zero-initialized output projection inside a shared low-rank backbone receives a gradient immediately, which a gradient-flow probe confirms directly. The gain isn't chain-of-thought compression. 23 of 57 LiveMath points beat the base model's best-of-8 sampling, and a logit-lens probe shows the operator amplifies the answer along the model's existing late-layer pathway, not writing it earlier. Gains track the base model's headroom across 13 base-task pairs, and skills compose as approximately linear operators that can be added, interpolated, and hot-swapped at inference time.
bullets: Reduces operator size from roughly 1.33M to 330K parameters while matching or exceeding the reinforcement-learned baseline; a 23K rank-4 version often suffices.
Compresses deliberation from 3,685 tokens to 6 decision tokens without accuracy loss.
Transfers across five tasks and three backbones, with out-of-distribution gains reported on later-released LiveMath problems.
Improved trainability comes from architecture and initialization: the shared low-rank backbone receives useful gradients immediately.
Operators can be added, interpolated, and hot-swapped, with skill composition behaving approximately linearly.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview. a: A shared low-rank backbone is injected at D=8 depths with per-depth inputdependent gate g; the operator is identity at initialization. b: The gate can be phase-conditioned on prompt vs. generation via zero-init increments. c: The identity anchor steers optimization: with up=0, the output projection gets gradient from step one, while baselines V=0 keeps both large matrices frozen until V moves. d: Trained skills act as composable residual objects.

Figure 4: Left: the rank–parameter–score ladder on SearchQA: 7.7K parameters already exceed the published 1.33M RL result, and the operator size scales linearly with the backbone width, so smaller models take smaller skills. Right: out-of-distribution generalization. A bundle trained only on problems released through February 2026, evaluated zero-shot on new LiveMath problems from April–June 2026 (zero id overlap): 79.0 versus base 25.4, and 7.5 points above the official released KV-Skill RL artifact under the identical evaluation protocol.

Figure 6: Left: decomposing the LiveMath gain. Base greedy 23.4; forced direct answering via prompt 38.7; base best-of-8 sampling 57.3; DecSteer 80.7. The last step exceeds the base model’s sampling budget: on 43 problems the operator is correct while all 8 base samples are wrong. Right: logit-lens readout of answer readability by layer. The answer becomes readable only within the last 1–6 layers in both arms; the operator amplifies the existing late-layer signal (3.4–6.4×, more for weaker bases) rather than writing the answer earlier.

Figure 3: Left: accuracy versus trainable parameters per task. DecSteer (BC) at 0.33M reaches or exceeds every KV-Skill variant at 1.33M, while KV-Skill’s own BC control (same signal, same examples) stays at the base. Right: median generated tokens, base versus DecSteer. LiveMath drops from 3,685 to 6 tokens (36× wall-clock), DocVQA from 289 to 11 (10.3×), with accuracy unchanged or higher; SearchQA already answers directly.

Figure 5: Left: gradient-flow probe over the first optimization steps. With up=0, the output projection B has gradient Θ( √ ds) at step 1; with KV-Skill’s V=0 anchoring, both large matrices have exactly zero gradient while only the small middle matrix moves. Right: accuracy versus rank, trained from scratch with BC. The knee sits between rank 2 and 4 on LiveMath; SearchQA saturates at rank 1. Rank-4 (23K parameters) reaches the 1.33M level.

Figure 1: A decision does not need a million parameters. Left: LiveMath accuracy vs. trainable parameters. A 23K-parameter model trained by behavior cloning matches a 1.33M-parameter one trained with RL, while the same BC fails on the prior one. Right: It collapses median output length from 3,685 to a 6-token decision.
Figure 8: Operator strength sweeps (mean ± SD over seeds). Stars mark each task’s best strength.
Figure 9: SearchQA calibration before and after skill injection: ECE (left) and answer-ranking AUROC (right) across the three backbones.

Figure 11: Left: RFT control on CSQA. Even when the training target contains full chains of thought (330/400 sampled solutions kept by the verifier, median target 1,445 characters), the operator still converges to 6-token direct answers with accuracy unchanged: the direct-answer mode is the operator’s least-effort solution, not an artifact of short targets. Right: RL stability. The published entropy bonus overwhelms the KL anchor by roughly 100× once entropy rises, driving divergence (reward 0.86 to 0.08); removing it restores stability. This supports using BC, which needs none of these controls.

Figure 7: Left: the headroom trend, an empirical relation. Skill gain versus base headroom (1− base score) over 13 base–task pairs on three backbones; the relation is monotone, and saturated bases (CSQA, OpenBookQA on 4B) sit at zero as the trend expects. Right: skill algebra. Adding, interpolating, and reordering two skills preserves the anchor skill in all 18 cells (zero interference); the one forbidden zone is a negative coefficient on a mode-switching skill, which reverses the modality it switches.

Figure 10: Left: multimodal extension on DocVQA. The identical BC recipe transfers to document VQA: 4B gains +2.3 ANLS (92.5 to 94.8, higher in 3/3 seeds) and 0.8B gains +23.8 (57.9 to 81.8), with a second confirmation of mild overshoot at full strength. Right: behavior on saturated 4B bases. Paired flip counts are almost perfectly symmetric (53/52, 58/59, 82/80, 7/7) and all skill arms sit within about a point of the base, the headroom trend’s expectation for a saturated base.

Figure 12: Commitment-point probe: applying a suffix intervention from generation step k measures how early the answer is fixed. The height of the curve at k=0 tracks the eventual skill gain across the four tasks probed and follows the headroom trend, so it serves as an auxiliary screening diagnostic; the informative quantity is the curve’s height, not its onset.

Table 1: Main results. Ours is a low-rank residual operator trained by behavior cloning on answer tokens only. KV-Skill, LoRA, Text Skill, SkillOpt, and Soft Skill rows quote published numbers; the Base rows are their published base scores. Rank rows are trained from scratch with the same recipe. In the smaller-backbone blocks, where no published baselines exist, the KV-Skill row is our faithful reimplementation trained with the identical BC recipe (Appendix A). Ours entries are means over 3 seeds; a uniform operator strength of 1.0 yields the same conclusions.

Table 2: Protocol and integrity checks behind the reported numbers: exact identity anchors for fair comparison, leakage and degeneracy screens, budget audits, and the import validation of the official KV-Skill artifact used as a baseline.

Table 4: Cross-carrier comparison: the KV-Skill operator is reimplemented exactly (V=0 identity init) and both operators are trained and evaluated under identical data, prompts, and decoding. Ours wins 6 of 8 cells and is never worse, with 1/4 the parameters.

Table 5: Training cost on a single A100-40GB. The BC recipe used for all main results trains in minutes because there are no rollouts; GRPO rows are the protocol-matched controls of Table 3. Inference additionally accelerates generation by up to 36× (LiveMath), 10.3× wall-clock (DocVQA).

Table 3: Behavior cloning matches GRPO under KV-Skill’s own protocol, at 1/4 the parameters. All BC seeds meet or exceed the KV-Skill RL reference (80.1 / 79.0). On LiveMath, GRPO from scratch trails both its KV-Skill counterpart and the BC warm start: the starting point matters more than the algorithm.

papers.selection_reason: Parameter-efficient low-rank activation steering reduces LLM decision cost by orders of magnitude.
papers.title: Learning to Decide, Not to Reason: Parameter-Efficient Decision Operators via Low-Rank Activation Steering
papers.tldr: DecSteer is a behavior-cloned, low-rank decision operator that equips frozen language models with transferable skills using far fewer parameters and much shorter inference than prior operators.

papers.abstract: Long-context decoding is limited by memory bandwidth, because every output token reads the KV cache of every layer. Sparse decoding reduces this cost by reading only part of the KV cache. We observe that the number of pages a query needs varies widely across KV heads, layers and steps. Fixed budgets are simple, but they are sized for demanding cases and tuned per workload; adaptive budgets follow this variation more flexibly, but existing designs pay for it with extra selection cost or training. At the kernel level, FlashAttention-3 (FA3) and FlashInfer are designed for rows of similar length: with page lists whose length differs per KV head, they either pad the lists (forfeiting much of the sparse saving), leave thread blocks unbalanced, or rely on a host-side plan that runs outside the CUDA graph. We propose MOIRA, a training-free sparse decode path in vLLM whose budget adapts per KV head and per layer. For every request, layer, KV head and step, a coverage rule keeps the smallest set of pages whose estimated attention mass reaches a fraction $γ$. A new kernel, self-planning attention, lets each thread block derive its own share of the work from the list lengths, so the whole decode step stays inside the CUDA graph. On an H200, at RULER's 128k context, MOIRA with $γ=0.99$ matches dense accuracy while reading about 30% of the pages and reduces the time per output token (TPOT) by 2.2-2.5$\times$ relative to dense FA3; with $γ=0.98$ it reduces TPOT by 2.7$\times$ and stays within the noise of dense. Under high serving load it raises throughput by up to 51%. These results suggest that a budget adapted per head and layer, paired with a kernel that keeps such budgets inside the CUDA graph, makes sparse decoding both flexible and fast.
bullets: Long-context decoding is memory-bandwidth-bound because each token accesses every layer’s KV cache.
MOIRA selects the smallest set of pages reaching a target attention-mass coverage per request, layer, KV head, and decoding step.
Its self-planning attention kernel handles variable page-list lengths without padding, imbalance, or host-side CUDA-graph breaks.
On an H200 with 128k-token contexts, it reads about 30% of pages at γ=0.99 and achieves 2.2–2.5× lower TPOT than dense FA3 while matching dense accuracy.
At γ=0.98, TPOT improves by 2.7× and serving throughput increases by up to 51%, according to the abstract.

papers.selection_reason: Sparse adaptive-budget KV-cache decoding for long-context LLMs; strong efficiency contribution.
papers.title: MOIRA: Mass-Oriented Indexing with Ragged Attention for Long-Context Decoding
papers.tldr: MOIRA enables fast, training-free long-context decoding by adaptively reading only the KV-cache pages needed by each layer and KV head while preserving dense-model accuracy.

papers.abstract: Existing geometry-aware Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) increasingly rely on external 3D encoders to provide structural priors, but executing these additional encoder paths at inference introduces substantial latency and computational overhead. We propose GeoThinker-$F$, an efficient framework that internalizes spatiotemporal perception by transforming causal MLLM hidden states into predictive latent world representations. Our key insight is that intermediate semantic representations contain sufficient information to predict useful representations of current geometry and future semantics, without requiring an exact reproduction of features from a dedicated 3D encoder. To realize this idea, GeoThinker-$F$ adopts a decoupled two-stage training strategy. In the first stage, the MLLM backbone is frozen while lightweight Latent Frame Prediction (LFP) heads learn from an offline 3D geometry expert and next-frame semantic targets. In the second stage, the external expert is removed, and the model is jointly optimized to generate and selectively integrate its self-predicted priors through a specialized Spatial-Grounded Temporal (SGT) Fusion module. Extensive evaluations show that GeoThinker-$F$ eliminates runtime dependence on external 3D geometry encoders while maintaining competitive performance across diverse spatial intelligence benchmarks. It achieves up to a $3.6\times$ inference speedup, reducing latency from $1.45\,\mathrm{s}$ to $0.40\,\mathrm{s}$ while retaining strong spatial reasoning performance.
authors: Haoyuan Li, Qihang Cao, Huanyuan Zhou, Xin Hu, Sijia Chen, Zihan Guo, Kun Xiang, Yunshuang Nie, Tao Tang, Xinlong Zheng, Jia-Wang Bian, Xianming Liu, Xiaodan Liang
bullets: Addresses the latency and computational overhead caused by external 3D geometry encoders in geometry-aware MLLMs.
Transforms intermediate MLLM hidden states into predictive representations of current geometry and future semantics.
Uses two-stage training: lightweight latent frame prediction heads first learn from geometry and next-frame semantic targets, then the external expert is removed during joint optimization.
Introduces Spatial-Grounded Temporal Fusion to selectively integrate self-predicted spatial-temporal priors.
Reports latency reduction from 1.45 s to 0.40 s while retaining competitive performance across diverse spatial intelligence benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the GeoThinker-F pipeline. The framework adopts two decoupled training stages to internalize geometric and temporal representations within the MLLM. Stage 1 (Left): With the MLLM backbone frozen, Latent Frame Prediction (LFP) heads attached to intermediate layers learn to predict latent geometry features produced by an offline 3D expert and semantic features of the next frame. Stage 2 (Right): The external geometry encoder is removed from the pipeline. The resulting geometry and future-semantic representations are selectively integrated by SGT-Fusion modules inserted at intermediate MLLM layers for spatial reasoning.

Figure 3: Efficiency and throughput comparison. (a) Compute vs. throughput trade-off, showing GeoThinker-F positioned in the ultra-efficient zone with minimal FLOPs and superior throughput. (b) Relative speedup over the highest-accuracy baseline among the compared methods within each backbone family, reaching an 8.8× acceleration on Qwen2.5-VL-7B compared to Cambrian-P and a 3.6× acceleration on Qwen3-VL-8B compared to GeoThinker.

Figure 4: Qualitative comparison between predicted geometry representations and VGGT feature targets. From top to bottom, we show the input RGB frames, geometry representations predicted by LFP head, and the corresponding feature targets from offline VGGT expert. The predicted features demonstrate remarkable structural alignment with the offline-expert feature targets.

Figure 7: Qualitative limitations of endogenous geometry prediction. For each sequence, we show the input RGB frames (top), LFP-predicted geometry representations (middle), and the corresponding VGGT feature targets (bottom). Top: In the presence of rapidly changing non-rigid structures, the predicted representations exhibit weaker correspondence with the VGGT targets. Bottom: The predicted maps display coarser spatial variation than the corresponding VGGT feature targets. These examples illustrate conditions in which endogenous geometry prediction does not fully recover the geometry-related structure captured by the external expert.

Figure 6: Qualitative semantic selectivity under visually ambiguous conditions. For each sequence, we show input RGB frames (top), LFP-predicted geometry representations (middle), and the corresponding VGGT feature targets (bottom). In these selected snow and driving examples, the VGGT targets exhibit comparatively diffuse or background-dominated activations, whereas the endogenous predictions remain concentrated around the primary human or vehicle. This case-level contrast suggests that prediction from MLLM hidden states can preserve semantically relevant spatial focus when low-level visual cues are ambiguous.

Figure 5: Qualitative structural correspondence in standard scenes. For each sequence, we show input RGB frames (top), LFP-predicted geometry representations (middle), and the corresponding VGGT feature targets (bottom). In these selected scenes with clear foreground subjects and structured motion, the endogenous predictions preserve coherent object-centered activation patterns and broad spatial correspondence with the VGGT targets across consecutive frames. This qualitative agreement illustrates that GeoThinker-F can recover useful geometry-related structure from intermediate MLLM hidden states.

Table 2: Cross-benchmark comparison on spatial intelligence benchmarks (Scaled regime). † indicates evaluation on reduced subsets. * indicates trained with official S1+S2 setting. Benchmarks include VSI-Bench(Yang et al., 2025a), MMSI-Bench(Yang et al., 2026c), MindCube(Yin et al., 2025), Viewspatial(Li et al., 2025a), SITE(Wang et al., 2025e), CV-Bench (Tong et al., 2024).

Table 1: Performance comparisons on VSI-Bench (Vanilla regime). By internalizing 3D geometry priors and incorporating temporal dynamics priors, GeoThinker-F completely eliminates the external VGGT encoder while outperforming the GeoThinker.

Table 5: Comparison of different VLA models on LIBERO. We train one policy for all 4 suites. All scores are averaged over 500 trials for each task suite (10 tasks × 50 episodes). Compared with GeoThinker, it reduces the spatial-prior integration overhead by 87.15%.

Table 6: Quantitative efficiency and spatial reasoning performance comparison across different model backbones. We report computational cost in FLOPs (T) and MACs (T), inference latency (s), and accuracy on VSI-Bench. * denotes leveraging estimated lower bound of latency. GeoThinker-F 32frame achieves substantial reductions in FLOPs, MACs, and inference latency compared to external 3D encoder baselines (e.g., GeoThinker), while maintaining highly competitive performance.

GeoThinker-F maintains competitive accuracy on ReVSI-Bench without executing a runtime external geometry encoder, while trailing its external-encoder GeoThinker counterpart.

Table 3: Ablation Study on VSI-Bench. All compared variants are trained on the same vanilla SFT data with Qwen2.5-VL-7B backbone, showing the individual and joint contributions of our endogenous Geometry-Prior LFP and Temporal-Prior LFP branches.

Table 8: Computational footprint and inference latency comparison on embodied robotic manipulation. Parameter size (M ), FLOPs (T ), and total latency (ms) are decomposed across the backbone and added auxiliary modules.

Table 9: Impact of general video data co-training. We evaluate performance changes (∆) when co-training with 430k general video instruction samples. While standard 2D MLLM baselines exhibit task interference of degrading 3D spatial accuracy on VSI, GeoThinker-F effectively mitigates cross-task degradation. By internalizing spatial-temporal priors directly within hidden representations, GeoThinker-F maintains robust spatial intelligence while simultaneously enhancing general temporal understanding.

Table 11: Performance comparison on VSTI-Bench. GeoThinker-FQwen3VL-8B achieves a competitive average score of 64.0%, outperforming several proprietary and open-source VLM baselines while eliminating the runtime external geometry encoder. Bold and underlined values denote the best and second-best results, respectively.

Table 4: Performance comparison on NAVSIM navtest. Compared with ReCogDrive, GeoThinker-F improves key driving metrics. Compared with GeoThinker, it reduces the spatialprior integration overhead by 52.91%. Evaluation includes Not-at-fault Collisions (NC), Drivable Area Compliance (DAC), Time-To-Collision within bound (TTC), Comfort (Comf.), Ego and Progress (EP).

Table 17: Ablation study on Stage-2 training strategies for GeoThinker-F. Evaluated on a Qwen2.5-VL-7B backbone across frame budgets (8 vs. 32 frames), General Video mixture integration, and LFP head fine-tuning status. Orange numbers at (·) denote performance gaps relative to GeoThinker. Jointly fine-tuning LFP heads alongside general video mixtures yields the optimal balance across specialized spatial and multi-modal benchmarks.
Table 15: Zero-shot frame scaling on ReVSI. Evaluates temporal extrapolation from 16 to 128 frames, where target ground-truth annotations dynamically adjust to the changing visual context.

Table 7: Resource efficiency and latency breakdown on autonomous driving evaluation. We report extra-module and total parameter counts (M ), computational complexity in FLOPs (T ), latency breakdowns (ms), and amortized Latency (Avg.).

Table 16: Ablation study on the influence of the OmniSpatial-Train data mixture. Controlled comparison between GeoThinker and GeoThinker-F with and without the OmniSpatial training dataset, isolating the core architectural contributions of endogenous feature prediction under strictly aligned training data distributions.

papers.selection_reason: Geometry-aware MLLM with predictive world representations and faster spatial intelligence inference.
papers.title: GeoThinker-$F$: Endogenous Predictive World Representations for Fast Spatial Intelligence
papers.tldr: GeoThinker-F internalizes spatial and temporal world representations in an MLLM, removing external 3D encoders and achieving up to 3.6× faster inference while maintaining strong spatial reasoning.

papers.abstract: Scaling up transformers has produced models with broad capabilities, deployed across heterogeneous hardware and fluctuating workloads. Yet, model families offer only a few fixed sizes (e.g., S, B, L), forcing users to commit to a model based on hardware and latency constraints. This rigidity is often suboptimal under varying query loads. We introduce a retraining-free method that elastifies pre-trained transformers into a single model that adapts on-the-fly across a continuum of computational budgets. Our key contribution is a differentiable relaxation of the functional unit-ranking problem: unlike prior work, which optimizes a single importance weight per MLP block or attention head, we rank every individual MLP neuron and attention head jointly, on a common scale, by minimizing the model's loss under soft pruning across many sparsity targets, all at once. Across 27 vision and text transformer encoders ranging from 22M to 8B parameters, our method yields smooth degradation up to 60% sparsity and outperforms one-shot baselines under deep pruning. For example, pruning DINOv3 ViT-H+/16 to 50% sparsity removes 427M parameters while reducing ImageNet-1k linear-probing accuracy by only 0.8%, without the need for weight correction or retraining. At 60% sparsity, a pruned AugReg ViT-B/16 model achieves up to $1.80\times$ higher throughput and $1.26\times$ lower single-query latency on an A100 GPU. Elastic models are produced in minutes, with construction time scaling sub-linearly with parameter count.
authors: Walter Simoncini, Dheeraj Varghese, Gertjan J. Burghouts, Cees G. M. Snoek
bullets: Addresses the rigidity of offering transformers in only a few fixed sizes under changing hardware and workload constraints.
Jointly ranks individual MLP neurons and attention heads on a shared importance scale using differentiable soft pruning across multiple sparsity targets.
Evaluated on 27 vision and text transformer encoders spanning 22M–8B parameters, with smooth degradation up to 60% sparsity.
Pruning DINOv3 ViT-H+/16 to 50% sparsity removes 427M parameters with only a 0.8% ImageNet-1k linear-probing accuracy drop.
At 60% sparsity, AugReg ViT-B/16 reaches up to 1.80× higher throughput and 1.26× lower single-query latency on an A100; models are built in minutes without retraining.

Figure 1 Differentiable soft pruning. Initial importance scores for MLP neurons and attention heads are transformed into learnable log-scores and median-centered by type, aligning their reference points without changing within-type rankings. At each optimization step, the joint ranking determines a threshold κb and soft mask Mb for each sparsity target b ∈ B. We run the same calibration batch through the frozen model under each mask, average losses across targets, and update only the log-scores. Mask gradients concentrate near each threshold, so multiple targets expose different regions of the ranking to useful gradients. The optimized ranking can then be hard-pruned to any inference budget without further optimization.

Figure 13 Pruned larger models can outperform smaller dense models. ImageNet-1k top-1 k-NN accuracy versus GFLOPs for the six-model DINO WebSSL family, pruned with our method from dense to 60% sparsity. Pruned 3B and 7B models pareto-dominate the dense 2B and 5B anchors.

Figure 6 Our method retains higher accuracy under deep pruning on DeiT-B/16. Top-1 k-NN (top) and linear-probing (bottom) accuracy versus GFLOPs on ImageNet-1k and the transfer average. Figure 5 Ranking optimization changes both cross-block sparsity allocation and within-block selection. Retained MLP neurons and attention heads at 50% sparsity for AugReg, DINOv3, and SigLIPv2 ViT-B/16. The top rows compare per-block allocations from plain and optimized scores with uniform pruning. Newly retained units appear even where block-level allocations remain nearly unchanged, showing that ranking optimization also reorders units within blocks rather than merely redistributing capacity across them.

Table 14 GPU-friendly tiling helps latency. Latency of dense and 60% pruned AugReg ViT-B/16 models across batch sizes, under eager execution and torch.compile, for unconstrained pruning, i.e., A = 1, and pruning in blocks of 8 or 64 neurons, reported as speedup over the dense model. Under eager execution, latency is launch-bound up to batch size 16 and pruning yields no speedup, while tiling accounts for most of the gains at larger batches. Compilation lifts speedups across the board, up to 1.79× at batch size 128, and at batch size 1 gains only materialize without launch overhead.

Groups are neuron groups per MLP block. All optimized variants use equal compute. Per-unit scores achieve the highest accuracy.

Table 3 Joint optimization across sparsity targets improves performance. ImageNet-1k top-1 k-NN accuracy for AugReg ViT-B/16. Joint optimization over 14 targets (Elastic) outperforms single-target optimization (Single) at all three sparsities.

Table 5 Elastic pruning generalizes to text. MTEB score for dense and elastically pruned models across the BGE, E5, E5-Mistral, and Qwen3 families. Shallow pruning is nearly free: at 20% sparsity, no model loses more than 3.3 points, and the E5 models lose under 1.0 points. Under deep pruning, bidirectional encoders degrade more gracefully than decoders: at 60% sparsity, BGE and E5 lose between 5.1 and 10.0 points, while E5-Mistral and Qwen3 lose between 11.5 and 19.5.

Table 8 Non-retrieval tasks are robust to pruning. MTEB score excluding retrieval tasks for dense and elastically pruned BGE, E5, E5-Mistral, and Qwen3 models. At 60% sparsity, BGE-L and E5-L lose 5.3 and 4.3 points, against 19.6 and 8.0 on retrieval tasks as shown in Table 9.

Table 9 Retrieval is sensitive to deep pruning. MTEB retrieval score for dense and elastically pruned BGE, E5, E5-Mistral, and Qwen3 models. Retrieval degrades faster than other tasks: at 60% sparsity, BGE-L loses 19.6 points and Qwen3 8B 22.1. On the other hand, models tolerate shallow pruning, and E5-B slightly exceeds its dense score at 20% sparsity.

Table 21 More unique calibration samples generally improve ranking optimization. Top-1 k-NN accuracy on ImageNet-1k for AugReg ViT-B/16 pruned with our method, varying the number of unique ImageNet-1k samples available to ranking optimization under fixed compute, i.e., 300 steps, at batch size 32. Superscripts give the change relative to 64 samples, and † marks our default. Using 9600 samples gains up to 14.3 points over 64 samples at 50% sparsity, and up to 2.6 points over the default at 40%, but trails it by 2.0 points at 60%.

Table 16 Pruning improves throughput. Throughput of dense and pruned AugReg ViT-B/16 models in fp16 at batch size 128, under eager execution and torch.compile, for unconstrained pruning, i.e., A = 1, and pruning in blocks of 8 or 64 neurons, reported as speedup over the dense model. In eager mode, ragged widths can be slower than the dense model, while pruning in blocks improves throughput by up to 1.63× over unconstrained pruning at 20% sparsity. Compilation nearly eliminates this gap, and models pruned to 60% sparsity reach up to 1.80× dense throughput.

Table 11 Our method is competitive against corrected baselines, and is compatible with weight correction. Top-1 k-NN accuracy on ImageNet-1k for pruned AugReg ViT-B/16, without (Plain) and with (Corrected) post-pruning weight correction. Uncorrected, our method outperforms SparseGPT and FPTP, only trailing corrected SnapViT by at most 4.0%. Corrected, it matches SnapViT at up to 40% sparsity and surpasses it beyond.

Table 12 Our correction-free method matches or outperforms weight-correction methods on DINOv3 ViT-H+/16. Top-1 k-NN accuracy on ImageNet-1k for DINOv3 ViT-H+/16 pruned with corrected SparseGPT and SnapViT, versus our correction-free method. At 10% and 20% sparsity, our method remains within 0.1% of the best corrected baseline. Our advantage grows with sparsity, to up to 18.2% over corrected SnapViT, the runner-up, at 60%.

Table 15 GPU-friendly tiling can affect accuracy at high sparsity. Top-1 k-NN accuracy on ImageNet-1k and transfer datasets for pruned AugReg ViT-B/16, with unconstrained pruning, i.e., A = 1, or pruning constrained to remove MLP neurons in blocks of 8 or 64. Superscripts indicate the delta relative to A = 1. Tiling costs little at up to moderate sparsity, but at 60% sparsity pruning in blocks of 8 and 64 trails unconstrained pruning by 3.4 and 3.2 points on ImageNet-1k, respectively.

Table 25 Our rankings interpolate to unseen sparsity targets. Top-1 k-NN accuracy on ImageNet-1k and transfer datasets for pruned AugReg ViT-B/16 with a ranking optimized over seven sparsity anchors, from 10% to 70% in 10% increments, and evaluated every 5%. Targets marked † lie between anchors. Performance degrades smoothly at the evaluated intermediate targets.

papers.title: Your Transformer Is Secretly Elastic
papers.tldr: A retraining-free method turns fixed-size transformers into smoothly adjustable models that trade accuracy for compute across a continuum of sparsity levels.

papers.abstract: Long contexts enlarge key--value (KV) caches, increasing memory use and attention costs during generation. Compressing these caches must preserve information for unseen questions. We introduce **Latent Compaction**, which learns a compact document-specific cache through test-time training. We initialize cache entries using reconstruction importance, teacher attention, and key-space diversity. Training first fits attention outputs and log-normalizers to those of the full cache, with reconstruction-selected entries held fixed. It then jointly optimizes the entire cache through end-to-end distillation from the full-cache model. Model weights remain frozen throughout, and training uses only generic prompts about the document, without access to downstream questions or answers. Experiments on RULER, LongBench, and Phonebook Lookup demonstrate substantial gains over budget-matched compression baselines. On a RULER, for example, our method achieves 96.7% accuracy at 32$\times$ compression, compared with 40.0% for KVZip+. The method also transfers across model scales and families, with retrieval gains on both Qwen3 and MiniCPM5. These results show that treating the KV cache as a neural network and optimizing it with test-time training can preserve retrieval accuracy under aggressive compression. The code is released at https://www.github.com/THUNLP/latent-compaction
authors: Yingfa Chen, Xingyu Shen, Chaojun Xiao, Xu Han
bullets: Targets the memory and attention costs of large KV caches during generation.
Initializes compact caches using reconstruction importance, teacher attention, and key-space diversity.
Distills attention outputs and log-normalizers from the full cache, then jointly optimizes the cache while freezing model weights.
Uses only generic document prompts, without downstream questions or answers.
Achieves 96.7% accuracy at 32× compression on a RULER task versus 40.0% for KVZip+, with gains across RULER, LongBench, Phonebook Lookup, Qwen3, and MiniCPM5.
