papers.abstract: Layer-wise post-training quantization methods let each layer compensate for the quantization error inherited from earlier layers. We ask under what assumptions such compensation guarantees a network output error no larger than without it. For linear networks of any depth, with the required calibration Gram matrices invertible, if the rounding error of each layer has zero conditional mean and a deterministic second-moment map common to both schemes, as under subtractive dither on an unbounded grid, then compensation with strengths in $[0,1]$ fixed in advance gives a mean-square output error no larger than no compensation, each scheme being followed along its own trajectory. The exact gain separates error removed directly from reduced excitation of later rounding noise. Outside this setting the comparison can fail. With rectified linear activations it fails for two independent reasons: noise changes activation states, and, even when no state changes, the correction moves error from samples on which a unit is inactive to samples on which it is active. With stable activations, commutators between the calibration projection and the activation patterns bound the excess. With a bounded codebook, even unique exact layer-wise minimizers with no overload can give a larger output error. For fixed rounding errors it already fails for two scalar linear layers, refuting a published universal guarantee. An exact residual identity gives the necessary and sufficient condition on a common layer input. All these comparisons hold the calibration input fixed. On two 8B models at 4 bits, fixed half-strength compensation beat uncompensated rounding in every model, text and draw tested, yet no rule for choosing the strength beat a layer-wise rule consistently, and lowering the full-network loss on the data used to choose did not reliably lower it on new text.
bullets: For arbitrary-depth linear networks, fixed compensation strengths in [0,1] do not increase mean-square error when calibration Gram matrices are invertible and rounding errors satisfy suitable zero-conditional-mean and shared second-moment conditions.
The gain comes from both directly removing inherited error and reducing the excitation of later quantization noise.
Guarantees can fail with ReLU activations, bounded codebooks, or fixed rounding errors—even for two scalar linear layers; stable activations admit bounds based on projection–activation commutators.

Experiments on two 8B models at 4 bits found fixed half-strength compensation consistently better than uncompensated rounding across tested models and inputs, but no strength-selection rule was consistently best or reliably transferable to new text.

papers.abstract: Structured pruning reduces the inference cost of large language models (LLMs) by permanently removing neurons and weight rows, yielding dense, hardware-agnostic speedup. Existing post-training methods couple neuron selection and weight reconstruction through a shared calibration dataset, introducing domain bias and out-of-memory failures at high sparsity. We propose SARATHI, a framework that decouples these two stages. A data-free \emph{NMF Residual Subspace Probe} scores neurons using intrinsic weight geometry, without accessing any calibration data, and carries a formal connection to Robust PCA. \emph{Adaptive OBS} then reconstructs the pruned weights with a localized calibration batch, operating in $\mathcal{O}(d^2)$ peak memory per layer and eliminating the global memory bottleneck of coupled methods. A \emph{Bias Shift Compensation} step corrects systematic activation drift in post-LayerNorm architectures that would otherwise cause perplexity collapse at high sparsity. Experiments across six models from two architecture families (gated and non-gated FFN) at 15--40\% sparsity show that SARATHI achieves competitive perplexity and matches or exceeds existing structured pruning baselines on zero-shot accuracy.
authors: Sankar Behera, Dhruv Singh, Satyadev Ahlawat, Yamuna Prasad
bullets: Addresses domain bias and out-of-memory failures caused by coupling pruning decisions with reconstruction on one calibration dataset.
Uses an NMF Residual Subspace Probe to score neurons from intrinsic weight geometry without calibration data.
Applies Adaptive OBS with localized calibration batches and O(d²) peak memory per layer for weight reconstruction.
Adds Bias Shift Compensation to mitigate activation drift and perplexity collapse in post-LayerNorm models.
Across six models at 15–40% sparsity, achieves competitive perplexity and matches or exceeds structured-pruning baselines on zero-shot accuracy.

papers.abstract: KV caches make long-context serving efficient by reusing past computation, but model switching breaks this reuse and forces the receiver to prefill the context again. We study \emph{zero-prefill cross-model context handoff}: translating a sender cache into a receiver-compatible state so that the receiver can continue directly without prefilling same context. Existing affine transport methods show that receiver KV states can be substantially reconstructed from sender caches. However, through extensive analyses, we find that reconstruction fidelity is a poor proxy for receiver utility. Similar K/V reconstruction errors can lead to substantially different attention patterns, predictive distributions, and downstream accuracy, because conventional reconstruction objectives overlook the query-dependent functional importance of K and V in receiver attention. We thus introduce CACHELINK, which learns a coupled K/V correction through the receiver behavior directly. Across four independently trained sender--receiver pairs and seven evaluation panels, CACHELINK improves the equal-weight mean over all methods for every pair. In matched diagnostics, CACHELINK changes K/V squared error by less than 0.4% while substantially changing receiver attention and next-token behavior. At 32K context, it reduces handoff latency by up to $7.27\times$ relative to receiver re-prefill. Our findings verify that reconstruction fidelity alone is insufficient and that preserving the receiver computation induced by the transported cache is important for effective cross-model KV transport.
authors: Haomiao Qiu, Yining Tang, Zijia Song, Ruizi Han, Ziyue Qiao, Miao Zhang
bullets: Cross-model switching normally forces the receiver to re-prefill the shared context, reducing KV-cache reuse.
The work finds that similar K/V reconstruction errors can produce very different attention patterns, predictions, and downstream accuracy.
CacheLink learns a coupled K/V correction guided directly by receiver computation and behavior.
Across four sender–receiver pairs and seven evaluation panels, it achieved the best equal-weight mean for every pair.
At 32K context, it reduced handoff latency by up to 7.27× versus receiver re-prefill.

papers.abstract: Recently, AutoRegressive Visual Generation (ARVG) models have emerged as a competitive paradigm for high-quality image synthesis. However, their substantial computational and memory demands make them difficult to deploy on resource-constrained edge devices. Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) provides a promising solution to reduce the computational and memory costs of ARVG models, yet existing methods often suffer from substantial image quality degradation under low-bit quantization. In this paper, we propose a training-free PTQ framework for ARVG, consisting of Tail-Aware Bounded-init Grid Refinement (T-BGR) and Coarse-to-Fine Activation Precision Scheduling (CAPS). T-BGR introduces a tail-aware reconstruction objective for weight quantizer calibration, assigning greater importance to distribution-tail coefficients and preserving fine-grained information without introducing additional parameters or high-precision branches. CAPS performs coarse-to-fine activation precision scheduling by jointly considering the importance and computational cost of different generation stages, enabling efficient mixed-precision allocation under a given bit budget. Extensive experiments on multiple ARVG backbones demonstrate that our framework consistently improves robustness under aggressive low-bit quantization. Notably, on Infinity, our framework achieves near full-precision image generation quality at an effective W4A5.6 activation precision, while existing methods at W4A6 still exhibit noticeable quality degradation or inconsistent performance. Code is available at https://github.com/lxm-lc/HGA-Quant.
authors: Xinmeng Liu, Xianglong Yan, Kaicheng Yang, Weisheng Dong, Yulun Zhang
bullets: Targets the high computational and memory costs that hinder ARVG deployment on resource-constrained edge devices.
T-BGR uses a tail-aware reconstruction objective to better preserve important weight-distribution information during quantizer calibration.
CAPS allocates mixed activation precision across generation stages based on stage importance and computational cost under a bit budget.
Experiments across multiple ARVG backbones show improved robustness to aggressive low-bit quantization.
On Infinity, it achieves near full-precision quality at effective W4A5.6 activation precision, while W4A6 existing methods show degradation or inconsistency.

papers.abstract: Implicit neural representations (INRs) are shaped by the spectral structure induced by their input encodings and activation functions. Existing methods improve fitting primarily by modifying which frequencies are available to the network, through coordinate encodings or periodic nonlinearities. However, frequency access is not the only bottleneck: signals with localized or spatially varying structure require the network to efficiently compose frequencies into multi-harmonic internal responses. We introduce learnable spectral activations (LSA), which replace fixed neuron-level nonlinearities with a residual truncated Fourier series whose harmonic amplitudes are learned during training. LSA does not expand the asymptotic function class. Instead, it changes the factorization of the representation: linear weights select features while activation coefficients control spectral shaping, and the two are updated by separate gradients. Because the activation output is affine in the coefficients given fixed pre-activations, spectral tuning becomes a more direct subproblem compared to architectures where it is entangled with feature selection. Empirically, this factorization concentrates more target-signal energy in the leading eigenmodes of the neural tangent kernel, consistent with improved optimization behavior. Across audio, image, neural radiance field, and neural acoustic field tasks, LSA also improves reconstruction quality.
bullets: Problem: Existing encodings and periodic activations expand frequency access but may struggle with localized or spatially varying structures requiring multi-harmonic composition.
Method: Replace fixed activations with residual truncated Fourier series whose harmonic amplitudes are learned during training.
Key idea: Linear weights select features while activation coefficients independently control spectral shaping, without expanding the asymptotic function class.

Result: The factorization concentrates more target-signal energy in leading neural tangent kernel eigenmodes and improves reconstruction quality across audio, image, neural radiance field, and neural acoustic field tasks.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards improves reasoning, while the allocation of learning signal shapes which solutions remain accessible under repeated sampling. Group-relative objectives assign equal advantages to equally rewarded responses, making aggregate credit proportional to sampled mode frequency. We introduce Exploration-Preserving Policy Optimization (ExPPO), a lightweight advantage-shaping rule that redistributes credit using prompt-relative, length-normalized response surprisal and prompt pass rate. ExPPO combines bounded shaping with shared normalization to preserve verifier polarity and approximately maintain each prompt group's total absolute sequence-advantage mass. Our analysis characterizes response-level credit allocation alongside sampled mode updates, deriving local conditions for gains in entropy and correct-mode discovery. Experiments show improved in-domain and out-of-domain reasoning coverage, higher aggregate response accuracy, and strong coverage at large sampling budgets. A controlled multi-answer evaluation further demonstrates increased correct-mode yield and gains in diversity among verified-correct responses. Code is available at https://github.com/jinhangzhan/ExPPO
bullets: Addresses group-relative objectives that can concentrate learning on frequently sampled solution modes.
Uses prompt-relative, length-normalized response surprisal and prompt pass rate to redistribute credit.
Applies bounded shaping and shared normalization to preserve verifier polarity and approximately conserve each prompt group’s absolute advantage mass.
Analysis links response-level credit allocation to entropy and correct-mode discovery.
Experiments report improved in- and out-of-domain coverage, aggregate accuracy, large-budget coverage, and diversity among verified-correct responses.

papers.abstract: Deep graph learning models deployed in real-world systems often need to cope with non-stationary environments, where the underlying graph distribution drifts continually over time. Prevailing solutions rely on training auxiliary generative modules to synthesize memory graphs for cross-domain adaptation, which incurs substantial computational overhead and scales poorly under prolonged distribution shifts. We argue that a more economical path exists: rather than generating memory, one can crystallize it. To this end, we propose Efficient Memory Crystallization (EMC), a training-free test-time framework that distills each incoming graph domain into a compact, semantically faithful memory through a closed-form solution to a memory-oriented distribution-matching objective, thereby eliminating redundant domain information under continual covariate shifts. To preserve both generalizability and adaptability as the model traverses a long sequence of target domains, EMC further models inter-domain dependencies through state-evolving memories and admits a theoretically grounded, tighter generalization error bound than direct adaptation. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superior performance of EMC over state-of-the-art baselines on graphs under non-stationary distribution shifts, while reducing average runtime by 87.4% and GPU memory consumption by 92.4% relative to the recent competitor, making continual graph adaptation practical at scale.
bullets: Addresses the computational and scalability costs of synthesizing memory graphs during prolonged graph distribution shifts.
Uses a training-free, test-time framework with a closed-form distribution-matching objective to distill each incoming domain into a compact, semantically faithful memory.
Models inter-domain dependencies with state-evolving memories to balance generalizability and adaptability across target domains.
Provides a theoretically tighter generalization error bound than direct adaptation.
Outperforms state-of-the-art baselines while reducing average runtime by 87.4% and GPU memory use by 92.4% relative to a recent competitor.

papers.abstract: Recent work on anchored diffusion language models improves denoising by shaping an intermediate latent space with supervised important-token targets. In this work, we introduce time-based (self-supervised) anchoring, which learns and reuses latent anchors without requiring such targets. Our key observation is that anchors encode persistent properties of the clean sequence, such as its semantic intent, global structure, or intermediate plan. Although their hidden representations become stale as the token canvas evolves, their semantic content remains useful across nearby diffusion times. This is implemented through a two-stage architecture consisting of a relatively expensive anchor network that generates the latent cache state and a lightweight denoising network that intelligently combines the cached latent state with the current state at each reverse step using a fusion module. This gives anchoring a latent-space caching interpretation: the anchor network is evaluated periodically, while its cached representation is reused across multiple reverse steps. We instantiate this framework as TADM:Post-train, which time-anchorizes pretrained DLMs, and TADM:Pretraining, which learns time-based anchors during pretraining. Applied to DiffusionGemma-26B, TADM:Post-train improves throughput by approximately 49% to 79% on several math, code, and STEM benchmarks (GSM8K, AIME26, GPQA-Diamond, LiveCodeBench-v6, HumanEval, MMLU-Pro). TADM:Pretraining reduces Transformer-layer computation by up to 38% relative to a standard single-stage DLM, achieves up to 73% higher measured throughput than ADLM.
bullets: Addresses the high per-step computation of diffusion language models and the need for supervised important-token targets in prior anchored approaches.
Uses a two-stage architecture: an expensive anchor network periodically creates a latent cache, while a lightweight denoiser fuses the cache with the current state across reverse steps.
Introduces TADM:Post-train for adapting pretrained DLMs and TADM:Pretraining for learning time-based anchors during pretraining.
On DiffusionGemma-26B, TADM:Post-train improves throughput by about 49–79% across math, code, and STEM benchmarks.
TADM:Pretraining cuts Transformer-layer computation by up to 38% and reaches up to 73% higher measured throughput than ADLM.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Time-Anchored Diffusion Model (TADM). The expensive anchor pathway is evaluated once every K reverse steps to produce a latent anchor ht′ , which is cached and reused. At each subsequent step, the lightweight shared network encodes the evolving state zt, and a gated fusion module combines its current representation ct with the cached anchor before denoising. TADM therefore replaces repeated evaluation of the expensive anchor network with learned latent-space reuse.

Table 1: TADM:Post-train performance. Results are averaged over three seeds across math, code, and STEM benchmarks and compared with the DiffusionGemma baseline under the same fixed-step evaluation setting. Increasing the anchor refresh interval enables progressively greater reuse of the cached latent representation, yielding substantial inference speedups. TADM preserves essentially the same task accuracy across benchmarks while achieving up to 1.79× higher generation throughput.

Table 2: We compare TADM diffusion baselines across sampling budgets. For TADM, we use refresh intervals K = {2, 2, 2, 8, 4, 4} for T = {128, 256, 512, 1024, 2048, 4096}, respectively. We report MAUVE, generative perplexity (Gen PPL), entropy, Transformer-layer evaluations normalized to MDLM over 5000 samples, and measured generation throughput over 20 generations of length 1,024. TADM periodically reuses its cached anchor representation, reducing Transformer computation while maintaining competitive generation quality.

The original cache-age notation k = {0, 1, 2} is reported here as anchor refresh intervals K = {1, 2, 3}. “Baseline” denotes naive reuse with the original DiffusionGemma weights and no fusion modules, while “Ours” denotes TADM:Post-train. papers.selection_reason: Time-anchored diffusion language models with latent-space caching for faster generation, relevant to efficient inference and LLM architectures.
papers.title: Time-Anchored Diffusion Language Models: Latent-Space Caching for Fast Generation
papers.tldr: Time-based latent anchoring caches persistent sequence information across diffusion steps, substantially accelerating diffusion language model generation without supervised anchor targets.

papers.abstract: Large-scale vision-language models (VLM) such as CLIP enable strong open-vocabulary reasoning, yet deploying these capabilities on resource-constrained edge devices remains challenging. EdgeVL addresses this problem by distilling CLIP representations into lightweight multi-modal encoders and applying quantization-aware training (QAT) for efficient Open-Vocabulary Classification (OVC) on edge hardware. However, its two-stage optimization applies different objectives for distillation and QAT, and contrastive learning is performed within the quantized student space, which can result in inconsistent optimization and reduced training efficiency. Moreover, identical supervision across RGB and non-RGB modalities may lead to modality imbalance. We propose a unified framework for quantized semantic distillation tailored to edge deployment. By jointly optimizing distillation and quantization within a unified teacher-anchored framework, our method ensures consistent training under quantization, suppressing hard negatives and enlarging decision margins. Additionally, we design a lightweight cross-attention adapter that enhances non-RGB representations through RGB-guided semantic transfer, narrowing the modality gap. Extensive experiments demonstrate consistent improvements on non-RGB modalities while maintaining deployment efficiency.
bullets: Targets the difficulty of deploying CLIP-like VLM capabilities on resource-constrained edge hardware.
Jointly optimizes semantic distillation and quantization-aware training to provide consistent learning under quantization.
Uses a lightweight cross-attention adapter for RGB-guided semantic transfer to reduce the gap between RGB and non-RGB modalities.
Suppresses hard negatives and enlarges decision margins through teacher-anchored optimization.
Experiments show consistent gains on non-RGB modalities while preserving deployment efficiency.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Comparison of edge-oriented VLM adaptation frameworks. (a) An edge device collects RGB and non-RGB sensory inputs from its environment and performs open-vocabulary classification. Our goal is to adapt the edge model by distilling knowledge from a large teacher model deployed on a server. (b) Existing approaches perform knowledge distillation and quantization-aware training (QAT) in separate stages with different objectives. During QAT, contrastive learning is applied by optimizing the distance between positive and negative samples in the quantized student embedding space. (c) Our method unifies distillation and quantization in a single step with teacheranchored contrastive supervision. Additionally, we introduce a lightweight cross-modal adapter that enhances non-RGB representations using RGB features.

Fig. 2: Overview of our method. A frozen CLIP encoder provides semantic supervision for a quantized student with a shared backbone supporting RGB and non-RGB inputs. RGB features are directly distilled toward the teacher embedding, while nonRGB features are enhanced through a cross-modal attention module using non-RGB queries and RGB keys and values. The student is trained with teacher-anchored contrastive learning and an RKD loss to preserve geometric structure in the embedding space. The student encoder and adapter are jointly optimized with quantization-aware training for efficient edge deployment, while the teacher remains frozen.

Fig. 3: Decision margin visualization. (a) Decision margin angle between the image embedding and the hardest negative class. Our method preserves alignment with the ground-truth text embedding while increasing angular separation from hard negatives. (b) Compared to EdgeVL, our model yields a larger angle between the ground-truth text embedding and the hardest negative class, resulting in a wider decision margin. (c) Cumulative density whose margin angle exceeds a given threshold. Our method retains more samples at larger margins, indicating improved separation from hard negatives.

papers.abstract: The BabyLM challenge measures how much language a model can learn from developmentally-plausible, child-scale data rather than internet-scale corpora, yet prior language models forgo the biological constraints of the neural circuitry that acquires human language: spiking neurons separated into excitatory and inhibitory populations wired by a recurrent lateral connectome. This paper presents URCHIN (Unified Recurrent Connectome with Horizontal Integrate-and-fire Neurons), which applies the Parallelized Hierarchical Connectome Spiking State-space Model (PHCSSM) to language modeling: leaky integrate-and-fire neurons coupled by a Dale's-law lateral connectome resolve each token through a multi-transmission loop that recirculates activity to a fixed point. The instantiation is deliberately minimal: a single horizontal layer of 128 neurons, no attention, and 4.23M parameters. Two implementations share one set of weights and produce identical benchmark scores, so URCHIN is trained once and deployed either way with no conversion step: a parallel state-space model (SSM) scan that is GPU-efficient for training, or an event-driven recurrent spiking neural network (RSNN) with constant-cost inference for CPU or neuromorphic edge deployment. Across all three BabyLM tracks (Strict-100M, Strict-Small, and Multilingual), URCHIN offers a biologically plausible, efficient, and directly deployable reference point.
bullets: Targets the BabyLM challenge and biologically constrained language learning.
Uses PHCSSM with leaky integrate-and-fire neurons, excitatory/inhibitory populations, and a Dale’s-law recurrent lateral connectome.
A minimal architecture with one 128-neuron horizontal layer, no attention, and 4.23M parameters.
The same weights support GPU-efficient parallel SSM training and constant-cost event-driven RSNN inference, without conversion.
Evaluated across BabyLM’s Strict-100M, Strict-Small, and Multilingual tracks as an efficient, directly deployable reference point.

figures.caption: Figure 1: URCHIN architecture. The embedding of the current token is injected as input current into a single layer of excitatory (red) and inhibitory (blue) LIF neurons joined only by lateral connections; a linear LM head reads the membrane voltage of the same neurons out to the 16,384-entry vocabulary. Each token is processed by a multi-transmission loop, a fixed number of lateral transmission steps that settles to a fixed point. Parallel URCHIN evaluates this with parallel scans for training; Serial URCHIN runs the identical dynamics event-driven for deployment.

Figure 2: Single-sequence inference throughput of Parallel URCHIN (24 transmission steps, evaluation setting) and Serial URCHIN (event-driven), the mean of the three homogeneous tracks. On the H200 GPU (a) parallel throughput scales with context length while serial is flat; on a single CPU core (b) the event-driven serial path is about seven times faster. Batch size one.

Table 5: Pretraining and fine-tuning hyperparameters for the three tracks. The architecture (a single 128-neuron layer, 80:20 E/I, full [1,1,1,1] lateral connectivity, LIF neurons, no STDP) is identical across tracks. Fine-tuning tasks: the strict tracks use the seven (Super)GLUE tasks (boolq, mnli, mrpc, multirc, qqp, rte, wsc); the Multilingual track uses nine tasks (arc, belebele, bmlama, include, mnli, sib200, truthfulqa, xnli, pos), each in English, Dutch, and Chinese. The Multilingual POS fine-tuning matches the Multilingual classification fine-tuning except for the learning rate and batch size marked in POS, and additionally uses a maximum sequence length of 128 and a warmup ratio and weight decay of 0.1 and 0.01.

papers.title: URCHIN: A Horizontal Spiking Language Model for Data-Constrained Pretraining
papers.tldr: URCHIN is a compact, biologically inspired spiking language model designed for efficient pretraining on child-scale data.

papers.abstract: Delayed Tensor Parallelism (DTP) removes the blocking all-reduce of tensor-parallel Transformer inference. Every device adds its own partial output to its residual stream (and broadcasts it) immediately, but only gathers (receives) the other devices' partials $δ$ modules later. A TP to DTP change therefore amounts to a real architecture change, and dense Transformer models need to be retrained or distilled after adaptation. We show that DTP breaks the permutation symmetry of neurons inside FFNs and of KV heads inside attention modules, and that this symmetry breakage makes the sharding itself a modelling decision. We show that maximising the affinity between the KV heads and the FFN neurons co-located on a device, by permuting the dense model before sharding, speeds up the distillation or retraining process. The affinity is measured with a first-order approximation of the damage that losing a head's contribution does to each neuron's output, and the co-located affinity is maximised with a coordinate-ascent optimiser that alternates an exact balanced assignment of neurons with an exhaustive search over the KV head partitions. The whole procedure takes under two minutes on one GPU for Qwen3-0.6B and Danube3-500M. On these models, at $δ=1$, the affinity-optimised layouts reach any distillation target in about half to two thirds of the steps needed by the naive contiguous layouts, over the whole 10k-step range we tested, and every optimised seed beats every contiguous seed and all but one of the sixteen random layouts. We also show that the co-located affinity score at initialisation predicts the KL to the base model after training, across seventeen layouts ranging from anti-optimised to optimised (Pearson $-0.81$ and $-0.89$).
bullets: DTP removes blocking all-reduce but changes the model architecture, requiring retraining or distillation.
DTP breaks permutation symmetry, making neuron and KV-head sharding choices important modeling decisions.
The method maximizes neuron–KV-head affinity using a first-order damage estimate and coordinate-ascent balanced assignments.
On Qwen3-0.6B and Danube3-500M, optimized layouts reached distillation targets in roughly half to two-thirds as many steps as contiguous layouts across 10k steps.
Initial affinity strongly predicted post-training KL divergence across 17 layouts, though results were evaluated on two small models and a fixed setting of δ=1.

papers.abstract: We generally perceive that training text-to-image diffusion models requires heavy compute: it is true if we aim at a comprehensive frontier model. This understanding prevents people from training their own models when getting started in the field. We develop MiniDog, a framework that enables pretraining diffusion transformers in 55 minutes and fine-tuning in another 15 minutes on four 3090 GPUs. For data, we use 26k dog images from ImageNet and caption them for pretraining and use 2k images generated by FLUX.1-schnell for fine-tuning. We precompute the image and text features and cache them for efficiency. For architecture, we use E2E-INVAE for its semantic latent space, a small transformer with 22M parameters, a small Qwen model for text encoding, and in-context conditioning. For training, we use iREPA and an EUPE perception encoder for acceleration. For evaluation, our repository supports FID, HPSv2 score, PickScore, and various VAE reconstruction metrics.
authors: Reyhaneh Esmailizadeh, Xingjian Leng, Zhanhao Liang, Liang Zheng
bullets: Targets the high compute barrier that discourages newcomers from training text-to-image models.
Uses 26k ImageNet dog images for pretraining and 2k FLUX.1-schnell-generated images for fine-tuning.
Combines cached image/text features, E2E-INVAE latents, a 22M-parameter transformer, Qwen text encoding, and in-context conditioning.
Applies iREPA and an EUPE perception encoder to accelerate training.
The framework supports FID, HPSv2, PickScore, and VAE reconstruction evaluation; the abstract does not report metric values.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models have advanced rapidly, but most remain optimized for single-image inputs. Multi-image reasoning is costly because each image adds many visual tokens, increasing encoding and attention demands. Existing techniques that address the above issue, including visual token pruning, token merging, visual token compression, learned resampling, hierarchical compression, retrieval-augmented visual reasoning, and memory-based architectures, have largely been designed for single-image scenarios, where redundancy is primarily spatial and local. Multi-image reasoning introduces additional challenges: redundancy may occur across images, task-relevant evidence may be sparse or distributed, and aggressive per-image compression can remove details needed for comparison, counting, temporal reasoning, retrieval, or evidence grounding. Moreover, existing token-reduction methods are often either (i) training-free but inference-inefficient, typically relying on accessing attention matrices to get token-importance that may be impractical to access with memory-efficient attention implementations such as FlashAttention, or (ii) training-dependent, requiring the base MLLM to be retrained or adapted to a new compressed-token paradigm. In this work, we study scalable multi-image reasoning and understanding without retraining the base model and without accessing attention matrices at inference time. To this end, we propose mmVB, a lightweight plug-and-play module that assigns query-conditioned per-image token budgets via cross-image context, adding only 1.6M trainable parameters while reducing visual input tokens by 9x. This reduction yields 5x faster time-to-first-token and 7x fewer prefill FLOPs, while maintaining 94.4% of full-resolution accuracy across eight multi-image reasoning benchmarks.
authors: Aimon Rahman, Joymallya Chakraborty, Vidit Bansal, Abhishek Dan
bullets: Multi-image inputs are expensive because each image contributes many visual tokens, with relevant evidence potentially sparse or distributed across images.
mmVB uses cross-image context to assign query-conditioned, per-image token budgets.
The lightweight plug-in adds 1.6M trainable parameters and reduces visual input tokens by 9×.
It delivers 5× faster time-to-first-token and 7× fewer prefill FLOPs while retaining 94.4% of full-resolution accuracy across eight benchmarks.
The approach targets multi-image reasoning without modifying or retraining the base model.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Introduction and Motivation. Existing multi-image methods scale poorly: dense attention breaks FlashAttention and excludes API-only models, token merging disrupts positional encodings and cross-image reasoning, and video-style compression assumes frame similarity. Our pre-encoding predictor instead assigns query-conditioned token budgets using only pixels, enabling compatibility with any MLLM, including closed models.

Figure 2: mmVB architecture. Frozen EfficientNetB0 encodes N images, while frozen LLM embeddings encode the query through mean pooling and a 64- dimensional bottleneck. A two-layer, four-head Transformer processes all N+1 tokens, after which a shared MLP maps each image token to four ordinal logits.

papers.abstract: Pixel-space diffusion models provide an appealing alternative to latent-space diffusion models by directly modeling raw images without relying on a learned tokenizer. However, scaling pixel-space models has predominantly followed dense strategies, tightly coupling model capacity with active computation. In this work, we show that standard LLM-style Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures can be effectively transferred to pixel-space diffusion. Building on this finding, we introduce PixelMoE, a pixel-space generative framework that sparsely scales model capacity with standard LLM-style MoE, without diffusion-specific routing mechanisms or auxiliary routing objectives. Specifically, PixelMoE combines standard Token-Choice (TC) routing with fine-grained routed experts for input-adaptive sparse computation, a shared expert for capturing common representations, and a bias-based load-balancing strategy. To complement sparse capacity scaling, PixelMoE further introduces Pixel-Space Hierarchical Flow Matching, which varies spatial resolution along the denoising trajectory from global structure formation to fine-grained detail refinement. At comparable active parameter counts, PixelMoE consistently outperforms its dense counterparts across model scales, demonstrating effective sparse capacity scaling in pixel space. On class-conditional ImageNet-1K, PixelMoE achieves FID scores of 1.47 at 256x256 and 1.53 at 512x512 without representation alignment or perceptual losses, comparing favorably with leading pixel-space and latent-space generative models. Code and models will be released soon.
authors: Ruixiao Dong, Jianmin Bao, Bozhi Luan, Zijie Meng, Xin Tao, Pengfei Wan, Kun Gai, Li Li, Houqiang Li
bullets: Addresses the challenge of scaling pixel-space diffusion, where dense models tie capacity to active computation.
Uses standard Token-Choice routing, fine-grained routed experts, a shared expert, and bias-based load balancing—without diffusion-specific routing or auxiliary routing losses.
Introduces Pixel-Space Hierarchical Flow Matching to shift from global structure formation to fine-detail refinement across denoising.
At comparable active parameter counts, consistently outperforms dense counterparts across model scales.
Reports FID 1.47 at 256×256 and 1.53 at 512×512 on class-conditional ImageNet-1K, without representation alignment or perceptual losses.

papers.abstract: Residual connections propagate information through a network by additively accumulating layer outputs. Recently proposed alternatives, such as Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections (mHC) and Attention Residuals (AttnRes), instead use more expressive depth aggregation mechanisms that improve language modeling performance at scale. In this work, we consider the mixing of representations over depth as a problem of storing and retrieving information across layers. Formalizing this perspective, we introduce Depth Memory (DM), a unified framework that describes the standard pre-layer-norm (PreLN) transformer, mHC, and AttnRes in terms of streams that carry representations through the network. One such stream, for example, could be an explicit memory stream that is queried to enrich the input to every layer, and whose output is subsequently written back into the memory for use by later layers. For AttnRes, this memory stream is a growing cache of explicit layer representations. For mHC, it is an expanded residual stream. Building on this view, we propose Linear Depth Memory (LDM), which formulates information retrieval across depth as a regression problem solved using recursive least squares. The resulting architecture propagates three streams across depth: the standard residual stream, a linear associative memory stream, and an inverse covariance stream. For high-throughput training and inference, we propose a hardware-aware implementation of LDM that reduces peak activation memory and memory traffic. LDM consistently achieves the lowest perplexities among PreLN, mHC and AttnRes baselines at the 400M and 1.5B parameter scales, alongside competitive zero-shot accuracy.
authors: David Gonz\'alez-Mart\'inez, Philipp Nazari, T. Konstantin Rusch, Shiwei Liu
bullets: Frames representation mixing across layers as storing and retrieving information through depth.
Unifies PreLN Transformers, mHC, and AttnRes as stream-based memory mechanisms.
Introduces LDM, using recursive least squares to retrieve information across depth.
LDM propagates residual, associative-memory, and inverse-covariance streams.
At 400M and 1.5B parameters, LDM reports the lowest perplexities among the compared baselines and competitive zero-shot accuracy.

papers.title: Depth Memory
papers.tldr: Depth Memory unifies residual-style depth aggregation as information storage and retrieval, and its Linear Depth Memory variant improves language-model perplexity with hardware-efficient execution.

papers.abstract: Speculative Decoding (SD) has demonstrated its efficacy in accelerating large language model inference, but for Vision-Language Models (VLMs), the diverse input modalities make it difficult for a small trained drafter to achieve consistently high throughput. Self-speculative decoding reuses parts of the target model as a drafter which retains the multi-modal capability of the VLMs, yet its efficiency depends on choosing a suitable draft configuration for each prompt. We propose Single-Peak SPeculative decoding (SP$^2$ec), a training-free bandit algorithm that adapts the draft configuration during generation. SP$^2$ec exploits the single-peak throughput pattern observed in existing self-speculative methods, including SWIFT, KnapSpec, SpecVLM, and our simple cosSim. Our algorithmic design explicitly minimizes a novel notion of wall-time regret for each given query, corresponding to the empirical wall-time latency. Theoretical guarantees on the wall-time regret show that SP$^2$ec can exploit the optimal draft configuration, with negligible exploration cost. Extensive experiments on Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct and LLaVA-NeXT-Mistral-7B across visual and textual tasks show consistent improvements of up to 11\% over the original self-speculative methods, demonstrating the wide applicability of the proposed SP$^2$ec algorithm.
authors: Yuqi Huang, Xingyao Li, Yunlong Hou, Fengzhuo Zhang, Jiachun Pan, Vincent Y. F. Tan
bullets: VLM inputs make it difficult for a separately trained draft model to deliver consistent speculative-decoding speedups.
SP²ec reuses parts of the target VLM and adapts its draft configuration separately for each prompt during generation.
It exploits the empirically observed single-peak relationship between draft configuration and throughput.
The method minimizes query-specific wall-time regret and has theoretical guarantees with negligible exploration cost.
Experiments on Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct and LLaVA-NeXT-Mistral-7B report improvements of up to 11% over original self-speculative methods across visual and textual tasks.

papers.abstract: Image-token compression must reduce computation without hurting the semantics. We introduce Varest, guided by semantic fungibility: tokens within a coherent semantic region can be summarized coarsely, while object boundaries and literal text require finer distinctions. Object and text localizers guide variable-resolution merging, preserving spatial coverage and finer detail at boundaries and text. Learned [REL] registers then prune visual tokens after early decoder processing. Training across budgets enables one checkpoint per backbone. Across three backbones and 13 benchmarks, Varest outperforms 15 baselines in mean performance retention at every evaluated budget, retaining 86.10-92.33% of full-token performance with only 5.56% of the original layer-averaged image-token count.
authors: Tianhao Fu, Austin Wang, Charles Chen, Roby Aldave-Garza, Victor Xie, Xiyue Jiao, Yucheng Chen, Martin Tin
bullets: Targets lower computation without sacrificing semantic understanding.
Uses semantic, variable-resolution token merging guided by object and text localization.
Preserves spatial coverage and finer distinctions at object boundaries and literal text.
Learned [REL] registers perform additional relevance pruning after early decoder processing.
Across 3 backbones and 13 benchmarks, retains 86.10–92.33% of full-token performance using 5.56% of the original layer-averaged image tokens, outperforming 15 baselines at every evaluated budget.

papers.abstract: The Key-Value (KV) cache constitutes a dominant source of memory consumption during large language model (LLM) inference, particularly in long-context and complex reasoning scenarios. Existing KV cache quantization methods have explored different compression granularities, including layer-wise precision adjustment and token-level information preservation. In practical deployment, however, the key challenge is not merely compression, but how to allocate limited quantization resources among heterogeneous precision preservation strategies under a fixed KV cache memory budget. We propose MultiAlloc, a profiling-guided precision allocation framework for KV cache quantization that adaptively distributes limited quantization resources between layer-wise precision enhancement and token-wise preservation. MultiAlloc employs lightweight offline profiling to characterize layer sensitivity and token importance, enabling adaptive precision allocation under a fixed memory constraint. Guided by the profiled memory--accuracy trade-off, it automatically derives an effective precision allocation strategy without online allocation search, and applies the resulting policy during inference. Extensive experiments on reasoning and long-context benchmarks demonstrate that MultiAlloc consistently improves over layer-wise, token-wise, and recent multi-granularity KV cache quantization methods under matched memory budgets across diverse models, including Mistral, Llama, DeepSeek-Qwen, and QwQ.
authors: Yangchengyu Zhou, Zhiping Wu, Runchang Jiang, Dongdong Ren, Youfang Han, Wei Zhao, Dongqi Cai, Wenbin Li
bullets: Targets KV-cache memory bottlenecks in long-context and reasoning-focused LLM inference.
Profiles layer sensitivity and token importance to guide adaptive precision allocation.
Balances layer-wise precision enhancement with token-wise preservation under a fixed budget.
Derives the allocation policy offline, avoiding online allocation search.
Shows consistent gains over existing single- and multi-granularity methods across diverse models and benchmarks at matched memory budgets.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of MultiAlloc. An offline profiling stage estimates layer-wise precision demands and token-wise preservation demands, followed by a budget-coupled precision allocation module that derives the static policy (q⋆,k⋆) under a fixed KV cache memory budget B. The policy is then directly applied during online inference.

Figure 1: Motivation for budget-aware precision allocation under a fixed KV cache budget. Different layers exhibit heterogeneous demands for layer precision enhancement and token preservation. Existing layer-wise and token-wise methods optimize individual preservation strategies, while MultiAlloc profiles these demands and allocates the shared memory budget across preservation strategies.

papers.tldr: MultiAlloc improves KV-cache quantization by allocating a fixed memory budget between layer- and token-level precision preservation using offline profiling.

papers.abstract: Different MRI modalities reveal different parts of a brain tumor. Segmentation models combine information from these modalities to outline tumor regions. Many models use a separate encoder for each modality. However, exchanging features among these encoders at several stages can increase model complexity. We introduce the Block-Wise Shared Adapter (BWSA), which combines compressed features from the modality encoders in a shared path and returns adapted features to each stream. In its fixed-blending form, BWSA adds the adapted features to the original features. Its trainable-gated variant (TG-BWSA) instead learns separate weights for the original and adapted features at each modality and encoder stage. We evaluate both variants on BraTS 2020 and BraTS 2023 with four segmentation backbones. On the official BraTS 2023 online validation set, BWSA increases average region-wise Dice by 1.3--7.6 percentage points relative to the corresponding unmodified backbones. TG-BWSA increases it by 2.8--7.7 points. Both variants add approximately 0.85--3.73% parameters and reduce average HD95 relative to the unmodified backbones.
authors: Milad Rostamian, Mohammadreza Mohammadi, Ender Konukoglu, Mohsen Soryani
bullets: Separate modality encoders can become complex when exchanging features across multiple stages.
BWSA compresses and combines encoder features in a shared path, then returns adapted features to each modality stream.
TG-BWSA learns stage- and modality-specific gates to balance original and adapted features.
Across four backbones on BraTS 2020/2023, both variants improve segmentation; TG-BWSA yields larger reported Dice gains on the BraTS 2023 validation set.
The adapters add approximately 0.85–3.73% parameters and reduce average HD95 versus unmodified backbones.

papers.abstract: Post-training pruning enables efficient deployment, but conventional methods do not explicitly preserve internal-gradient alignment between sparse and dense models. We study novel connections between downstream performance of compressed models and the ability to retain gradient information via influence-function preservation. Central to this connection is a curvature-aware objective that accounts for both layer activations and backpropagated gradients. Despite its promise, this objective remains underexplored in pruning due to a lack of efficient solvers. We introduce $\texttt{CACTUS}$, a novel ADMM-based optimizer supporting both pruning and sparse-plus-low-rank decompositions of pre-trained weights. Compared to LLM-Surgeon which targets the same objective, $\texttt{CACTUS}$ can achieve over an order-of-magnitude speedup. At $50\%$ pruning of Qwen3-4B, $\texttt{CACTUS}$ reduces the C4 perplexity gap to the dense model by $45\%$, improves compressed-to-dense per-sample gradient cosine similarity on WikiText-2 from $0.670$ to $0.755$, and runs over $28\times$ faster than LLM-Surgeon on substantially weaker hardware. By preserving influence functions, $\texttt{CACTUS}$ supports effective data selection. On Llama-3.2-3B, fine-tuning a fresh dense model on the $5\%$ of data selected by $\texttt{CACTUS}$ achieves $49.44\%$ accuracy on BIG-Bench Hard, compared with $47.22\%$ using ALPS and $49.54\%$ using dense-model selection. Finally, integrating $\texttt{CACTUS}$ with LoGRA, a recent gradient-projection strategy, on Qwen3-4B with MLP layers pruned to 2:4 sparsity and a rank-64 correction retains a $0.711$ cosine alignment with dense LoGRA-projected C4 gradients.
authors: Mehdi Makni, Natalia Ponomareva, Rahul Mazumder
bullets: Targets the gap between efficient pruning and preservation of internal-gradient alignment with dense models.
Optimizes layer activations and backpropagated gradients through a curvature-aware objective.
Supports both pruning and sparse-plus-low-rank weight decompositions via ADMM.
At 50% Qwen3-4B pruning, it narrows the C4 perplexity gap by 45%, raises WikiText-2 gradient cosine similarity from 0.670 to 0.755, and runs over 28× faster than LLM-Surgeon on weaker hardware.
Preserved influence functions enable effective data selection; 5% CACTUS-selected data reaches 49.44% BIG-Bench Hard accuracy, close to dense-model selection at 49.54%.

papers.abstract: Few-step distillation reduces the sampling cost of diffusion and flow models, but existing approaches often require auxiliary score models or specialized architectures. We show that simple on-policy velocity regression already provides a strong foundation for 4-NFE generation. To represent teacher velocity variation within each coarse transition, we introduce Pivot, a training-only residual proxy that separates local corrections from the student's interval-mean prediction. We further repel the student from weaker teacher predictions, providing a lightweight mechanism for avoiding undesirable modes. The resulting framework, Simplified Matching Distillation (SMD), remains entirely regression-based, requires neither online score estimation nor adversarial training, and leaves the deployed generator unchanged. We evaluate SMD on image generation and editing, 3D generation, video synthesis, and joint audio--video generation, scaling to 33 billion parameters. At 4-NFE, SMD outperforms strong few-step baselines and surpasses multi-step teachers on several benchmarks. It also supports cross-model, multi-teacher, and causal-video distillation.
authors: Jiawei Zhang, Ziyu Wan, Nanye Ma, Long Zhao, Dong Chen, Hongyu Liu, Qifeng Chen, Dongdong Chen
bullets: Uses on-policy velocity regression as the foundation for few-step distillation.
Introduces Pivot, a training-only residual proxy that captures teacher velocity variation within coarse transitions.
Repels the student from weaker teacher predictions to reduce undesirable modes.
Evaluated across image, 3D, video, and joint audio–video generation, including models up to 33B parameters.
Supports cross-model, multi-teacher, and causal-video distillation; reports outperforming strong few-step baselines and surpassing multi-step teachers on several benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Visual token pruning for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) appears highly effective, with existing methods retaining over 95% of unpruned performance on common VQA benchmarks using a quarter of the visual tokens or fewer. However, our extensive evaluation of ten methods across three MLLM families and five ability groups reveals a critical gap: strong general performance often comes at the cost of severe degradation on fine-grained tasks such as OCR and visual grounding. We trace these failures to two limitations of the prevailing paradigm of retaining the highest-ranked native patches. A single importance ranking overlooks the complementary evidence required by different tasks, while sparse patch selection disrupts both image content and spatial integrity. To address these limitations, we propose Bifocal, a training-free, two-stage pruning method built on a mixed-granularity framework. It allocates separate budgets to query-focused and image-intrinsic evidence, complemented by a pooled coarse representation of the entire image. Before the LLM, Bifocal matches question words to visual regions through a soft conjunction balanced against norm-debiased image saliency, while selecting image-intrinsic evidence to maximize representational coverage. Inside the LLM, it further prunes tokens using density-adjusted text-to-image attention. With roughly a quarter of the original visual tokens, Bifocal is the only evaluated method to retain over 90% of unpruned performance in every ability group across all three models, and ranks first on average in all nine model-budget settings. The code is available at: https://github.com/EIT-NLP/Bifocal
authors: Peiran Yin, Hao Wu, Zihao Yang, Fengyu Zhou, Yijuan Liang, Haozhe Hu, Xudong Wang, Wei Zhang, Xiaoyu Shen
bullets: Existing pruning methods can retain strong overall performance but substantially harm OCR and visual grounding.
Bifocal uses mixed-granularity pruning with separate query-focused and image-intrinsic token budgets plus a pooled whole-image representation.
It matches question words to regions, balances this with norm-debiased image saliency, maximizes coverage, and applies density-adjusted text-to-image attention pruning inside the LLM.
Using roughly one-quarter of the visual tokens, it retained over 90% of unpruned performance in every evaluated ability group across three MLLM families.
The method was evaluated across ten pruning methods, five ability groups, and nine model-budget settings; code is publicly available.

papers.abstract: Equivariant machine learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) promise atomistic simulations with accuracy approaching that of quantum-mechanical calculations. However, the high computational cost of their core Clebsch--Gordan tensor product (CGTP) convolutions severely limits model scalability and efficiency. In this paper, we rethink the parallel execution of CGTP convolutions and introduce LunaTP. Built on node-centric execution, LunaTP exploits path-group parallelism and multi-level reuse to accelerate CGTP convolutions and higher-order derivative computation while preserving the underlying mathematical formulation. On an NVIDIA H100 GPU, LunaTP achieves kernel speedups of up to 250.0$\times$ over e3nn and 17.1$\times$ over OpenEquivariance. It also delivers end-to-end training throughput gains of up to 28.7$\times$ over e3nn and 3.11$\times$ over OpenEquivariance. Finally, LunaTP demonstrates scalability and robust performance across models, workload scales, and GPUs, delivering substantial acceleration for training and atomistic simulation with high-accuracy equivariant MLIPs.

Achieves end-to-end training throughput gains of up to 28.7× over e3nn and 3.11× over OpenEquivariance.
Shows robust performance across models, workload scales, and GPUs, supporting faster training and atomistic simulation.

papers.abstract: Post-training quantisation reduces the memory cost of large language models, but it remains unclear whether compression preserves language skills of regional varieties as reliably as their standard-language counterparts. We study this question for Bavarian, Standard German, and English using BAVGROUND, a multiple-choice benchmark, where 206 source questions are aligned across all three languages. Across 14 open-weight 7B--10B instruction models, we compare BF16 with 8-bit GPTQ and two 4-bit settings, GPTQ and AWQ. Eight-bit GPTQ remains close to BF16 and largely preserves the relative behaviour of the three languages, while 4-bit quantisation was found to be much less stable. The two 4-bit methods reduce average accuracy by about 1.4--1.5 percentage points and change 11.9--16.0% of BF16 decisions, with changes concentrated on examples where the BF16 model is already uncertain. This instability does not translate into a consistent Bavarian disadvantage. Although Bavarian, a low-resource dialect, has lower baseline accuracy than German and English, the language most affected at 4 bits varies across models and quantisation methods. Calibration further shapes these cross-language effects: the relative Bavarian--German effect changes with calibration language, while changing the calibration source has little average effect on GPTQ-4 but can affect AWQ-4 much more strongly. Free-form evaluation on five models further shows that 4-bit compression can degrade generated responses even in settings where multiple-choice accuracy changes only modestly, while 8-bit GPTQ remains comparatively stable. Overall, our results show that quantisation robustness for regional language varieties depends on the model, quantisation method, calibration data, and evaluation setting, and cannot be measured by aggregate multilingual accuracy alone.

papers.abstract: Random features provide a standard approach to scaling kernel methods to large datasets by approximating the kernel with a finite-dimensional feature map. Existing works of random feature methods primarily focus on well-specified models and light-tailed noise conditions, leaving a gap in understanding their performance under more general conditions, such as misspecified models and heavy-tailed noise. In this paper, we provide a comprehensive and improved analysis of kernel ridge regression with random features (KRR-RF) under general conditions. In the light-tailed noise setting, we improve upon the worst-case uniform bounds of the feature map used in the previous works and lead to the minimax optimal learning rates with $2r+\gamma>\alpha_0$, where $(r,\gamma,\alpha_0)$ denote the regularity of the target function, the effective dimension of the kernel, and the embedding index of the RKHS, respectively. In the heavy-tailed noise setting, we leverage a recently developed Hilbert-valued Fuk-Nagaev inequality and extend the same optimal results under finite weak moment conditions. The additional cost to achieve robustness is a mildly stronger explicit sample-size requirement than in the light-tailed case. For both settings, our results recover the conditions random features budgets (up to log factors) required in the previous works. In the most benign case when $\alpha_0=\gamma$, KRR-RF are minimax optimal for all $r \in (0,1]$. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to establish optimal learning rates for KRR-RF under weak moment conditions in the misspecified setting. Numerical experiments and a real data analysis validate the derived learning rates and demonstrate their practical relevance in the presence of mis-specification and heavy-tailed noise.

papers.abstract: Guardrail approaches that rely on reasoning-based large language models (LLM) improve safety decisions, but come with substantial inference overhead due to the explicit reasoning. We introduce LR-Guard (Latent Reasoning Guardrail), an efficient and explainable guardrail that jointly learns structured latent reasoning and on-demand reasoning reconstruction. Our method distills a frozen teacher's analysis of safe and unsafe prompt interpretations and their comparison into compact latent representations. Joint training optimizes these representations for both safety prediction and reconstruction of the teacher's explicit reasoning traces, enabling human-readable explanations without requiring intermediate text generation for every decision. Experiments show that LR-Guard outperforms its explicit-reasoning teacher in most in-domain and out-of-domain settings on safety classification and explanation extraction, while achieving a 19.4x inference speedup at batch size one. Further, reconstructed reasoning traces from the latent information exhibit high semantic similarity to the teacher's explicit reasoning.

bullets: Addresses the inference overhead of reasoning-based LLM guardrails.

Achieves a 19.4× inference speedup at batch size one, with reconstructed traces showing high semantic similarity to the teacher’s reasoning.

papers.abstract: Benchmarks are essential for evaluating and improving large language models (LLMs). Yet many widely used benchmarks are redundant, making evaluation unnecessarily expensive. Benchmark compression lowers this cost by estimating full-benchmark scores and rankings from a partial evaluation. Research in this area has grown rapidly since 2024, but to our knowledge no survey has systematically organized its methods and findings. We review 119 papers to explain how methods choose what to evaluate, recover full-benchmark results, and verify their reliability. From this analysis, we develop a taxonomy covering compression within individual benchmarks, across benchmark suites, and during adaptive evaluation, together with work on redundancy and reliability. We compare their information needs, total costs, reliability checks, and limitations. Methods reduce evaluation costs by selecting representative subsets, using cheaper or reusable information, and testing adaptively, but risk poor coverage, inaccurate estimates, and sequential delays. The resulting taxonomy and practical guide help researchers choose, validate, and deploy methods for more efficient and reliable LLM evaluation.
authors: Guoming Ling, Yupei Lin, Zhongzhan Huang, Junxin Li, Junjie Liu, Shanshan Zhong, Hefeng Wu, Liang Lin
bullets: Identifies redundancy in widely used LLM benchmarks as a major source of unnecessary evaluation expense.
Taxonomizes methods for compression within benchmarks, across benchmark suites, and through adaptive evaluation.
Analyzes how methods select evaluations, reconstruct full-benchmark scores and rankings, and verify reliability.
Finds that representative subsets, cheaper or reusable information, and adaptive testing can reduce costs.
Highlights risks including poor coverage, inaccurate estimates, and delays from sequential evaluation, and offers practical guidance for method selection and validation.

papers.abstract: Prefix reuse improves LLM inference by sharing the KV cache of common prompt prefixes. This helps only if the scheduler can execute a matched branch in the current worker round. Schedulers assume that a matched prefix is ready, which holds for full attention but fails for hybrid LLMs. There, a branch (the consumer) may need recurrent state that another branch (the producer) is still computing in the same round. The native scheduler stops its waiting-queue scan at this blocked consumer, and the resulting head-of-line blocking creates \emph{execution bubbles}: idle batch slots that independent work could fill. We introduce RadixFlow, which decouples prefix matching from state readiness. Its state-ready traversal turns a global scan barrier into a local wait: only the consumer is blocked until the next round, while feasible independent branches keep filling the batch under the native state check. On five hybrid models, RadixFlow lowers mean latency by 3\% to 24\% and worker rounds by 11\% to 44\% at almost unchanged reuse. On the larger Qwen3.5 models, ablations show that most of the gain comes from traversal, which adds little on a full-attention control. Heavier rounds limit how much of this saving reaches latency.
authors: Huihao Jing, Wenbin Hu, Shaojin Chen, Haochen Shi, Haoyu Huang, Sirui Zhang, Yuxuan Liu, Zhongwei Xie, Haoran Li
bullets: Prefix matching can fail when a hybrid-LLM consumer depends on state still being computed by a producer in the same round.
The native scheduler stops scanning at the blocked consumer, causing head-of-line blocking and idle batch slots.
RadixFlow decouples prefix matching from state readiness through state-ready traversal, turning a global scan barrier into a local wait.
Across five hybrid models, it reduces mean latency by 3%–24% and worker rounds by 11%–44% with nearly unchanged prefix reuse.
Traversal provides most gains on larger Qwen3.5 models; heavier rounds limit latency improvements, while full-attention workloads see little added benefit.

papers.abstract: Running large language models (LLMs) on consumer hardware is bottlenecked by the key-value (KV) cache, which grows with every decoded token and quickly exhausts the memory and bandwidth of a single consumer GPU. We present SparPR (Sparse Partial Recomputation), a runtime KV-cache recovery mechanism that does not modify model weights and requires no offline training. SparPR couples three online decisions: Query-Aware key-block selection scores historical blocks against the current query; dynamic budget control estimates per-block copy and recompute costs to decide how many blocks to retain; and on-demand local recomputation with cost-aware fallback merges retained blocks into continuous spans and switches between sparse recomputation and full recovery according to a runtime cost comparison. Implemented on FlexGen/FlexLLMGen, SparPR is evaluated on a single consumer laptop (RTX 3070 Ti 8GB, Ryzen 9 6900HX, 16GB RAM). It cuts end-to-end latency by 31%, 52%, and 63% at 1k, 2k, and 4k prompt tokens respectively, with 1.4x-2.7x higher throughput, and completes an 8k-token workload in 44 minutes where the FlexGen baseline times out. Under a fixed cache budget, SparPR retains a Needle Accuracy that stays well above StreamingLLM and H2O at every keep ratio, and ablation studies confirm that the three mechanisms act jointly.
authors: Jieyun Deng, Keming Hu, Yanghe Liu, Li Feng
bullets: Targets KV-cache growth that can exhaust single consumer GPUs during long-context decoding.
Combines query-aware key-block selection, dynamic retention budgets, and cost-aware local or full recomputation.
Requires no model-weight changes or offline training and integrates with FlexGen/FlexLLMGen.
On an RTX 3070 Ti laptop, it reduces latency by 31%–63% across 1k–4k prompts and achieves 1.4×–2.7× higher throughput.
Completes an 8k-token workload in 44 minutes, while the FlexGen baseline times out; cache retention remains strong across keep ratios.

papers.abstract: Training-free diffusion-based compression methods repurpose the generative priors of a diffusion or a flow model to compress data without retraining them as task-specific codecs. Recent codebook-based approaches such as Turbo-DDCM achieve strong perceptual quality at ultra-low bitrates, but their reliance on dense Gaussian codebooks remains costly in both memory and computation, and scales poorly with the large latent dimensions of modern image and video generators. Their combinatorial bitstream encoding further becomes computationally heavy at this scale. We introduce H-DDCM, a scalable generative compression framework that replaces Gaussian codebooks with implicit randomized Hadamard dictionaries. The fast Walsh-Hadamard transform allows for implicitly synthesizing full-dimensional dictionaries with $O(d \log d)$ compute for projection and reconstruction and $O(d)$ memory, without materializing the full-dimensional dictionary. We further introduce an efficient table-free lexicographic coding scheme that makes combinatorial encoding practical at larger dimensions. Beyond images, we adapt the framework to an autoregressive video flow model and develop a streaming compression scheme that periodically re-encodes recently reconstructed frames into a fresh KV-cache prefix, preserving temporal context across segments at no additional transmitted bits. This enables long-form, close to real-time generative video compression on a single GPU. Across image and video benchmarks, H-DDCM achieves competitive rate-distortion-perception performance while substantially reducing the memory and computational overhead of codebook-based training-free generative compression.
authors: Or Ronai, Vladimir Kulikov, Tomer Michaeli
bullets: Targets the memory, computation, and encoding costs of codebook-based generative compression at large latent dimensions.
Uses randomized Hadamard dictionaries with fast Walsh-Hadamard transforms, requiring O(d log d) projection/reconstruction compute and O(d) memory.
Introduces table-free lexicographic coding to make combinatorial bitstream encoding practical at larger dimensions.
Extends the framework to autoregressive video with streaming re-encoding of reconstructed frames to preserve temporal context without extra transmitted bits.
Reports competitive rate-distortion-perception performance with substantially lower codebook-related overhead, including long-form near-real-time video compression on a single GPU.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Quantitative comparison of image compression methods. We compare H-DDCM with training-free diffusion-based and other compression methods in terms of rate, distortion, and perception. Distortion is measured by PSNR, perceptual quality by FID (presented in log-scale), and runtime by round-trip encoding and decoding time. GPU memory refers to the excess memory used by training-free methods for dictionary storage, while tables memory refers to disk storage required by Turbo-DDCM’s precomputed combinatorial tables. The first row corresponds to training-free methods utilizing the SD 2.1 backbone (512 × 512, d = 214) and other compression methods. The second row corresponds to FLUX backbone (1024 × 1024, d = 218). The dashed gray vertical line denotes the VAE encoder-decoder bound. H-DDCM achieves competitive results on the ratedistortion-perception tradeoff, all the while being the fastest training-free method, avoiding explicit codebook materialization. Error bars represent the standard error of the mean (SEM).

Figure 3: Quantitative comparison of video compression methods. We compare H-DDCM OC (B = 8) with training-free methods using the same CF backbone and other compression baselines in terms of rate, distortion and perception. Distortion is measured by PSNR, and perceptual quality is measured by DOVER and FVMD (presented in log-scale). Encoding and decoding FPS report compression and decompression throughput, and are compared among methods using the CF backbone. H-DDCM achieves competitive rate-distortion-perception performance among the CF-based training-free methods while providing the highest measured encoding and decoding throughput, without codebooks materialization. Error bars represent the standard error of the mean (SEM).

papers.abstract: Vision Transformers achieve strong performance but incur high computational costs from quadratic token interactions. Training-free token reduction methods improve efficiency, but their robustness remains underexplored. We propose Prune-and Merge ViT, a training-free framework for off-the-shelf models. It combines class attention-based pruning with similarity-based merging to reduce redundancy while preserving semantic information. To evaluate robustness we introduce two metrics. Relative Accuracy Drop (RAD) measures relative accuracy degradation under transformations, and Prediction Flip Rate (PFR) quantifies prediction consistency. On pretrained ViT and DeiT, Prune-and-Merge reduces computation competitively while maintaining robustness and better accuracy than existing token reduction methods. Our analysis suggests that hybrid token reduction does not introduce hallucination-like behavior and preserves prediction stability for common image transformations.
authors: Vatsal, Soumil Malhotra, Priyanshu Chahal, Sanjeev Kumar
bullets: Addresses the quadratic cost of token interactions and limited understanding of robustness in training-free token reduction.
Uses class-attention pruning to remove less-important tokens and similarity-based merging to reduce redundancy.
Introduces Relative Accuracy Drop (RAD) and Prediction Flip Rate (PFR) to assess robustness under image transformations.
Evaluated on pretrained ViT and DeiT models, it achieves competitive compute reduction with better accuracy than existing token-reduction methods.
Finds that hybrid token reduction preserves prediction stability and does not produce hallucination-like behavior for common transformations.

papers.abstract: Some observation-window-based KV cache compressors use prompt attention to identify important tokens but allocate uniform or predefined budgets across heads, overlooking input-dependent differences in budget demand. We propose ChampionKV, an input-adaptive head-wise budget allocator for long-context KV cache compression. It uses the maximum aggregated observation-window attention score as a lightweight empirical proxy for attention concentration, assigning larger budgets to heads with dispersed attention and smaller budgets to concentrated heads. An abnormal-head mask and a floor-budget mechanism improve robustness under weak attention responses. ChampionKV plugs into compressors such as SnapKV and PyramidKV without changing their token-selection procedures. On LongBench and RULER, both Champion variants consistently improve over their SnapKV and PyramidKV base compressors; the improvements are largest and statistically significant on Llama3.1-70B-Instruct, especially under tight budgets, whereas results on the tested 7B/8B models remain competitive but mixed. ChampionKV does not uniformly outperform Ada-KV, whose global cross-head Top-K selection retains an advantage in several settings. Controlled analysis further shows improved retained attention mass over the corresponding base compressors at negligible overhead.
authors: Yuechuan Chen, Yanda Guo, Xiaoxi Liu, Weilin Ruan, Huanbo Xu, Ruyi Wang, Wei Zhu

papers.abstract: Non-prefix KV cache reuse is a promising approach for improving inference efficiency in multi-agent systems as agents share the same context blocks. However, when agents have conflicting tasks, directly reusing non-prefix KV caches across agents can severely degrade model performance, causing up to a 90% drop. Existing remedies, including selective recomputation and offset-based calibration, recover a limited fraction of this loss. We argue that the problem lies not only in contaminated KV representations but also in the agent's difficulty interpreting reused context under its own instructions. To this end, we introduce LatentRemedy, which uses a few task-conditioned latent tokens to help the target agent leverage reused context without recomputing the shared block. Specifically, we use an MLP to map the last hidden state of the target prefix into a small number of latent tokens, which are placed after the reused KV block to interact with the shared context. To guide subsequent predictions toward the target task, we train the MLP through full-prefill distillation. Experiments show that LatentRemedy consistently outperforms existing reuse baselines on conflicting tasks while maintaining TTFT close to direct reuse as cache size grows. Code and data are available at https://github.com/chenzhwsysu57/kvreuse.
authors: Zhiwei Chen, Zhongtao Rao, Waikit Xiu, Yuxiang Zhang, Shuting Cui, Jian Chen, Tianxiang Zhao
bullets: Non-prefix KV reuse improves inference efficiency but can cause up to a 90% performance drop when agents have conflicting tasks.
The method maps the target agent’s final prefix hidden state to a small set of latent tokens using an MLP.
These tokens are inserted after the reused KV block to help the target agent interpret shared context under its own instructions.
Full-prefill distillation trains the MLP to guide predictions toward the target task.
LatentRemedy consistently outperforms existing reuse remedies while keeping TTFT close to direct reuse as cache size increases.

papers.abstract: Long-running agents retain KV caches across turns and sessions for hours or days. Compressing these persistent caches requires reducing storage while controlling reconstruction error. We present AlignPred, a codec that combines local alignment with predictive coding under a configurable KV reconstruction-error budget. Local orthogonal transforms align related heads or layers into a common coordinate frame, allowing AlignPred to combine token-wise prediction with same-token prediction across heads or layers. Residuals are quantized on an error-bounded lattice and entropy-coded, without learned predictors, encoder-side mode search, or large joint transforms. Across three attention mechanisms, AlignPred requires less storage than the evaluated baselines at comparable measured reconstruction error. Against the evaluated CPU codec implementations, it decodes at least 1.6 times faster while matching or improving encode time. AlignPred achieves near-native task scores at substantially compressed operating points on LongBench-Pro at 128K context. AlignPred's SGLang HiCache integration reduces persistent target-KV storage by 42-72% relative to native HiCache, with comparable latency.

bullets: Targets long-running agents that retain KV caches across turns and sessions.

Uses error-bounded lattice quantization and entropy coding without learned predictors or large joint transforms.
Uses less storage than evaluated baselines at comparable reconstruction error and decodes at least 1.6× faster than evaluated CPU codecs.
Reduces SGLang HiCache persistent target-KV storage by 42–72% with comparable latency and near-native LongBench-Pro scores at 128K context.
