papers.selection_reason: Presents an error-controlled KV cache compression codec, directly targeting memory-efficient inference.
papers.title: AlignPred: Error-Controlled KV Cache Compression via Alignment and Predictive Coding
papers.tldr: AlignPred compresses persistent KV caches with bounded reconstruction error while reducing storage and maintaining fast decoding and near-native long-context performance.

papers.abstract: Long-context inference makes the key-value (KV) cache a major memory bottleneck for large language models. We propose BELT, a low-rank KV cache compression framework. Its key-side objective targets attention distributions rather than raw keys or pre-softmax logits, yielding a quadratic surrogate with a closed-form low-rank solution. A learned global rank allocator uses differentiable soft selection during training and hard selection at deployment to meet a user-specified component budget. Experiments demonstrate improved model quality under aggressive compression and increased decoding throughput at comparable accuracy. Evaluated across three LLMs and multiple benchmarks, BELT achieves up to 70% low-rank KV cache compression while outperforming the strongest baseline by up to 23.3 points on LongBench, and up to 17.8x overall KV cache reduction when combined with quantization. With Triton-based GPU kernels and a quantized cache, BELT delivers up to 2.7x speedup for the attention module and 3.3x end-to-end decoding throughput.
authors: Yaoyang Liu, Shuwei Shen, Jincheng Tang, Jinguang Liu, Jinbao Xue, Hailong Yang, Ke Zhang, Yinjun Wu
bullets: Targets attention distributions rather than raw keys or logits, producing a quadratic objective with a closed-form low-rank solution.
Learns global top-k rank allocation using differentiable soft selection during training and hard selection at deployment.
Across three LLMs and multiple benchmarks, achieves up to 70% low-rank KV-cache compression and up to 17.8× reduction with quantization.
Reports up to 23.3-point LongBench gains over the strongest baseline and up to 3.3× end-to-end decoding throughput.
Uses Triton GPU kernels and quantized caches to reach up to 2.7× attention-module speedup.

papers.selection_reason: Low-rank KV cache compression with learned rank allocation for long-context LLM inference, directly targeting KV-cache memory efficiency.
papers.title: BELT : BEhavior-Aligned Low-Rank KV Cache Compression with Learned Top-k Rank Allocation
papers.tldr: BELT compresses long-context KV caches with behavior-aligned low-rank representations and learned rank allocation, improving memory efficiency and decoding speed while preserving quality.

papers.abstract: The design of attention mechanisms in long-context large language models faces an ``impossible triangle'' among KV cache size, training and prefill FLOPs, and model quality. GQA achieves strong quality but incurs high KV cache overhead; alternative approaches such as MLA and MFA can compress the cache, but MLA suffers from quality loss while MFA substantially increases training and prefill compute. We propose Virtual Head Attention (VHA), which simultaneously improves all three vertices through two lightweight linear operations: Q Premix applies a near-identity transformation to queries within each KV group to recover virtual head diversity from halved physical query heads, and Linear Postmix fuses inter-head features via a low-rank $I + AB^\top$ residual structure. Since VHA introduces no nonlinear operations, Premix can be folded into the query projection and Postmix into the output projection at inference time, reducing the model to a standard GQA-2 architecture that directly reuses all existing GQA inference optimizations. With only two KV heads, the group size in large models readily reaches 64, fully exploiting Tensor Core parallelism during decoding. Across four scales with 4K-context 50B-token pretraining, VHA consistently surpasses the standard GQA baseline at every scale ($+$0.05\% to $+$0.81\%), while reducing KV cache by $4\times$ vs.\ GQA-8 at dense scales and $2\times$ vs.\ GQA-4 at the MoE scale, and lowering training and prefill FLOPs by 7.9\% (1.7B, $S{=}4096$). On an industrial 30B-A3B MoE model trained on 500B tokens at 8K context, VHA outperforms both MLA and GQA-4 by $+$0.70\,/\,$+$2.60\,\% on a 12-benchmark base-model evaluation suite; in a separate matched 10B-A1B MoE comparison after long-context mid-training, VHA attains an average RULER score of 84.4 over 8K--128K versus 73.0 for GQA, while using two rather than four KV heads in the full-attention layers.
authors: Xibo Ding, Guoxia Wang, Jinle Zeng, Jiabin Yang, Sirui Tao, Chao Yang, Dianhai Yu
bullets: Targets the trade-off among KV-cache size, training/prefill compute, and model quality in long-context LLMs.
Uses two lightweight linear operations: Q Premix restores virtual query-head diversity, while Linear Postmix fuses inter-head features with a low-rank residual structure.
The operations can be folded into existing projections at inference, yielding a standard GQA-2 model compatible with GQA optimizations and Tensor Core decoding.
Across four model scales, VHA improves over GQA while reducing KV cache by 2–4× and training/prefill FLOPs by 7.9% in one reported setting.
On industrial MoE evaluations, VHA outperforms MLA and GQA and achieves higher long-context RULER scores than GQA while using fewer KV heads.

papers.title: Virtual Head Attention
papers.tldr: Virtual Head Attention (VHA) reduces KV-cache and compute costs while maintaining or improving long-context language-model quality over standard attention alternatives.

papers.abstract: Traditional time-series classification methods often operate as black boxes, providing a class prediction without indicating which time point or time interval within the series led to that prediction. To improve temporal interpretability, MILLET (Multiple Instance Learning with Temporal Explanation), which combines an InceptionTime encoder with Conjunctive Pooling, provides both classification and temporal explanations. However, MILLET contains approximately 424 K parameters, making it unsuitable for deployment on resource-constrained micro-controllers, and it achieves an overall time-series accuracy of 0.888 and an explanation score of 0.681 NDCG@n. We therefore propose SEA-Net, a lightweight architecture using small multi-scale depthwise-separable convolutional TSC encoders and improved Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) pooling heads. Our SEA-Net bottleneck encoder with Top-k pooling achieves 0.931 accuracy and 0.765 NDCG@n with only 41 K parameters. Another variant, using a gated encoder with Top-k pooling, achieves 0.955 accuracy and 0.750 NDCG@n with 62 K parameters. These results demonstrate that lightweight architectures can maintain strong classification performance and temporal explanations while substantially reducing model size. The proposed variants address specific limitations of the pooling strategy used by MILLET, providing a practical direction for interpretable time-series classification on resource-constrained edge devices.
bullets: Addresses black-box time-series classifiers that do not identify influential time points or intervals.
Uses small multi-scale depthwise-separable convolutional encoders with improved multiple-instance-learning pooling heads.
The bottleneck encoder with Top-k pooling achieves 0.931 accuracy and 0.765 NDCG@n using 41K parameters.
The gated encoder with Top-k pooling achieves 0.955 accuracy and 0.750 NDCG@n using 62K parameters.
Targets practical deployment on microcontrollers and edge devices while preserving temporal interpretability.

papers.selection_reason: Lightweight interpretable time-series architecture for resource-constrained deployment; relevant to Efficient AI.
papers.title: Sea-Net: A Small and Inherently Interpretable Neural Network for Time Series Classification
papers.tldr: SEA-Net delivers interpretable time-series classification on resource-constrained devices with far fewer parameters than MILLET while achieving strong accuracy and temporal explanation quality.

papers.abstract: As generative language models become more capable and widely used, inference demand grows, making efficient serving increasingly important. Discrete diffusion language models (dLLMs) offer a promising path to more efficient inference through parallel token generation. Prior dLLM decoding methods, however, focus on improving inference efficiency for individual sequences. We formulate fixed-budget dLLM batch decoding and introduce Batch-Paced, a training-free method that jointly optimizes the allocation of decoding compute across requests to improve overall batch quality. Across two dLLM backbones, five benchmarks and their representative mixtures, Batch-Paced improves batch performance under matched budgets; gains generally grow with batch size and largely persist across decoding configurations. Analysis of requests' decoding trajectories suggests that these gains arise largely by raising the committed-token confidence of lower-confidence requests. We further show that Batch-Paced's batch decode time remains competitive and that adding a decoding-depth allowance during Batch-Paced decoding can shorten it further at a modest performance cost.
authors: Shuai Zhang, Zhanchao Zhou, Huachuan Qiu, Anqi Li, Zhenzhong Lan
bullets: Targets inefficient batch serving when inference compute is limited.
Introduces a training-free scheduler that jointly allocates decoding effort across requests.
Improves batch performance across two dLLM backbones, five benchmarks, and representative mixtures under matched budgets.
Benefits generally increase with batch size and persist across decoding configurations.
Maintains competitive batch decode time; limiting decoding depth can reduce latency with modest performance cost.

After a denoising forward pass assigns confidence scores to masked-token predictions, Uniform commits a fixed number of positions per sequence, whereas Batch-Paced ranks positions across the batch.

Figure 3: Batch-Paced gives requests different commit schedules within a fixed-budget batch. Matched panels show the same illustrative mixed B = 16 batch with requests aligned row by row; the shared center separates Uniform’s leftward and Batch-Paced’s rightward token-progress axes. Segment width, height, color, and row-end marks encode per-forward token count, mean confidence, commit size, and final correctness, respectively.

Figure 2: Batch-Paced’s largest confidence shifts and performance gains occur in the low-confidence group. The panels show (a) variation in commit allocation across requests and forwards, (b) confidence shifts by Uniformconfidence group, and (c) paired performance differences between Batch-Paced and Uniform.

Figure 5: Depth limits trade Batch-Paced performance for shorter decode time. The plot compares Uniform, Fast-dLLM, and original and depth-limited Batch-Paced across task mixtures and budgets; larger circles denote larger depth allowances. Batch-Paced generally outperforms Uniform at comparable decode time; tighter allowances move it toward Fast-DLLM’s runtime; larger ones recover the original policy’s performance and runtime.

Figure 7: LLaDA-8B-Instruct shows the same pattern, with its largest confidence shifts and performance gains in the low-confidence group. The panels show (a) variation in commit allocation across requests and forwards, (b) confidence shifts by Uniform-confidence group, and (c) paired performance differences between Batch-Paced and Uniform.

papers.title: Batch-Paced: Fixed-Budget Batch Decoding in Discrete Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: Batch-Paced improves fixed-budget batch decoding for discrete diffusion language models by allocating compute across requests rather than decoding each sequence independently.

papers.abstract: Post-hoc linearization is an attractive way to accelerate pretrained Video Diffusion Transformers (Video DiTs), yet existing methods largely treat the quality loss induced by attention replacement as a recovery problem. We show that a more fundamental bottleneck lies upstream: \emph{initialization}. Random initialization discards pretrained knowledge, whereas manual weight reuse transfers it through rigid and incomplete source--target correspondences. We introduce \textbf{LinMorph}, which recasts Video DiT linearization as a learnable softmax-to-linear weight transformation problem. Instead of copying predefined counterparts, LinMorph learns a cross-parameter morphism that lets each target Gated DeltaNet (GDN) parameter draw jointly from pretrained query, key, value, and output projections, including for parameters with no direct softmax counterpart. A single morphism is shared across layers and learned through local teacher alignment, while producing layer-specific initializations from their respective pretrained weights. The resulting weights are then materialized as independent GDN modules for progressive distillation and joint recovery.Since the morphism operates in weight space rather than token space, it can be learned on short, low-resolution clips and directly reused at larger video scales. Across pretrained Video DiTs, LinMorph enables markedly faster recovery and better final generation quality than random initialization and heuristic weight reuse. Results show that efficient linearization depends not only on how a converted model is recovered, but critically on how pretrained knowledge is transferred before recovery. Project page: https://lonelyling.github.io/LinMorph.
authors: Lingyi Long, Congyue Zhao, Xiaoou Li, Yanmin Qian, Tao Huang
bullets: Identifies initialization—not only post-conversion recovery—as a key bottleneck in Video DiT linearization.
Learns a shared cross-parameter softmax-to-linear morphism instead of relying on random initialization or rigid weight copying.
Allows each GDN parameter to combine information from pretrained query, key, value, and output projections, including unmatched parameters.
Uses local teacher alignment on short, low-resolution clips, then applies layer-specific transformed weights for progressive distillation and recovery.
Reports faster recovery and better final generation quality across pretrained Video DiTs than random or heuristic initialization.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of LinMorph. A shared weight morphism is first learned from the frozen softmax teacher and used to generate GDN initialization weights. After materialization, the mapper is discarded and the GDN modules are progressively introduced and recovered by prediction distillation. papers.selection_reason: Presents a weight-morphing method to linearize Video Diffusion Transformers, improving efficiency of video DiT inference.
papers.title: LinMorph: Learning to Morph Weights for Efficient Video DiT Linearization
papers.tldr: LinMorph learns how to transfer pretrained attention weights into linear Gated DeltaNet modules, enabling faster Video DiT linearization with better recovered quality.

papers.abstract: Long-context training of large language and multimodal models couples structured attention masks (document, prefix-LM, share-question, sliding-window, block-sparse) with multi-node context parallelism, making the mask a dominant bottleneck. FlashMask's column-wise sparse mask compresses them from $O(n^2)$ to $O(n)$ via four query-axis boundary vectors, covering broad structured patterns. Implemented for Ampere GPUs, it neither exploits FlashAttention-3's TMA/WGMMA warp-specialized pipeline on Hopper nor supports distribution. The column-wise sparse mask is indexed by key positions but stores query-axis interval boundaries. Under any multi-chunk context-parallel assignment, it reduces per-rank mask localization to a provably zero-communication \emph{clip--shift--max} on the boundary vectors, compatible with the single-GPU kernel. FlashMask-3 introduces a mask-aware Hopper kernel with three-role warp specialization atop FlashAttention-3's TMA/WGMMA pipeline, plus a mask-aware distributed extension: zero-communication mask localization, a sparsity-aware load balancer (HCC-IPO), and a mask-aware compute-communication overlap with mask-driven communication pruning, whose forward all-gather uses topology-aware hierarchical routing. On a single H100 across 12 masks at 4K--128K context, it improves achieved TFLOPs over FlashMask, FlexAttention, and MagiAttention by 45--141%, 34--71%, and 2--44%. At context-parallel degrees 4--32 with 8K sequence per device, it attains 31--75% compute-communication overlap efficiency and improves throughput over Megatron-Core CP ring, Megatron-Core CP all-gather, and MagiAttention by $1.80\times$--$3.71\times$, $1.71\times$--$2.92\times$, and $1.09\times$--$1.46\times$. In end-to-end training of a 118B-A14B MoE at 128K on 128 H100 GPUs, it raises throughput by 7.3--11.0% over a Dual Chunk all-gather baseline, with attention forward+backward 24.5--44.9% faster.
authors: Guoxia Wang, Qianyue He, Siming Wu, Haoyang Xie, Qiwen Bao, Jinle Zeng, Jiabin Yang, Tian Wu, Dianhai Yu
bullets: Targets the bottleneck of structured attention masks in long-context, multi-node training.
Uses a Hopper-optimized FlashAttention-3 kernel with TMA/WGMMA and three-role warp specialization.
Provides zero-communication mask localization via a clip–shift–max operation, plus load balancing and mask-aware communication overlap with pruning.
On a single H100, improves achieved TFLOPs by 2–141% over prior mask-aware attention systems across 12 masks and 4K–128K contexts.
Across 4–32 context-parallel degrees, improves throughput by up to 3.71×; in 128K end-to-end MoE training, raises throughput by 7.3–11.0%.

papers.selection_reason: Mask-aware distributed attention for long-context LLM training; directly improves attention efficiency and long-context capability.
papers.title: FlashMask-3: Efficient and Expressive Mask-Aware Distributed Attention
papers.tldr: FlashMask-3 makes structured, mask-aware attention efficient on Hopper GPUs and across distributed context parallelism, delivering substantial kernel and end-to-end training speedups.

papers.abstract: Extended chain-of-thought reasoning improves problem-solving performance but increases inference cost and latency, motivating more accurate answers with shorter reasoning. We introduce PaceReasoner, a label-free test-time reinforcement learning framework that uses a model's LONG responses to improve its SHORT-mode accuracy. Both modes share a trainable policy, creating a need for reliable supervision, sufficient SHORT training samples, and continued LONG responses to guide learning. PaceReasoner combines all-response and LONG-only answer consensus through progressive, confidence-weighted supervision. A behavior reward gradually shifts from encouraging SHORT exploration to rewarding agreement with LONG answers, while a ratio controller regulates the balance between modes. Across three model backbones and four benchmarks, PaceReasoner improves average SHORT accuracy over the baselines by 7.4--13.5 percentage points, with fewer than 25 reasoning tokens per response on average. Ablations support the key components, and cross-dataset results demonstrate transfer beyond the adaptation set.
authors: Changguo Jia, Zhiyou Xiao, Xinbei Ma, Geng Chen, Weiming Zhang, Yiming Xu, Tianqi Zhao, Minghui Zhou
bullets: Addresses the inference cost and latency of extended chain-of-thought reasoning.
Uses a shared policy with label-free test-time reinforcement learning to train SHORT responses from LONG responses.
Combines all-response and LONG-only consensus with progressive, confidence-weighted supervision.
Gradually shifts rewards from encouraging SHORT exploration to matching LONG-answer guidance, while regulating the mode balance.
Across three backbones and four benchmarks, improves average SHORT accuracy by 7.4–13.5 percentage points; results transfer beyond the adaptation set.

papers.selection_reason: Label-free test-time RL to shorten LLM reasoning while preserving accuracy, directly targeting reasoning efficiency and LLM inference cost.
papers.title: PaceReasoner: Label-Free Learning to Answer Briefly from Long Reasoning
papers.tldr: PaceReasoner uses long responses as label-free guidance to improve short-answer accuracy while keeping reasoning under 25 tokens on average.

papers.abstract: Multi-agent Large Language Model (LLM) systems typically commit to a deliberation protocol before inference. A fixed protocol cannot allocate computation differently to resolved and unresolved instances, and it may mistake repeated support for independent confirmation. We study this failure as semantic false consensus: a confident group answer supported by narrow, duplicated, or correlated rationales. We introduce ECMR, an evidence-aware controller over frozen role-conditioned LLMs. At each step, ECMR summarizes answer concentration, support diversity and independence, contradictions, role behavior, verification history, and remaining budget, then selects whether to propose, challenge, verify, arbitrate, diversify, correct a role, or stop. We formulate this decision as finite-horizon budgeted control and derive sufficient conditions under which state conditioning, risk-triggered verification, and role correction improve cost-adjusted utility. Across a declared held-out evaluation of 9,000 records from MedQA, CaseHOLD, and FinQA, ECMR-Full increases pooled accuracy from 62.1% to 84.9%, reduces false-consensus rate from 40.7% to 17.0%, and raises evidence-support rate from 58.0% to 88.7%. State shuffling loses 11.7 accuracy points with only 0.7 fewer rounds, while harder traces shift from early stopping toward arbitration. ECMR-Full uses the largest token budget, yielding the strongest absolute reliability rather than uniformly superior token efficiency.
authors: Yuan Liu, Haoyue Peng, Fanliang Hu, Lei Huang, Wenli Cai
bullets: Targets fixed deliberation protocols that waste computation and can mistake duplicated or correlated support for independent confirmation.
Controls frozen, role-conditioned agents by choosing among proposing, challenging, verifying, arbitrating, diversifying, correcting roles, or stopping.
Tracks answer concentration, evidence diversity and independence, contradictions, role behavior, verification history, and remaining budget.
On 9,000 held-out records across MedQA, CaseHOLD, and FinQA, pooled accuracy rose from 62.1% to 84.9%, while false-consensus rate fell from 40.7% to 17.0%.
The full controller uses the largest token budget, achieving stronger absolute reliability but not uniformly better token efficiency.

figures.caption: Figure 1: ECMR separates trainable deliberation control from frozen LLM execution. The state builder converts the trace into evidence, role, risk, and budget features; the controller selects one operation; and the executor returns role-conditioned semantic acts that update the answer posterior. Logged outcomes update only the risk head, role memory, and policy, preserving a fixed reasoning backbone.

Figure 4: Three-domain held-out reliability. Panel (a) traces domain accuracy and uncertainty for every method; panel (b) shows ECMR-Full accuracy gain, FCR reduction, and ESR gain over Direct with independently propagated uncertainty.

Figure 2: Inference budget and marginal return. Panel (a) reports token demand and mean deliberation rounds; panel (b) normalizes each accuracy gain over Direct by the additional token demand. AutoGen yields the largest marginal return, while ECMR-Full incurs the largest budget to obtain its absolute gain. Whiskers propagate the registered uncertainty.

Figure 3: Where evidence-aware control pays. Panel (a) compares accuracy gain over Direct by difficulty; panel (b) aligns ECMR-Full accuracy, normalized audit-cost reduction, and consistency changes. Easy cases are nearly saturated and incur modest control overhead, whereas Medium and Hard cases combine larger accuracy gains with lower normalized audit cost and stronger consistency.

Figure 5: Ordered compliance ablation over 9,000 records per variant. Panel (a) compares role-violation and false-consensus incidence as controls are added; panel (b) relates the derived role-compliance score to evidence-support rate. The full loop matches the ECMR-Full macro endpoint; whiskers are binomial standard errors.

Figure 6: Difficulty-conditioned controller actions. Panel (a) reports the explicit-verification trigger rate for every policy and difficulty stratum. Panel (b) shows ECMR-Full reallocating complementary terminal routes from early stopping on Easy cases to arbitration on Hard cases; whiskers mark routing uncertainty.

papers.selection_reason: Evidence-aware budgeted control for multi-agent LLM reasoning, addressing reasoning reliability, false consensus, and token-budget allocation.
papers.title: ECMR: Evidence-Aware Deliberation Control for Multi-Agent LLM Reasoning
papers.tldr: ECMR adaptively controls multi-agent LLM deliberation using evidence quality and disagreement signals to reduce false consensus and improve reliability.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models apply bidirectional attention over the whole context at every denoising step, so a longer context makes each step substantially more expensive. Sparsifying only at inference leaves the pretrained weights unchanged, so the model is never trained under the sparse pattern it runs with. We propose Prefilling-dLLM v2, which continues training a diffusion language model so that it routes with its native mask token. One mask is appended at the end of each chunk, and a learned role offset marks it as a routing slot. On every fourth layer, a query keeps a bidirectional local window and the top-K chunks scored from that mask; the other layers use a bidirectional sliding window. Starting from Dream-v0-Base-7B extended to 16K with YaRN, we compare Prefilling-dLLM v2 with bidirectional NSA, DSA, and SWA under the same layout, key budget, and dense initialization, using the same Fast-dLLM decoder. With the YaRN factor scaled to the evaluation length, Prefilling-dLLM v2 leads the other sparse methods on all three RULER tasks from 16K to 128K. Its mean accuracy at 128K is 7.4 points above NSA, the next sparse model, while DSA and SWA remain near zero. At the same length, decoding is 172x faster than with full dense attention.
authors: Qi Han, Jing Xiong, Ziyuan Zhang, Ngai Wong
bullets: Addresses the high per-step cost of bidirectional full-context attention in diffusion language models.
Adds one learned routing mask per chunk; every fourth layer selects the top-K chunks while other layers use local sliding-window attention.
Continued training aligns the model with the sparse attention pattern used at inference.
Outperforms bidirectional NSA, DSA, and SWA across three RULER tasks from 16K to 128K; at 128K, it is 7.4 accuracy points above NSA.
Achieves 172× faster decoding than dense attention at 128K, within the evaluated setup and context range.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Mean accuracy of the four sparse methods on the three RULER tasks. The YaRN factor scales with the evaluation length.

Figure 2: What query q can see. Each chunk is three cells, and q sits in the middle so the local window extends both ways. Teal cells are the local window and orange cells are selected. The bar above each NSA chunk is its summary. DSA reads scattered tokens, and Prefilling-dLLM v2 marks the last cell of every chunk as a mask.

Figure 3: Computation on a route layer. A chunk is S − 1 content tokens followed by one routing mask. The role offset r is added to that mask at the input. Its query pools the content keys with an intra-chunk softmax, and the weighted sum is the summary key sc. A content query adds a lowrank residual and scores these summaries. Inside a GQA group (Ainslie et al., 2023) the scores are reduced by a maximum, and the top K chunks are shared by every head in the group. Attention mass puts the selected chunk scores and the local-window log-sum-exp in one partition, then a second softmax distributes each chunk’s mass over its content tokens.
Figure 7: Training loss of the continued-training runs. Each line averages the previous 25 steps. The dashed vertical line marks the end of the DSA indexer warmup.

Figure 4: Cosine between the mean content key of each chunk and the summary key of each routing slot on the 16K single-needle probe, averaged over route layers and 100 examples. Each panel is binned to 32×32. On the clean probe the diagonal pairs a slot with its own chunk. Shuffle summaries permutes the summaries across chunks.

Figure 6: Prefill time and decode time per generated token under the same Fast-dLLM decoder. Both vertical axes are logarithmic. The number above each full-dense and hybrid-dense bar is the ratio of that latency to the latency of Prefilling-dLLM v2. The YaRN factor is the evaluation length divided by 2048.

Figure 5: 16K single-needle accuracy for the routing mask, a new learned token, and EOS. Shuffle summaries permutes the summaries across chunks and leaves the text in place. Move needle places the intact needle in another chunk. Each bar is 100 examples.

Table 2: LongBench-v1 at the 16K training length. The upper block is dense attention. Full dense keeps dense attention in every layer through the same number of continued-training steps as the other variants. Hybrid dense uses three sliding-window layers and one dense layer. The lower block is sparse attention. In the dense block, ∗ marks the best score in each column. In the sparse block, the best score is bold and the second best is underlined.

Table 3: Layer configurations. Each variant occupies two rows. The first row is every fourth layer, and the second row is the other 21 layers. Local window is a bidirectional radius. Remote budget is the set of keys gathered beyond that window. Total budget is the number of key positions on that row. The sparse rows share a budget of about 2560. A dense layer reads every key.

Table 5: Continued training. Each variant is initialized from the dense step-500 checkpoint and trains for 1000 steps with a cosine schedule on four GPUs, at learning rate 10−4 with 50 warmup steps. The base weights stay frozen. Low-rank adapters of rank 16, scale 32, and dropout 0.05 train the query, key, value, and output projections. The rows below are the parameters that differ across variants.

Table 1: Three RULER tasks at 16K, 32K, 64K, and 128K. The upper block is dense attention. Full dense keeps dense attention in every layer through the same number of continued-training steps as the other variants. Hybrid dense uses three sliding-window layers and one dense layer. The lower block is sparse attention. Fixed uses YaRN factor 8. Scaled sets the factor to the evaluation length divided by 2048. MK is multi-key multi-query. Avg. is the mean of S-N, MK, and VT. In the dense block, ∗ marks the best score in each column. In the sparse block, the best score is bold and the second best is underlined.
Table 4: Dense context extension. The run continues Dream-v0-Base-7B under dense attention. The base weights stay frozen, and the listed low-rank adapters are the trainable parameters.

Table 7: Routing-token ablations on the three RULER tasks. The YaRN factor is held at 8 at every length. MK is multi-key multi-query. Avg. is the mean of S-N, MK, and VT. Mask is the native mask used by Prefilling-dLLM v2, copied from its Fixed row in Table 1. EOS and New token replace the mask in the routing slot, both in training and at evaluation.

papers.selection_reason: Learned chunk routing and sparse attention for long-context diffusion language models directly address efficient attention and long-context processing.
papers.title: Prefilling-dLLM v2: Learned Chunk Routing for Long-Context Diffusion Language Models
papers.tldr: Prefilling-dLLM v2 trains a diffusion language model to route attention through learned chunk-level mask tokens, enabling efficient long-context decoding while preserving strong retrieval performance.

papers.abstract: Multi-agent deliberation can improve recognition by criticizing and revising candidate answers, but fixed controls cannot respond to changes in disagreement or reasoning quality. We present an adaptive multi-agent controller (ADMA) that learns continuous policies for proposal, challenge, arbitration, and coordination while keeping the task model frozen. Shared trace features describe quality, agreement, and progress, while role-specific features support decentralized control during inference. One controller trained on legal and financial reasoning is transferred without policy updates to four textual and multimodal benchmarks and two successive task-model versions. With Qwen3.5 held fixed, ADMA-Full improves accuracy by 6.2-14.2 percentage points over Direct and by 2.8-3.0 points over ADMA-Fixed. Paired bootstrap ranges for the Full-Fixed comparison are positive on three tasks. Outcome decompositions show that recoveries exceed introduced errors, while process assessment records fewer false-consensus events and more supported correct outcomes. Transfer to Qwen3.6 remains task dependent, which bounds the generality of the learned policy. Median token and latency ratios are 14.3-18.7 and 7.8-16.5 relative to Direct. These results show that adaptive deliberation can improve fixed-model recognition when its task-dependent gains justify the additional computation.
authors: Yuan Liu, Haoyue Peng, Fanliang Hu, Lei Huang, Wenli Cai
bullets: Fixed deliberation controls may fail when disagreement or reasoning quality changes.
ADMA learns continuous proposal, challenge, arbitration, and coordination policies from shared and role-specific trace features.
A controller trained on legal and financial reasoning transfers without policy updates across four textual/multimodal benchmarks and two model versions.
With Qwen3.5, ADMA-Full improves accuracy by 6.2–14.2 points over Direct and 2.8–3.0 points over ADMA-Fixed; recoveries exceed introduced errors.
Transfer to Qwen3.6 is task dependent, while token and latency costs are substantially higher than Direct.

figures.caption: Figure 1: ADMA controller learning and adaptive inference. During centralized training, joint transitions from four frozen role models are stored in replay and evaluated by role-specific critics. During decentralized inference, the learned actors adapt role behavior and collaboration from the evolving trace until termination. The final prediction is evaluated separately for accuracy, reliability, and resource use.

Figure 5: Reliability and deliberation depth within Qwen3.5. a–b, paired false-consensus and supported-correct incidence among all 500 observations per task, separated into shared and method-exclusive outcomes. c, ADMA-Full round distributions within paired correctness groups defined against Direct. Gray denotes two rounds and gold at least three; labels report the latter’s percentage, count, and group denominator. papers.abstract: Edge-cloud collaboration combines the lower inference overhead and greater data locality of edge-side execution with the stronger capabilities of cloud-hosted models. However, as LLM agents increasingly operate in long-horizon scenarios, cloud participation becomes interleaved throughout execution rather than a one-shot decision for each query. Such interleaved participation introduces trajectory-level effects that remain insufficiently understood. To address this gap, we introduce EC2-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating edge-cloud collaboration in long-horizon agent execution. It provides executable digital-workspace agent tasks and a unified evaluation framework covering task performance, resource usage, and privacy exposure. Using this benchmark, we empirically study diverse forms of edge-cloud collaboration. Our study reveals three findings. First, collaboration achieves a favorable balance among task performance, resource usage, and privacy exposure compared with edge-only and cloud-only execution. Second, as edge models become stronger, collaborative execution approaches cloud-only performance, and performance differences across strategies shrink, while privacy exposure remains strongly strategy-dependent. Third, stronger edge capability shifts preferred collaboration from externally controlled cloud participation and direct cloud execution toward more edge-controlled collaboration. Further analyses identify cloud-invocation decision-making and instruction following as important edge-side abilities for effective collaboration. These findings provide a systematic understanding of edge-cloud collaboration in long-horizon agent execution and insights for designing future edge agents that effectively collaborate with cloud models. Code and resources are available at https://github.com/OpenBMB/EC2-Bench.
authors: Pengcheng Huang, Zhenghao Liu, Shixin Ren, Shi Yu, Sijia Yao, Yukun Yan, Chaojun Xiao, Maosong Sun
bullets: Introduces executable digital-workspace tasks and a unified evaluation framework for task performance, resource usage, and privacy exposure.

Stronger edge models narrow the performance gap with cloud-only execution, while privacy exposure remains dependent on the collaboration strategy.
As edge capabilities improve, preferred designs shift toward more edge-controlled collaboration.
Cloud-invocation decisions and instruction following are key edge-side abilities for effective collaboration.

papers.abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) achieve strong performance by externalizing explicit reasoning traces before producing the answer, yet suffer from overthinking challenge that allocates uniformly heavy computation to queries of varying difficulty. While proprietary models mitigate this via opaque routing, open-source LRMs still lack an efficient mechanism to internalize adaptive reasoning due to both expensive training cost and limited disclosure of training recipes. In response, we introduce RPO (Root-token Policy Optimization), a framework that enables LRMs to self-determine when to reason by training only the initial root token (e.g., whether to invoke the tag) via group relative reward and group-wise advantages. By focusing on this pivotal branching point, RPO drastically reduces training overhead and VRAM usage. Across multiple model families and scales, RPO learns difficulty-aware adaptive thinking at just ~2% of the training compute of prior adaptive-reasoning methods.
authors: Taehyeon Kim, Hyunsoo Lee, Youngsoo Jang, Moontae Lee
bullets: Addresses overthinking caused by applying equally heavy reasoning to queries of different difficulty.
Optimizes only the initial root token that decides whether to invoke explicit reasoning.

The abstract does not specify detailed datasets, baselines, or inference-time gains.

papers.abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) often underperforms full fine-tuning. We investigate this performance gap through a tangent-space lens: factorized updates are confined to the tangent space of the current low-rank factors, leaving gradient components outside this space unexploited. An analysis of ten representative LoRA variants reveals that these residual components account for most of the gradient energy and exhibit strong spectral concentration. Motivated by this finding, we propose Dynamic Tangent LoRA (DT-LoRA), which partitions a fixed rank budget into a stable branch and a dynamic branch to capture the principal residual gradient directions. We show that these directions define the optimal update of a local quadratic model under orthogonal-complement and rank constraints. Matrix-free randomized SVD recovers them without materializing the residual gradient, while controlled write-back preserves accumulated updates and stabilizes training within the allocated rank. DT-LoRA adds no trainable parameters or inference cost over LoRA. Experiments across computer vision and natural language processing tasks demonstrate consistent improvements over LoRA and its variants. Moreover, despite being a general-purpose adaptation method, DT-LoRA outperforms task-specific approaches to open-vocabulary domain generalization for semantic segmentation, achieving state-of-the-art results. Code is available at https://github.com/Snipine/DT-LoRA.
authors: Yangming Zhang, Ling Yi, Datong Li, Jinliang Ding, Xiaojie Wang, Tiecheng Song, Zhaolong Ning
bullets: LoRA misses substantial, spectrally concentrated gradient components outside the tangent space of its low-rank factors.
DT-LoRA divides a fixed rank budget into stable and dynamic branches to capture principal residual-gradient directions.
It uses matrix-free randomized SVD and controlled write-back to identify useful directions while preserving accumulated updates and stabilizing training.
Experiments across vision and NLP show consistent gains over LoRA variants; it also achieves state-of-the-art results for open-vocabulary domain generalization in semantic segmentation.
The method is evaluated within a fixed rank budget and is designed to add no inference overhead over LoRA.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of DT-LoRA. A fixed rank budget is split into a Stable branch and a Dynamic branch. Every τ steps, Matrix-Free Randomized SVD extracts the principal directions of the tangent-space residual gradient from the cached activations X and output gradients R, yielding a candidate update H . Controlled Write-back then merges H into the Dynamic branch, keeping the branch at rank q. After training, both branches are merged into the pre-trained weights, so inference costs the same as LoRA.

Figure 1. Analysis of the tangent-space residual gradient. (a) Tangent-space residual gradient energy ratio ρ of ten LoRA variants. (b) Cumulative spectral energy Ek of the tangent-space residual gradient. (c) Gradient coverage 1 − ρ of four LoRA variants and DTLoRA during training. For various LoRA variants, the tangent-space residual gradient accounts for a large proportion of the gradient energy and exhibits spectral concentration. Our DT-LoRA explicitly accounts for this property, and its gradient coverage keeps increasing during training, indicating that the principal directions of the tangent-space residual gradient are effectively exploited.

papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) improves reasoning but incurs substantial autoregressive rationale cost. Continuous CoT moves intermediate computation into recurrent hidden states, yet typically uses a fixed number of updates even though the best budget varies across questions and accuracy need not improve monotonically with $K$. We introduce Dynamic K-Head, a question-conditioned, pre-rollout budget selector. It is jointly trained with the reasoner under selected budgets, using difficulty supervision based on scores assigned from the question alone. We also show that latent-update count can misrepresent end-to-end cost because a short latent rollout can shift computation into a longer explicit continuation. We therefore count latent updates, implementation-specific special tokens, and all decoded text. Instantiated with CoDI on Llama 3.2 1B and GSM8K, Dynamic K-Head reaches 54.44% exact-match accuracy at 12.03 average reasoning/output tokens, compared with 52.31% at 15.21 tokens for fixed-$K=6$ CoDI---a 2.12-point gain with 20.9% lower token cost. Across three out-of-distribution arithmetic datasets, it reduces cost by 19.3--25.7% while improving accuracy by 0.30--2.22 points. These results demonstrate that difficulty-supervised budget selection can improve both accuracy and efficiency, while stable budget selection remains a central challenge.
authors: Ying Li, Yuqi Chen, Sixuan Li, Yunfeng Cai
bullets: Fixed latent-update budgets are inefficient because question difficulty varies and accuracy may not increase monotonically with computation.
The method jointly trains a question-conditioned budget selector and reasoner using difficulty supervision derived from the question alone.
It measures end-to-end cost using latent updates, special tokens, and decoded text, rather than latent updates alone.
On GSM8K with CoDI and Llama 3.2 1B, it achieves 54.44% exact match at 12.03 average tokens versus 52.31% at 15.21 tokens for fixed K=6.
Across three out-of-distribution arithmetic datasets, it lowers cost by 19.3–25.7% while improving accuracy by 0.30–2.22 points; stable budget selection remains challenging.

papers.abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) frameworks place teacher and student on the same GPUs, so per-GPU memory limits the teachers that fit. DisaggKD separates them across nodes: teacher replicas stream hidden states to the student, a KD loss over row windows and vocabulary shards equals the full-vocabulary loss in exact arithmetic without forming the full-vocabulary logits, and a prefetch ring paces producer and trainer. Closed-form memory and traffic models locate the memory limits of each layout. On the Qwen3.5-35B-A3B to 9B pair, the disaggregated layout matches the LM loss of the colocated run with the same loss and is faster than that run; our fused loss also lets a colocated run train on as few nodes at faster speed, while the split is memory efficient when the student spans several nodes. On the larger pairs, colocated runs with a fused loss still run OOM where the split trains, because teacher weights and student states fill the budget.
bullets: Teacher replicas stream hidden states to student nodes, avoiding colocated teacher-memory limits.
A row-window and vocabulary-shard KD loss matches the full-vocabulary loss in exact arithmetic without materializing full logits.
A prefetch ring coordinates teacher production and student training, while memory and traffic models identify layout limits.
On Qwen3.5-35B-A3B to 9B, the split matches colocated LM loss and runs faster; larger pairs fit in split layouts when colocated runs OOM.
The fused loss also reduces node requirements and increases speed for colocated training.

papers.selection_reason: Disaggregated knowledge distillation reduces per-GPU memory and enables training larger teacher-student pairs.
papers.title: DisaggKD: Efficient Knowledge Distillation through Teacher-Student Disaggregation and a Fused Loss
papers.tldr: DisaggKD separates teacher and student across nodes and uses a fused, memory-efficient distillation loss to enable larger KD workloads without changing the loss.

papers.abstract: Since scaling laws were introduced for modern LLMs (Kaplan et al., 2020), several works have extended them to account for quantization, tracking the emerging low-precision data types supported on AI accelerators. We develop a more accurate scaling law for quantized pretraining with mixed precision across the forward and backward passes, grounded in optimization theory and validated empirically. Our formulation separates the effects of quantization on model capacity and on optimization efficiency, and explicitly models the persistent optimization error from forward and backward quantization identified through convergence analysis. To select the regimes for fitting and evaluating our law, we first decompose existing 4-bit training recipes into their forward and backward components, isolating those that most affect loss. Our Qwen3 experiments under selected 4-bit regimes, together with published Llama-style experiments, show that our law predicts loss with up to $11\times$ lower MSE than existing laws as model size and token count scale. Finally, we extend our law to layer-wise mixed precision and identify the optimal quantized-pretraining recipe, i.e., model size, training tokens, and per-layer forward/backward precision, under a hardware-aware compute budget. Unlike prior precision scaling laws, our law predicts that the optimal precision increases with the compute budget.
authors: Jinuk Kim, Rajarshi Saha, Muhammed Fatih Balin, Youngsuk Park
bullets: Separates quantization effects on model capacity from optimization efficiency.
Models persistent optimization error from forward and backward quantization using convergence analysis.
Decomposes 4-bit training recipes to identify forward/backward regimes most affecting loss.
Validated on Qwen3 and published Llama-style experiments, achieving up to 11× lower MSE than prior laws.
Extends to layer-wise mixed precision and predicts that optimal precision increases with compute budget.

papers.selection_reason: Scaling laws for mixed-precision quantized pretraining directly target compute and memory efficiency of LLM training.

papers.abstract: Complex and long-horizon agent tasks often rely on frontier models deployed in the cloud to achieve strong performance. However, using these models for every step of a long-horizon trajectory incurs substantial inference cost, even though not all steps may require the same level of model capability. In this paper, we find that allocating the LLM to only a small subset of key steps can achieve performance comparable to full LLM execution while significantly reducing inference cost. Motivated by this observation, we propose EdgeWise, an edge-cloud collaboration framework that deploys an SLM on the local device as the primary solver and selectively delegates critical steps to a cloud LLM when stronger model capacity is needed. To enable autonomous delegation without additional models at inference time, we introduce a step-level RL method that jointly optimizes task solving and delegation, with fine-grained credit assignment for individual delegation decisions. We also introduce an external judge-based delegation strategy and use it to systematically investigate key design choices in edge-cloud collaboration, including when to delegate, how delegation decisions should be made, what context should be shared, and how frequently the cloud LLM should be invoked. Experiments show that EdgeWise matches or outperforms pure-LLM execution while reducing inference cost up to 62% on SWE-Rebench and 34% on Terminal-Bench 2.1. We further deploy EdgeWise on a local workstation, demonstrating comparable cost savings in a practical edge-cloud setting.
authors: Zeru Shi, Jindong Jiang, Ryo Hachiuma, Yonggan Fu, Byung-Kwan Lee, Peter Belcak, Saurav Muralidharan, Ayush Agarwal, Ruixiang Tang, Ambrish Dantrey, Pavlo Molchanov, Anjul Patney, Subhashree Radhakrishnan

Uses an edge SLM as the primary solver and delegates only critical steps requiring greater capability.
Introduces step-level reinforcement learning with fine-grained credit assignment for autonomous delegation.
Also evaluates an external-judge delegation strategy and design choices around timing, context, and invocation frequency.
Reports cost reductions of up to 62% on SWE-Rebench and 34% on Terminal-Bench 2.1, with comparable or better performance than pure-LLM execution.

papers.selection_reason: Reduces inference cost via selective cloud delegation for long-horizon agent tasks, fitting efficiency-focused AI research.
papers.title: EdgeWise: Bringing Long-Horizon Agents to the Edge via Selective Cloud Delegation

papers.abstract: Recent video super-resolution (VSR) models achieve efficient one-step generation through diffusion distillation. However, high-resolution inference remains costly, and distilled models are difficult to align with human preferences. These challenges call for improvements in both model architecture and training strategy. We present \textbf{FlashVSR+} to address both limitations. On the architecture side, we introduce hybrid attention based on the strong locality observed in pretrained VSR models, while retaining sparse global interaction for long-range consistency. It achieves up to $2\times$ DiT speedup and 45\% lower peak memory, enabling spatially untiled 4K VSR on a single 24GB RTX 4090. On the training side, we propose Reward-Yield Distribution Matching Distillation (Ry-DMD) for preference-aligned one-step generation. Ry-DMD uses reward-weighted teacher rollouts to incorporate black-box rewards into distribution matching, without backpropagating through the reward model. We further show that Ry-DMD generalizes beyond VSR to T2I generation. Together, FlashVSR+ delivers stronger restoration quality and substantially improves high-resolution efficiency, with consistent gains in user preference. We release our code, models, and training data at \href{https://www.flashvsr.tech}{\textcolor{FlashBlue}{\textbf{www.flashvsr.tech}}}.
authors: Ruchang Yao, Shi Guo, Junhao Zhuang, Mingde Yao, Xin Cai, Jiahao Zhan, Bin Fu, Xinyuan Chen, Yu Qiao, Tianfan Xue
bullets: Targets the high inference cost of high-resolution VSR and the difficulty of aligning distilled models with human preferences.
Uses hybrid attention that emphasizes local interactions while preserving sparse global context for long-range consistency.

papers.abstract: While it is known that quantization of large language models (LLMs) reduces memory usage via lower-bit weights, studies quantifying the resulting impact on energy usage and carbon intensity are scarce. We present the first unified evaluation of weight-only quantization strategies for LLM inference across varying input/output lengths and GPUs, highlighting differences in energy efficiency in addition to accuracy degradation and runtime. We study quantized inference on Llama 2 7B, Phi 3.5 Mini Instruct, OLMo 1B, Qwen 2.5 7B, and Qwen 2.5 14B across GLUE MNLI, MMLU, HumanEval, and GSM8K datasets, evaluating 10 post-training quantization (PTQ) strategies on NVIDIA H100, A6000, A100, and L4 GPUs. We identify a novel trend showing that quantization techniques tend to exhibit peak energy efficiency relative to full-precision baselines when inputs are sufficiently long and outputs are short. Furthermore, we show that quantization strategies become marginally more energy-efficient relative to full-precision models as batch sizes increase, though gains are modest. Notably, fused-kernel implementations such as EETQ int8 and Bitsandbytes int8 offer the highest energy savings, up to 4x compared to FP32 on short text generation, with negligible accuracy loss. Finally, we observe that energy usage closely tracks runtime on our evaluated benchmarks, indicating that, in practice, latency optimization can serve as a reliable proxy for reducing the environmental footprint of LLM services. We conclude with suggested directions for strategically selecting low-carbon quantization strategies based on specific inference requirements.
bullets: Quantization is assessed for energy use, carbon intensity, runtime, and accuracy across five LLMs, four GPUs, four benchmarks, and 10 PTQ strategies.
Energy efficiency relative to full precision is strongest when inputs are long and outputs are short; batch-size increases provide modest additional gains.
Fused-kernel methods, particularly EETQ int8 and Bitsandbytes int8, achieve up to 4× energy savings versus FP32 on short-text generation with negligible accuracy loss.
Energy consumption closely follows runtime, making latency optimization a practical proxy for reducing inference environmental impact.
The findings support selecting quantization methods according to workload and low-carbon inference requirements.

papers.abstract: We propose a unified spatial-density signal to score token importance for both inference phases: bipartite merge for prefill and KV eviction for decode, yielding measurable gains in each stage. To isolate the two phases, we split benchmarks by scoring logic. Prefill probes (MMBench, POPE, ScienceQA) evaluate only the first decoded token; their accuracy reflects prefill logits argmax before any decode KV eviction. Full-pipeline probes (TextVQA, DocVQA, MM-Vet) assess the complete generated sequence and capture both phases. We identify a critical evaluation pitfall: decode pruning claims validated solely on prefill probes measure prefill quality, not decode performance. Experiments show discarding all visual KV during decode barely affects prefill-probe accuracy but degrades TextVQA and MM-Vet drastically; this insensitivity stems from the scoring rule, not compression intensity.Evaluated on seven model variants (InternVL-3.5, Qwen3-VL, LLaVA-1.5) and three full-pipeline benchmarks, our method achieves a three-way Pareto frontier across compute, memory and accuracy. Density-based prefill compression maintains strong accuracy, scales linearly with visual token count, and delivers 100x faster token selection at high resolution. For decode, density top-k KV eviction consistently outperforms strong baselines H2O, SnapKV and StreamingLLM on TextVQA and MM-Vet across three retention ratios. At 0.125 keep ratio on TextVQA, it surpasses H2O by 9.6 points; InternVL-3.5 models (2B to 38B) maintain a 7 to 10 point advantage. Compression scales favorably with model size: every measured 8B to 38B model transition reduces accuracy loss instead of worsening it. We suggest MM-Vet or DocVQA as mandatory full-pipeline validation for any decode-phase claims. Our code is available at https://github.com/Kai-Liu001/TwinPrune
authors: Kai Liu, Anqi Li, Junxian Li, Zhixin Wang, Zhikai Chen, Renjing Pei, Yulun Zhang
bullets: Motivation: Prefill-only probes can hide severe decode-phase quality degradation, so pruning claims require full-pipeline evaluation.
Method: Apply density-based scoring for bipartite visual-token merging during prefill and top-k visual KV eviction during decode.
Contribution: Establishes separate benchmarks and evaluation guidance, recommending MM-Vet or DocVQA for decode-pruning validation.
Results: Prefill selection is up to 100× faster at high resolution; decode pruning outperforms H2O, SnapKV, and StreamingLLM across tested retention ratios.
Scope: Evaluated across seven model variants and multiple vision-language benchmarks; performance gains are reported for both stages.

figures.caption: Figure 3: TwinPrune pipeline. A single spatial density signal ρ, defined as each visual token’s average cosine dissimilarity to its w×w neighborhood (b), drives both phases. One signal, two levers, and a three-axis Pareto trade-off over compute, KV, and accuracy (a).

papers.selection_reason: Proposes density-aware token pruning and KV eviction for vision-language models, directly addressing efficiency in both prefill and decode phases.
papers.title: TwinPrune: Density-Aware Two-Phase Token Pruning for Vision-Language Models

papers.abstract: Training recipes are tuned by hand for one model, cluster and workload, and every new model, accelerator, framework version or dataset means tuning again. Automated tuners search a fixed space of knobs and check only that a job runs, yet a configuration can run to completion while it silently changes training. ATTUNE is a single coding agent that tunes any working recipe for the workload and stack at hand, unattended, within a GPU-hour budget the user sets. It diagnoses each run and changes one lever at a time, guided by a catalog of lessons from past campaigns, and ships a recipe only if it passes a correctness gate: a configuration check against objective-changing settings and known stack defects, and a convergence check of its loss curve against the baseline's. On four held-out models at 64-128 GPUs, ATTUNE raises mean throughput over the strongest public recipe run on our stack by 6.7% on Llama-3.1-405B (best campaign 11.9%) and 33.9% on GLM-4.5 (54.7%), whose public recipe was written for H100. It keeps Mixtral-8x22B's recipe, where nothing it finds clears the noise band. Under a common GPU-hour budget it beats OptiCo, Bayesian optimization and random search on GLM-4.5 and MiniMax-M2; on GLM-4.5 its mean gain is more than four times the best alternative's at less than half the GPU-hours, and on both models its tuning pays for itself within a day of training. The gate rejects no legitimate run and catches 16 of 24 faulty runs, missing only ones that barely move the 20-step loss. Ablations tie its best campaigns to one of its search rules: retrying an out-of-memory layout with recomputation. We release ATTUNE's code and TrainingThroughputBench, a leaderboard of the fastest known recipes for MoE models up to 744B parameters on up to 256 GPUs, each with its throughput, cost per million tokens and a passed correctness check, at https://github.com/amazon-science/attune.
authors: Leo Fan, Hongyang Wang, Wenbo Chen, Jingguo Liu, Xian Li, Xuan Wang, Ruochen Wen, Yiming Yan, Hao Wu, Zheshen Wang, Benoit Dumoulin
bullets: Addresses the need to retune recipes across models, hardware, software stacks, and datasets, while avoiding silent objective-changing configurations.
Uses a coding agent that diagnoses runs, changes one lever at a time, and reuses lessons from prior tuning campaigns within a user-defined GPU-hour budget.
Accepts a recipe only after configuration checks and a loss-curve convergence check against the baseline.
Improves mean throughput by 6.7% on Llama-3.1-405B and 33.9% on GLM-4.5; it leaves Mixtral-8x22B unchanged when gains remain within noise.
Outperforms competing search methods on GLM-4.5 and MiniMax-M2 under a common budget; the correctness gate catches 16 of 24 faulty runs.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) on mobile devices can act as agents that call external software tools to complete complex tasks, but the major challenge of supporting on-device mobile agentic AI with LLMs is the long latency of LLM tool calling on mobile devices. In particular, the decode phase is the main contributor of such long latency, but is hard to speed up on mobile processors as it is bound by memory bandwidth rather than compute power. To address this limitation, in this paper we present SchemaWeaver, a new on-device mobile agentic AI technique that enforces schema-guided parallel decoding in the decode phase of LLM tool calling, to reduce its latency by producing multiple tokens in each decode pass. SchemaWeaver can be generically applied to the LLM inference engine on mobile devices without involving any training efforts or changes on LLMs, and our experiment results on major mobile SoCs and LLM families show that SchemaWeaver can reduce the LLM tool calling latency by up to 3.9 times, compared to the competitive baselines.
bullets: Targets the decode-phase latency bottleneck in mobile LLM tool calling, which is constrained by memory bandwidth.
Enforces schema-guided parallel decoding to generate multiple valid tokens in each decode pass.
Integrates generically with mobile LLM inference engines without training changes or LLM modifications.
Evaluations across major mobile SoCs and LLM families report up to 3.9× lower tool-calling latency than competitive baselines.

papers.abstract: Training large language models is constrained by both wall-clock time and memory footprint, and recent matrix-aware optimizers sharpen this tradeoff: Muon can improve optimization but its dense polar update remains expensive. We propose Monarch-Muon, a structured matrix-aware optimizer for weights parameterized by Monarch factors. The resulting structure reduces weights, gradients, and optimizer state, and exposes small independent update subproblems in place of a single dense orthogonalization; we formalize this through a blockwise trust-region interpretation. In quality runs, Monarch-Muon improves over Monarch-AdamW at fixed structure: 3.06 vs. 3.09 in the dense 257M model and 2.68 vs. 2.77 in the 1B MoE model; the two-block MoE variant also matches dense AdamW while using 15% fewer active and 25.4% fewer total parameters. In 6.89B-parameter systems measurements, Monarch-Muon reduces peak memory from 68.9 to 52.9 GB, Muon optimizer state from 14.60 to 6.77 GB, and the Muon optimizer step from 1288 to 304 ms.
authors: Alexander Miasnikov, Ruslan Kabirov, Gleb Molodtsov, Dmitrii Vlashchuk, Vladimir Aletov, Nail Bashirov, Daniil Tikhonov, Maxim Krutikov, Aleksandr Shestakov, Aleksandr Beznosikov
bullets: Targets the compute and memory costs of dense Muon updates for large language models.
Parameterizes weights with Monarch factors, reducing weights, gradients, and optimizer state.
Replaces dense orthogonalization with independent blockwise update problems, formalized via a trust-region view.
Improves over Monarch-AdamW in reported dense and MoE quality runs, and matches dense AdamW with fewer parameters in a two-block MoE.
For 6.89B-parameter systems, reduces peak memory from 68.9 to 52.9 GB and the Muon optimizer step from 1288 to 304 ms.

papers.abstract: Dynamic Sparse Training (DST) periodically prunes and regrows connections, inducing a discrete dynamical mechanism over network topologies. At extreme sparsity ($\ge 99\%$), this dynamic tends to destroy input-output information pathways, and performance with standard magnitude/random updates degrades sharply. We formalize forward, backward, and functional reachability on layered sparse graphs, derive closed-form expectations for reachable neurons and edges, and show that Monte Carlo realizations match the theory. Guided by this reachability-based structure, we bias pruning toward non-functional edges and regrowth toward functionally consistent candidates. We introduce this reachability-driven modification of topology evolution as Reachability-guided in DST, referred to as guided DST. On CIFAR-10/100 and Tiny ImageNet, guided DST recovers large accuracy gaps versus unguided DST (up to $+14.4$ points at $99.9\%$ sparsity on CIFAR-100), and on MLP-Mixer guided DST remains trainable at $99.99\%$ sparsity while unguided random regrowth degrades sharply. These results cast extreme-sparse training as a connectivity-preserving dynamical process. Our implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/mzjaworski/ea_dst.
authors: Mohammad Pasande, Mateusz Jaworski, Jeroen Rook, Elena Mocanu
bullets: Extreme Dynamic Sparse Training can destroy input–output pathways, causing sharp performance degradation at sparsity levels of 99% or higher.
The paper formalizes forward, backward, and functional reachability in layered sparse graphs and derives expected reachable neurons and edges.
Reachability-guided DST prunes non-functional edges preferentially and regrows connections that maintain functional consistency.
Theory agrees with Monte Carlo realizations of sparse topologies.
On CIFAR-10/100 and Tiny ImageNet, guided DST recovers substantial accuracy gaps; it remains trainable at 99.99% sparsity for MLP-Mixer, where unguided regrowth degrades sharply.

papers.title: When Sparsity Breaks Connectivity: Functional Reachability and Guided Topology Dynamics in Extreme Sparse Training
papers.tldr: At extreme sparsity, preserving functional connectivity during dynamic pruning and regrowth substantially improves sparse-training viability.

papers.abstract: Vision Transformers incur high computational costs when processing long visual token sequences. Existing reduction methods typically rank tokens independently and discard those deemed unimportant or redundant. We propose a reconstruction-guided framework for visual token condensation (ReConV), which summarizes the complete visual sequence with a compact Summary Bank (SMB) and retains tokens whose information is not adequately captured by the SMB, as indicated by their reconstruction residuals. At each compression layer, a lightweight position-conditioned decoder reconstructs the current tokens, leaving shared information compressed in the SMB while explicitly preserving poorly reconstructed details. Experiments on image classification and multimodal understanding demonstrate favorable performance-efficiency trade-offs: ReConV surpasses the uncompressed baseline with 48\% fewer GMACs on ImageNet and enables reusable image-level representations for efficient multi-turn inference. Code is available at TokenDrop.
authors: Xiaoya Tang, Shilong Liu, Daniel Smolyak, Xiwen Li, Quynh Nguyen, Tolga Tasdizen
bullets: Targets the high computational cost of Vision Transformers on long visual token sequences.
Uses a position-conditioned decoder to reconstruct tokens from a Summary Bank at each compression layer.
Retains tokens with large reconstruction residuals, rather than ranking tokens independently.
Achieves favorable performance-efficiency trade-offs in image classification and multimodal understanding.
On ImageNet, surpasses the uncompressed baseline with 48% fewer GMACs and supports reusable image-level representations for efficient multi-turn inference.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of ReConV, the proposed reconstruction-guided token pruning framework. Given N token embeddings from a vision encoder or transformer layer, each compressive layer uses a small set of learned summary bank (SMB) tokens to summarize the input via cross-attention, reconstructs the original tokens using the SMB representation and positional information, and retains the top-k tokens with the largest reconstruction residuals (approximately N · r, where r is the keep ratio). Tokens that are well reconstructed are dropped as redundant, while the retained tokens are passed to the next layer. For classification, the model uses the CLS token when available, or pooled SMB features otherwise; for other tasks, it uses the retained visual tokens with SMBs.

Figure 3: Patch-to-SMB assignments for tokens entering the first, second, and third compression layers of our A1A3A5 classification model, which use keep ratios of 0.75, 0.25, and 0.0, respectively. The model’s performance is reported in Table 2. Green numbers identify the SMB tokens assigned to reconstruct the corresponding patches, and patches assigned to the same SMB are masked with the same color. Unnumbered patches have been dropped by preceding layers. Examples are randomly selected from the ImageNet validation set.

Figure 6: Patch-to-SMB assignments in our single-layer A5 classification model with a keep ratio of 0.0 and our three-layer A1A3A5 classification model with keep ratios of 0.75, 0.25, and 0.0. From left to right, the figure shows the patch-to-SMB assignments and corresponding color-coded masks at the single compression layer of the A5 model, followed by the patch-to-SMB assignments for the tokens entering the first, second, and third compression layers of the A1A3A5 model. For example, the visualization at the first layer therefore includes all input patch tokens; this layer subsequently drops 25% of them, and the retained tokens enter the second compression layer. Green numbers identify the SMB tokens assigned to reconstruct the corresponding patches, with patches assigned to the same SMB sharing the same color. Patches without a number have been dropped by preceding compression layers. The examples are randomly selected from the ImageNet validation set.

Figure 7: Samples are randomly selected from the MME evaluation set, covering five subtasks from left to right: artwork, existence, landmark, OCR, and scene. The figure visualizes the 64-token setting of our model, which contains 56 kept tokens and 8 SMBs. From top to bottom, the panels show: the question-answer pair, the input image, SMB allocation at the first compression layer, SMB allocation at the second compression layer after the first token-dropping step, and the final SMB allocation after the second token-dropping step. The color from light to dark yellow indicates SMB indices from 0 to 8. The letters on each patch indicate the assigned SMB index, while patches without letters have already been dropped.

Figure 4: Examples from the MT-VQAv2 test split, where the number of questions associated with each image varies across samples. In the multi-turn setting, each image is encoded and optionally compressed only once, and the resulting visual embeddings are reused across all associated questions.

Figure 1: Illustration of visual token pruning. Prompt-independent saliency emphasizes irrelevant regions, while prompt-conditioned pruning can still discard task-relevant details, especially at high pruning ratios. ReConV instead preserves information through SMB summaries and residual tokens.

Figure 5: ImageNet1K top-1 accuracy percentage vs computation cost (GMACs) tradeoff. Left: Models with 1-2 compressive layers with varying number of SMBs and layer placement. Right: Models with 3 compressive layers (A1A3A5) with varying number of SMBs and keep ratios.

The baseline scores 76.4 and 72.4 on the dev splits of MMB and MMBCN, respectively
Table 6: Ablation studies on model components and architectural design choices.

The percentage in GMACs indicates the reduction computation relative to the backbone, and the percentage in accuracy indicates the retained performance relative to the backbone accuracy. The configurations “0.75,0.25,0” denote the keep ratios of the three compressive layers, corresponding to ρ1, ρ2, ρ3 in Section 3.3. Ourdistill indicates that a DeiT-S teacher trained from scratch is used for distillation.
Table 8: Efficiency analysis on POPE. We report prefill latency per sample, measured on an A800 GPU (40GB). Speedup is computed relative to the Baseline.

Table 3: Comparison on MT-VQA-v2 and ConvBench at a 95% visual token reduction rate. Amort. denotes latency per question with image encoding amortized across questions, while Mean Total Prefill denotes total prefill latency averaged across conversations.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes reconstruction-guided visual token condensation, directly fitting token pruning/eviction for efficient vision and multimodal inference.
papers.title: Bottlenecked semantic compression by representation reconstruction
papers.tldr: ReConV compresses long visual token sequences by reconstructing shared information in a compact summary bank and retaining tokens with unrecovered details, improving efficiency while preserving performance.

papers.abstract: Diffusion language models accelerate generation by decoding multiple masked positions per forward pass. However, accuracy is known to drop when parallel decoding trajectories deviate from their sequential counterparts, which are slow and expensive "oracles" that adhere to the joint distribution of language. In this paper, we propose Parallel Inconsistency Guidance (PIG), a new paradigm that uses a trained auxiliary model to directly estimate the inconsistency between parallel and sequential generation from a single model forward pass. During inference, masked positions are traversed by decreasing confidence, and tokens are added to the parallel decode set one-at-a-time until the total estimated inconsistency between the parallel and sequential generation exceeds a threshold. Surprisingly, it suffices to train a lightweight ~2M parameter auxiliary model on a small mixture drawn from OpenCoder, GSM8K-train, MATH-train, and MBPP-train. For LLaDA-8B Instruct and NemotronDiffusion-3B Instruct, PIG extends the accuracy-TPF frontier on GSM8K, MATH500, MBPP, HumanEval, and MMLU, when compared to the industry standard Fast-dLLM and measures favorably on LLaDA-8B Instruct against DAPD, KLASS, EB-sampler, and other learned unmasking policies.
authors: Quentin Fruytier, Anton Xue, Sanjay Shakkottai, Sujay Sanghavi
bullets: Diffusion language models decode multiple masked positions in parallel, but accuracy can suffer when their trajectories diverge from slower sequential decoding.
PIG uses a lightweight auxiliary model to estimate parallel–sequential inconsistency from a single forward pass.
Tokens are considered in decreasing confidence order and added one at a time until estimated inconsistency exceeds a threshold.
A roughly 2M-parameter auxiliary model is trained on a small mixture of coding, math, and reasoning data.
On LLaDA-8B Instruct and NemotronDiffusion-3B Instruct, PIG extends the accuracy–throughput frontier across several reasoning, coding, and language benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Parallel Inconsistency Guidance (PIG). Left: from one forward pass, PIG estimates how likely each parallel commit is to disagree with the unseen sequential decode and defers the risky ones (M3). Right: on Nemotron-3B HumanEval (64-token blocks), PIG.INT and PIG.EXT extend the accuracy–TPF frontier of the model’s own confidence decoder and baseline reported result.

Figure 2: PIG.INT controls single-round regret. One forward pass (NFE) predicts every masked slot and ranks them by confidence; that ranking is the traversal order (I). Candidates are iteratively added to S, each with its predicted incremental regret bi = p̂ν(νi, µ̂i(S)) (II), and admitted only while the predicted regret R̂(S) fits the budget φ (III); the first candidate that does not fit closes the round. We then greedily decode all tokens in S in parallel, before starting the next round.

Figure 3: Cross-round regret measures the value of waiting. On the canvas and confidence order of Figure 2 (I), PIG.EXT admits each candidate and then prices the next candidate N(S): ci is how much the mismatch risk of i would drop after first committing S (II). The round continues while R̂(N(S)) − R̂(N(S) | S) ≤ θ (III): committing “are” changes little for M3, so the walk widens; committing “blue” would turn M2 from “look” into “are”, so waiting is worth more than θ, the round closes and commits only “are” and “blue”. We implement with |N(S)| = 16 look-ahead positions.

Figure 8: The calibrated mismatch table p̂ν read by PIG.INT, one per backbone (left LLaDA-8B-Instruct, right Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion-3B). Rows: the committing position’s confidence νi at the fixed edges of Algorithm 5; columns: its aggregate coupling µ̂i to the higher-confidence members of the set, at the quantile edges of each model’s own fit. A cell is the empirical rate at which a parallel commit differed from its sequential replay, pooled over the GSM8K-train and OpenCoder probes; a cell holding fewer than 50 commits is left blank and is read by the decoder at the pooled rate of its row.

Figure 4: Finite Differences Estimator (FDE). The frozen DLM’s pass feeds a learned adapter (≈2.2M parameters), which returns in the same pass the full directed matrix D̂ of entropy finite differences of Equation (4), D̂ij ≈ Hi(xt)− Hi(xt⊕x̂j), the change in uncertainty at i if j were committed.
